papers.title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.

papers.title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
papers.summary: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

papers.title: Mixed-Methods Exploration of Sociotechnical Factors to Improve Adoption of Crime-Reporting Apps in Urban Communities
papers.summary: Crime-reporting mobile applications can enhance community safety and engagement in urban areas, yet their adoption remains low, partly because developers prioritize technological features over residents' social realities. This study used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to identify and validate the sociotechnical factors that drive adoption. Two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews revealed that users' initial sense of usefulness fades, whereas sustained engagement depends on perceived value (PV), comprising six dimensions: safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility. A survey of 505 urban residents, analyzed with PLS-SEM, validated PV as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of these dimensions (safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie). PV was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and performance expectancy, and behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explained 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% in actual use. The findings offer design principles for community-centered crime-reporting technologies.

papers.title: Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks
papers.summary: Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark ends with a scoring rule that converts a model's response, often free-form text rather than a clean option letter, into a right/wrong verdict, buried in its code. Unlike the dataset, this rule is chosen without justification and left unexamined, yet it sets the published number. We reproduce the official scorers of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks on five open vision-language models (VLMs) that fit a single 16 GB GPU, and introduce a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge adjudication (Cohen's kappa=0.956) that recovers what the model actually answered. The scoring rule alone moves accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, yet exactly 0 wherever a model emits clean option letters, so it hides on strong-model leaderboards. It is the fallback and not the rambling that does the damage: the benchmark with the highest non-compliance we measure has an artifact of exactly zero, because its scorer abstains instead of guessing; a reasoning model with non-compliance 0.000 still swings 9.5 points with which regex match of its trace the parser keeps. No standard rule is reliable: snapping a non-answer to its closest option credits answers never given yet buries correct ones, abstention discards answers stated in words, and likelihood scoring follows answer-token priors, so a single grade conflates capability with luck rather than measuring either. We release all code, labels, and the protocol, and argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two rules, not one unexamined grade.

papers.title: Can We Stop the Backtest Yet? Anytime-Valid Promotion Tests for Adaptive Financial Research Agents
papers.summary: Financial research agents can generate and monitor trading rules faster than a human can document the resulting selection process. Candidates appear at data-dependent times, weak rules are abandoned, and promising ones are watched until they cross a reporting threshold. We introduce PROMOTE, a protocol that assigns every candidate predictable testing wealth at birth and accumulates a cost-aware e-process only from subsequent returns. If lifetime allocations sum to at most one, a weighted Ville argument bounds the probability of ever promoting a rule whose declared bounded net score has always had nonpositive conditional mean. The result permits dependent candidates, adaptive births, and indefinite monitoring. We audit the implementation in two settings. A retrospective pseudo-out-of-sample replay contains 24 panel--rule hypotheses, 3,000 shared-sign null paths, injected alternatives, and public ETF and industry data. Repeated unadjusted tests produce a family crossing in 94.5% of null paths, versus 0.0% for PROMOTE; at a 15-bp aligned ETF-component perturbation, PROMOTE has 70.1% target power and median crossing session 2,327. A separate exact mean-zero experiment lets an agent select candidate identities and birth times from past scores; the funded gate has 1.77% false-family crossings across 3,000 programs. The market replay produces zero promotions after costs. The certificate controls historical false promotion under the declared null; it is not a certificate that an earlier edge remains profitable at deployment. AI-use disclosure. Generative AI tools, including OpenAI Codex, assisted manuscript preparation. For this preprint version, Codex assisted with LaTeX editing, author and venue metadata, compilation, and layout checks.

papers.title: LAND: Learning an Adaptive Number of Draws for Bayesian Best-of-N Selection
papers.summary: Best-of-N decoding improves generation quality by sampling multiple candidates and selecting the best, but it allocates equal compute to sources regardless of how much they benefit from additional sampling: the expected benefit is small for sources with low-variance score distributions and potentially much larger for those with high-variance distributions. To address this shortcoming, we propose LAND (Learning an Adaptive Number of Draws), which dynamically allocates samples according to their posterior-predictive marginal value. LAND learns a discrete empirical mixture of source-conditioned score distributions from calibration data, updates its belief about a source as completion scores are observed, and stops sampling when the expected improvement of another draw falls below a shared compute price. Across machine-translation experiments with multiple models and language pairs, LAND achieves better MetricX scores than fixed best-of-N at matched average compute. Conversely, at matched translation quality, LAND requires approximately 20-40% fewer candidate generations. Adaptive allocation therefore provides a simple way to retain the benefits of best-of-N while substantially improving its compute efficiency.

papers.title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
papers.summary: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Its 11 projects, spanning financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting, are reconstructed with 13 domain experts from real materials and chain 150 subtasks through 2-15 rounds of new materials and client feedback. Because no reference outputs are injected, agents inherit their own errors from one task to the next. Expert rubrics then score every checkpoint as well as the final package. Across seven model-harness systems, even the best system scores only 65.0 out of 100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. The failures are often failures of carrying work forward: in one audit project, all seven systems addressed the review findings, but only one preserved traceability. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery, which also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

papers.title: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels
papers.summary: Generative models increasingly simulate users at different skill levels in education and AI evaluation. Yet it remains unclear whether lower-skill behavior reflects less internal knowledge or a different use of retained knowledge. This distinction is difficult to study in natural language, where proficiency and relevant knowledge are hard to measure. In this work, we study Maia-2, a chess transformer that predicts human moves conditioned on player skill, using quantitative skill ratings and deterministically labeled chess concepts. We hold board positions and model weights fixed and analyze positions where skill conditioning changes the prediction from a blunder to the best move. First, we measure encoded knowledge by training probes to predict the presence of 172 chess concepts from Maia-2's internal states. Probe accuracy remains nearly constant across skill conditions, and probes trained at one level transfer accurately to the others. To test whether stronger decisions can be recovered from this retained knowledge, we fine-tune only Maia-2's final output layer, raising best-move accuracy in the lowest skill band from 14.4% to 82.8%. Training this layer only on highest-skill representations retains most of the improvement at lower levels, showing that recovery does not require direct training on lower-skill states. Steering concept-relevant features learned by a sparse autoencoder also improves lower-skill decisions while leaving probe-measured concept encoding practically unchanged. These results support an account in which skill conditioning changes how retained concept knowledge influences move selection, showing that weaker behavior can understate the knowledge available within a model.

papers.title: Online Label-Free Gradient Matching for Continual Language Model Training
papers.summary: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.

papers.title: Can AI Do Formal Demography? Why Vaccinating the Oldest Saves Both the Most Lives and the Most Years of Life
papers.summary: Can AI contribute to formal demography? We report an experiment in which an AI model, Claude, was asked to explain and then simplify the proof of an earlier result: that vaccinating the oldest against COVID-19 saves both the most lives and the most years of life, because the years saved per person treated rise with age. The model proposed a new proof that is shorter, more intuitive, and somewhat more general than the original, built from a known life-table identity and the definition of convexity. It states the condition for the result as the convexity of the reciprocal of the hazard, which can be checked from the hazard alone and holds for most familiar parametric models, and it yields a lower bound on life expectancy whenever that condition is met. Prompted by a further question, the model also gave an exact form of the condition, showing how far convexity can be relaxed. The model traced these identities and related results in earlier literature. An edited record of the sessions is provided, and complete transcripts are available on request. The exercise suggests that AI can revisit established results, make them easier to understand, and prove valuable generalizations.

papers.title: Grading the Unannotated: Insights from the WorkRB Skill Extraction Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026
papers.summary: Skill extraction benchmarks score models against a few human-annotated positives and treat every other skill in the vocabulary as equally wrong. At the scale of ESCO (13,939 skills) this binary view can reward models that rank the annotated positive high for the wrong reason, and hides semantically nonsensical predictions. The WorkRB Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026 replaces it with graded relevance: every candidate skill in a model's ranking window carries a 0 to 4 grade, and the leaderboard scores nDCG@100 against these grades. Since ternary judgements proved too coarse for objective annotation, relevance is decomposed into a cascade of four binary questions (same domain, activity mentioned, right granularity, replacement of a gold positive) that a smaller LLM judge can answer reliably; the labels are validated with blind human and frontier-model re-annotation. This paper documents the annotation methodology, the construction of five benchmark datasets (four with vacancy sentences as queries, one with lexically distant skill surface forms), the validation of the LLM cascade, and insights from the submissions. The field converged on multi-stage retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, whose gains come from clearing nonsense out of the ranking window rather than finding more positives: at the top of the leaderboard, the graded ordering is uncorrelated with what binary evaluation would have said. Graded labels expose much bigger gaps between top submissions and baselines than binary evaluation does, and show that semantic-understanding skill recommendation is still wide open. The clear next direction is bringing efficiency back: every submitted system we could size uses at least 42x, typically several hundred times, more parameters than the baselines it beats.

papers.title: An Agentic Framework for Automated Power System Studies and Grid Connection Assessment
papers.summary: Connecting new generation and demand to the grid depends on two scarce skills: checking applications against a large, changing body of regulation, and running the network studies that decide where and how a project connects. We present Grid Agents, an AI system that brings both together, and the methodology we use to evaluate it. The Grid Ontology is its knowledge system. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable, and evolves as the agents learn from use. Every answer drawn from it rests on evidence the agents cite. Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment with domain tools and a study framework, draws on the Grid Ontology, and relies on established solvers for every number it reports. In both, engineers make the decisions. We bring eight published power-system benchmark families, previously scattered across separate papers, into one suite of 519 tasks, and we verify not only each answer but the work behind it, by replaying the agent's tool calls. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. Grid Studio scores highest on the 519 power-system tasks and is the fastest of all the systems we compare, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33-67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.

papers.title: FedReady: Bounded Agents for Federation Formation
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.

papers.title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game
papers.summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.

papers.title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
papers.summary: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

papers.title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
papers.summary: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.

papers.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
papers.summary: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

papers.title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

papers.title: Output-Aware Block Influence: Jacobian-Lens Weighting for Depth Pruning
papers.summary: Depth pruning removes entire transformer blocks and therefore depends on a reliable criterion for identifying which blocks can be removed. Block Influence (BI) ranks blocks by how minimally they rotate the hidden state. However, local redundancy does not necessarily imply downstream irrelevance. We address this limitation using the Jacobian Lens (J-Lens) neural artifact, a map transporting perturbations at a layer to the final residual stream. At a common sparsity level, pruning scores applying J-Lens transportation to $BI$, what we call $J-BI$, were found to improve post-pruning accuracy by up to 19 points over $BI$ while reducing damage to perplexity for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-IT, and Gemma-3-12B-IT. We also perform a single-block ablation study and use J-Lens probing to explain why the proposed scores improved performance.

papers.title: Beyond the Last Layer: Global Inter-Layer Aggregation for AI-Generated Image Detection
papers.summary: The rapid development of generative models has made AI-generated images increasingly close to real images. It has also brought several challenges to detectors, including rapid generator updates, large changes in data distribution, and limited cross-dataset generalization. Many existing methods based on pretrained vision encoders primarily use the global representation from the last layer, potentially leaving useful information from intermediate layers underexplored. To address this issue, we propose Global Inter-Layer Aggregation (GILA). GILA extracts global representations from different depths of a frozen encoder, models interactions among layer representations through inter-layer self-attention, and adaptively aggregates the resulting contextualized representations. The method is not tied to a single pretraining objective and does not require fine-tuning the pretrained encoder. We evaluated GILA on three vision backbones with different pretraining objectives, ten seen generators, and three external datasets. The experimental results show that GILA makes better use of multi-layer information in pretrained encoders and improves detection performance and cross-dataset generalization.

papers.title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
papers.summary: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity Top-1 accuracy over concept-based methods by 1.2-8.5 percentage points and attains H3 forecast Top-1 accuracy within 1.9-2.2 points of matched black-box forecasters. Intervention experiments show concept-node edits correct 25.6-34.4% of initially incorrect H3 forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and concept steering achieves the requested target activity in up to 90.0% of cases.

papers.title: SFA: A Statistical Physics-Inspired Diffusion Transformer for Efficient and High-Quality Image Generation
papers.summary: Diffusion transformers have achieved remarkable success in image generation, but accelerating attention while preserving generation quality remains a major challenge at high resolutions. Inspired by statistical physics and the widespread occurrence of scale-free laws in nature, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA), which preserves fine local interactions while summarizing distant regions at progressively coarser scales. For $N$ tokens, mean pooling, token-count correction, and a shared softmax over a scale-free spatial hierarchy give SFA $O(N\log N)$ complexity in both forward and backward passes. Our Triton implementation achieves $357.3\times$ forward and $265.6\times$ backward attention speedups over FlashAttention at 262,144 tokens. After 40 epochs of PixelFlow training from scratch on ImageNet at $256\times256$ resolution, SFA achieves the best generation quality among five attention mechanisms, including full attention. Fr\'echet inception distance evaluated on 50,000 generated samples (FID-50k) improves from 13.25 for full attention to 12.51, and the advantage over full attention persists through 80 epochs. SFA also achieves the best generation quality among the compared efficient-attention methods on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ). Beyond training from scratch, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with attention replaced by SFA retains the generation quality of its full-attention counterpart under matched fine-tuning budgets. We obtain similar results when fine-tuning pretrained PixelFlow on ImageNet. SFA establishes scale-free structure as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers.

papers.title: A Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support Framework for Brain Tumor MRI Classification: Integrating Attention-Guided Learning, Explainable AI, and Out-of-Distribution Validation
papers.summary: Deep learning models for brain tumor diagnosis need to do more than achieve high classification accuracy. For practical use, they should also provide understandable predictions, recognize unsuitable inputs, and work within a usable clinical system. This paper presents a framework for classifying brain MRI into four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. The model uses InceptionResNetV2 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), while Grad-CAM provides visual explanations of its predictions. A two-stage out-of-distribution (OOD) mechanism screens unsuitable inputs using an initial grayscale check followed by Mahalanobis distance, softmax confidence, and predictive entropy. These components are brought together in NeuroScan AI, a real-time web application. Evaluated on a Mendeley brain tumor MRI dataset of 12,064 images, the framework achieved 98.70% validation accuracy, 96.73% test accuracy, and a macro-average AUC of 0.9965. The OOD pipeline achieved 99% detection accuracy on a preliminary 100-image benchmark. Grad-CAM visualizations showed qualitative correspondence with clinically established tumor locations across all four classes. Overall, the work brings classification, explainability, input validation, and deployment into one framework, while recognizing that broader clinical and OOD validation is still required.

papers.title: From Single-Shot QA to Continuous Perception: Revisiting the Energy Composition and Optimization Boundary of Edge VLMs
papers.summary: Visual-prefill energy conclusions for edge vision-language models (VLMs) are commonly drawn under single-shot workloads; we revisit them under continuous perception. Profiling nine VLMs across three architecture families on Jetson AGX Thor and Orin (4,508 records, calibrated with a pure-text task), we find two mutually independent energy laws: the per-output-token decode cost grows monotonically with model scale, whereas the visual-prefill (image-encoding) cost is dominated by visual-encoder architectural efficiency, not scale. Under continuous perception ($N{=}10$) with sparse output, visual-prefill energy reaches 92--97\% of total. We derive optimization strategies---visual frame reuse, adaptive output truncation, task-aware routing, and encoder throughput optimization---for edge VLM deployment.

papers.title: Beyond Black Boxes: An Ontology Based Vision Framework for Transparent Fruit Disease Detection
papers.summary: Efficiency and reliability in the timely identification of phytopathogens would help minimize crop loss in agricultural sectors but existing deep learning based methods, although accurate, would require a large annotated dataset and are black-boxed in their operation, thus, restricting flexibility and transparency. The current paper presents a hybrid detection framework that is able to overcome these drawbacks through the unified real-time vision with a semantic knowledge base. Web Ontology Language (OWL) was used to develop a comprehensive ontology of the disease of fruits that formally codifies phytopathological knowledge, such as symptom phenotype, spectral phenotype (HSV), and morphological phenotype. Such knowledge-guided configuration guides the image processing pipeline, making it possible to diagnose using this knowledge under expert specified rules without a large training dataset. The ontology underwent a computationally verified test of its structural soundness and commonsensical practical usefulness and scored an overall of 7.4/10. On the public set of MangoFruitDDS, the diagnostic performance was an F1 Score of 85.00%, precision of 85.00%, and a recall of 85.23%. These findings are very competitive and similar to other known deep learning models like the VGG16 that prove that the knowledge-driven approach provides an accurate, transparent, and scalable solution on automated fruit disease diagnosis.

papers.title: Real-Time Obstacle Detection and Distance Estimation on Smartphones for Visually Impaired and Distracted Pedestrians
papers.summary: According to the World Health Organization, at least 2.2 billion people worldwide live with visual impairment, including tens of millions with severe vision loss. Traditional aids such as white canes or guide dogs remain costly, limited in capability, and inaccessible to many. At the same time, smartphone distraction in public spaces has been linked to elevated risks of collisions with vehicles, trips, and falls. These dual challenges motivate lightweight, smartphone-based solutions that combine accessibility with low latency. We present a Kotlin-based Android application that uses a YOLOv8 detector, retrained to recognize eighteen common urban obstacle classes, to deliver real-time obstacle alerts for both user groups. The detector was optimized with pruning, quantization, and early-exit branches, and deployed through the Android Neural Networks API (NNAPI), which can dispatch inference to GPU, NPU, or DSP accelerators when available. On a mid-range smartphone, these optimizations reduced average inference latency from about 3.2 s for the off-the-shelf YOLOv8n to 0.39-0.48 s; the recommended configuration (INT8 quantization with early exit) runs in 0.42-0.48 s while retaining a recall of 0.81. The application combines the optimized detector with ARCore-based or monocular focal-length distance estimation, so it works with a single smartphone camera and requires no LiDAR, depth camera, or other specialized sensor. Multimodal feedback, including Text-to-Speech guidance for visually impaired users and vibration alerts for distracted pedestrians, supports use across different contexts.

papers.title: Think Before You Locate: Clinical Chain-of-Though Supervision for Sequential Medical Image Grounding
papers.summary: Clinicians rarely localize a finding from one image alone. They compare current and prior scans, follow structures across slices, and match regions across views or modalities. Yet vision-language models for sequential medical grounding usually learn only from bounding boxes. Boxes show where the target is, but they do not explain why that region in that image answers the question. We study whether explicit, image-grounded reasoning can improve localization, and which tasks benefit from it. We introduce method, whose core is MedChain, a corpus of 182,573 filtered rationales spanning eight sequential grounding tasks and ten imaging modalities. A medical VLM (FlemingVL-38B) first drafts a caption-like rationale, and a multimodal refiner (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) then re-examines the images, question and annotated box to write a box-conditioned explanation with explicit cross-image reasoning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 on these rationales with deliberative chain-of-thought supervision (dCoT-SFT). Across 4B, 9B, and 27B models, dCoT-SFT sets a new state of the art on MedSG-Bench. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5, improving over the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points. In a paired comparison using fixed 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13--4.00). The gains mainly come from change detection and object tracking, while performance drops on three appearance-matching tasks. Replacing a model's own rationale with a rationale from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points, showing that localization depends strongly on the reasoning context. Finally, adding GRPO with an IoU reward after dCoT-SFT gives only small and task-dependent gains, which we analyze through controlled multi-seed development experiments.

papers.title: Out-of-distribution AI-generated image detection with zero-phase deconvolution for residual whitening
papers.summary: Current AI-generated image detection methods struggle in out-of-distribution testing conditions because detectors are usually not robust when evaluated on generators not included in the training set. This work explores a way to mitigate the forensic bias between sources of images -whether real or generated -by removing generator-specific fingerprints. This new training process can be approximated by pre-processing involving a deconvolution operation designed to remove correlated noise patterns inducing loss of generalization. Indeed, we show that whitening the spatial distribution of the image noise residuals can significantly improve the performance of detectors on images coming from generators unseen during training. In particular, an end-to-end CNN model trained on whitened image residuals improves detection by 12.6% on average compared to a training involving original images.

papers.title: ReactionBench: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Modeling Reactions to Video
papers.summary: Understanding what happens in a video is not sufficient for socially responsive multimodal systems: such systems also aim to relate what a person observes to how that person responds. Existing video benchmarks largely evaluate events, temporal reasoning, or people depicted in the video, while affective and viewer-response datasets often focus on emotion labels, aggregate responses, or prediction from the stimulus alone. This leaves an underexplored question: can current multimodal models ground an observed viewer reaction in the stimulus context associated with it? We introduce ReactionBench, a human-anchored benchmark for reaction-specific video understanding. Built from a candidate pool of 31,834 synchronized stimulus-reaction clips spanning 433 hours and eight domains, ReactionBench evaluates three complementary abilities: ranking the intensity of a viewer's reactions within a video, matching a reaction to its temporally aligned stimulus, and explaining the concrete stimulus cues linked to that reaction. Human annotation provides 14,894 ratings over 3,257 moments, and the frozen evaluation comprises 250 intensity profiles, 112 matching items, and 200 rationale items with 447 blind-written human references. Across seven multimodal models, reaction-specific grounding remains challenging: the best model reaches 50.9% accuracy on four-way stimulus-reaction matching, while GPT-5 shows no detectable loss under reaction substitution. Performance is also sensitive to evaluation protocol. Project page: https://yibozh.github.io/ReactionBench-page/

papers.title: SemaNorm: Stain Normalization via Semantic and Morphology Alignment for Robust Cross-Hospital Computational Pathology
papers.summary: Stain variability remains a major source of domain shift in computational pathology, yet existing normalization methods largely optimize color consistency without explicitly preserving morphology or diagnostic semantics. We propose SemaNorm, a self-supervised stain canonicalization stain normalizer to recover clean patches from strongly perturbed inputs, avoiding paired transfer, adversarial instability, and identity collapse. It further combines a frozen pathology foundation-model consistency loss with a differentiable nuclei-structure loss to preserve semantic and cellular organization. SemaNorm is evaluated across Camelyon17-WILDS and NCT-CRC-HE-100K using cross-hospital tumor classification, cell-graph morphology metrics, and semantic stability measured with an independent held-out foundation encoder. SemaNorm improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 5.9% over the strongest normalization baseline and by 13.5% over no normalization, while achieving the best morphology preservation. Independent foundation-model and cell-graph analyses further confirm improved semantic and structural stability. These results establish morphology- and semantics-aware optimization as a principled alternative to color-only stain normalization.

papers.title: Memorix: Managing Memory Selections for AI Agents
papers.summary: AI agents now handle a growing share of tasks across sessions within a persistent project. Their behavior depends not only on the model, but heavily on the persistent state they read from the environment. Existing systems assemble this memory at use time, splicing selected files into the prompt as a one-off payload. As a result, per-task assembly is costly and can still miss critical material, failures cannot be traced or replayed, and agents can read documentation written for the wrong version. Our key insight is that what an agent should read is mostly determined by its project, so the selection can be computed once, ahead of time, and reused across tasks. We propose Memorix, an agent memory system that realizes this insight. Memorix achieves this via three key mechanisms: (1) an immutable and versioned Store pins every source by identity and reproduces historical layouts cheaply, (2) a View that splits selection (Derivations) from composition (Environment), making the result reproducible and shareable, and (3) Quests and Profiles keep a delivered view refreshable and available inside the project as sources evolve. We implement Memorix and evaluate it on SWE-ContextBench and LibEvolutionEval against mainstream agent memory systems. Precomputed Environments raise resolved rate by up to 1.5X and deliver the correct library version on every version-conditioned task, while cutting amortized cost by up to 100X and build time by up to 38X.

papers.title: SAMP: Self-Adaptive Margin Prioritization For Robust Diffusion Watermarking
papers.summary: Diffusion models have made high-fidelity visual generation widely accessible, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries and complicating content provenance. Existing watermarking methods typically use a fixed embedding strength throughout denoising or treat all watermark dimensions equally. As a result, they may introduce unnecessary distortion when some watermark dimensions are already reliable, while failing to sufficiently reinforce those that are more vulnerable to subsequent perturbations. Therefore, robust watermarking requires adapting both the embedding strength during denoising and the optimization priority across watermark dimensions. To address this problem, we present SAMP, a self-adaptive framework consisting of global margin regulation and vulnerability-sensitive allocation. Global margin regulation adjusts the embedding strength according to the separation between the target codeword and competing codewords, together with the estimated effects of common attacks. Vulnerability-sensitive allocation identifies watermark dimensions that are more easily weakened by local perturbations and gives them higher optimization priority. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMP achieves an average information recovery accuracy of 0.993. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, SAMP improves PSNR by 16.8% and reduces LPIPS by 47.1%. These results validate the effectiveness of SAMP for reliable and high-quality diffusion watermarking.

papers.title: CRaFT-XDet: Causal and Robust Fusion Transformer for Dual-Energy X-ray Prohibited Item Detection
papers.summary: Automated prohibited item detection in X-ray security imagery is fundamentally constrained by severe object overlap, scanner-dependent domain shifts, and spurious correlations induced by cluttered baggage composition. Existing detectors largely rely on appearance-driven supervision, limiting their robustness and cross-scanner generalisation. We introduce CRaFT-XDet, a causality-grounded and physics- motivated detection framework that reformulates X-ray threat detection as invariant representation learning under attenuation-driven modality variation. Our approach is grounded in a Scanner-Invariant Causal Detection formalisation (Theorem 1), which establishes that minimising the proposed Causal Invariance Regularisation (CIR) objective across partitioned scanner environments approximates the interventional distribution P (Y | do(Xobj)) under standard identifiability assumptions, providing a principled causal formulation for dual-energy X-ray detection. CRaFT-XDet integrates: (i) causal feature disentanglement to suppress context-induced shortcuts; (ii) physics-motivated regularisation to enforce material-consistent embeddings; and (iii) transformer-based cross-energy interaction modelling for structured reasoning in cluttered scenes. With 29.2 M parameters, 89.5 GFLOPs, and 345 FPS (1.7 ms inference), CRaFT-XDet is real-time deployable. Trained on SIXray with five-fold cross-validation, the framework achieves 0.9389 mAP@0.5 and 0.8021 mAP@0.5:0.95. Without domain adaptation, CRaFT-XDet maintains strong cross- dataset performance on OPIXray and HiXray, indicating robust generalization across heterogeneous scanner distributions. In category-agnostic binary threat detection, the model attains 93.92% recall and 0.9031 mean IoU, highlighting reliability in safety-critical screening where missed detections are costly.

papers.title: CRAFT: Corrective and Robust Multi-Agent Framework for Text-to-Parametric CAD
papers.summary: Text-to-CAD generation has the potential to make mechanical CAD more accessible, but existing approaches face a trade-off between data dependence and output fidelity. Supervised methods rely on large paired text-model datasets, while zero-shot prompting strategies are often brittle and tend to lose the parametric structure needed for downstream editing and customization. We present CRAFT, a corrective and robust multi-agent framework that produces parametric OpenSCAD programs from natural language without task-specific training. At its core is a JSON intermediate representation that carries symbolic parametric expressions throughout the generation process, so the resulting models remain editable and retain their parametric structure. CRAFT combines semantic understanding, parametric planning, compilation, rendering, self-correction, and component-level verification within a layered recovery process, using multi-view visual feedback to detect and repair geometric errors. Across NopSCADlib, ABC, and Slice-100K, CRAFT is competitive with direct zero-shot baselines in perceptual and geometric quality while exposing substantially more editable parametric structure.

papers.title: Evaluating Context Sensitivity of Collaboration Behavior in Multi Party Simulation Frameworks
papers.summary: Group Social Behavior is increasingly used as a lens to study Large language model (LLM) simulations to aid model training and evaluation. However, little prior work has examined how contextual factors such as team size and goal type manifest in long running simulations. To overcome this gap, we conduct a controlled, full-factorial study examining how contextual factors affect collaboration behavior across multi-party simulation frameworks. Using well established social science taxonomies, we quantify context sensitivity of collaboration behavior in simulated teams. Our analyses reveal significant effects of contextual factors such as simulators consistently favor smooth collaboration over disagreement, negotiation pressure, and coordination breakdown. These findings provide the first systematic evidence of how contextual factors influence emergent collaboration in LLM based multi-party simulation frameworks, offering both guidance and empirical results for the use of such simulations.

papers.title: Pano2BIM: A Geometry-Constrained Vision-Language Agent for As-Built BIM Generation from a Floor Plan and a Single 360$^\circ$ Image
papers.summary: Digital twins require accurate, up-to-date building information models (BIM) that reflect physical conditions, yet generating and maintaining as-built models remains costly and labor-intensive. Emerging image-based methods can capture visual appearance without inherently producing structured BIM information, while vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with reliable metric object placement. This paper presents Pano2BIM, a geometry-constrained VLM agent that generates approximate IFC4 models at Level of Development (LOD) 200 from a floor plan with known room dimensions and a single 360-degree photograph. The VLM identifies landmarks and objects, while deterministic tools estimate camera pose, compute metric positions through ray casting, and check spatial constraints. An optional second stage enriches the presentation model through render-and-compare feedback without modifying the primary furniture geometry. In a preliminary evaluation on one laboratory, the proposed Measure workflow achieved a mean furniture-footprint intersection over union (IoU) of 0.53, compared with 0.44 for a single-response baseline using identical modeling instructions, and matched an average of 4.0 versus 2.3 of seven fixed furniture elements across three runs. Centroid disagreements were similar for the four elements consistently identified by both approaches. The measurement stage averaged 3.8 minutes and USD 1.63 in API costs per run, while the complete demonstrated workflow required approximately 42 minutes and USD 11. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of rapid, low-cost as-built BIM generation, with potential applications in maintaining digital twins that reflect changing physical conditions.

papers.title: A Novel Lightweight Multi-Scale Branching Encoder for Few-Shot Image Classification
papers.summary: Few-Shot Learning (FSL) addresses classification scenarios in which only a small number of labeled examples are available for each class. This paper presents the Sum12 Multi-Scale branching encoder, a lightweight convolutional architecture designed to improve the embedding stage of Prototypical Networks without substantially increasing computational cost. The encoder uses seven parallel convolutional branches whose kernel-size combinations sum to 12, allowing local and broader spatial structures to be represented within a unified Multi-Scale feature space. The proposed architecture was evaluated on Omniglot, CIFAR- FS, FC100, and miniImageNet under controlled few-shot learning protocols and compared with the original Prototypical Network encoder and Inception-inspired branch variants. Additional ablation studies have investigated fusion strategies, dilated convolutions, branch compositions, and receptive field budget. Beyond few-shot learning, the encoder was also tested on the MedMNIST 2D benchmark to assess its behavior in conventional supervised medical image classification. Across these experiments, Sum12 generally improved the low-shot classification performance with respect to the basic ProtoNet encoder while preserving a compact model size. These properties suggest that the proposed encoder may be suitable for low-data visual recognition and resource-constrained intelligent imaging applications. However, complete end-to- end validation on the target embedded platform, including resolution of the observed implementation discrepancies, remains future work.

papers.title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
papers.summary: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.

papers.title: DTP-OPSD: Reinforcement Learning with Distractor-Aware Temporal-Privilege On-Policy Self-Distillation for Temporal Video Grounding
papers.summary: Temporal Video Grounding (TVG) aims to localize the start and end times of an event described by a language query in a video. The task becomes particularly challenging when the same video contains multiple repeated, similar, or opposite events. On these hard examples, all responses sampled by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) may miss the target and receive zero temporal Intersection-over-Union (tIoU). Their group-relative advantages are then all zero, leaving no useful policy gradient signal. To address this, we propose DTP-OPSD, a reinforcement learning framework with distractor-aware temporal-privilege on-policy self-distillation. The student observes the clean video and generates responses on-policy, while a shared-weight teacher observes a privileged video in which the target window is marked by red full-frame borders and same-video distractor windows by blue full-frame borders. For the distillation loss, the teacher evaluates student-generated prefixes and provides dense token-level Jensen-Shannon divergence supervision. This supervision remains informative even when GRPO provides no policy gradient signal. We suppress distillation when the teacher does not outperform the student and strengthen it for groups where the teacher performs better but all student rollouts receive zero tIoU. We also construct a compact hard-interference training set through VLM screening and human verification. With only 300 additional post-training examples, DTP-OPSD achieves the highest mIoU among the compared open-source 8B models on Charades-TimeLens, ActivityNet-TimeLens, and QVHighlights-TimeLens, reaching 55.93, 54.77, and 66.71, respectively. Compared with Pure GRPO trained on the same data, DTP-OPSD improves all 12 reported metrics, with R1@0.7 gains of 1.28, 1.62, and 1.78 points on the three benchmarks. Code will be released at https://github.com/nian1125/DTP-OPSD

papers.title: SPARQLcirc: Probabilistic Query Evaluation with Provenance Circuits
papers.summary: Probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) computes the probability of every answer of a query over a tuple-independent probabilistic knowledge graph. We study exact PQE for SPARQL over graphs accessed through SPARQL 1.1 endpoints. Shared triples among the derivations of an answer make exact PQE #P-hard in general. Knowledge compilation of the Boolean provenance of every answer yields exact probabilities, and the provenance formulas of different answers can share subformulas. We propose SPARQLcirc, which rewrites a SPARQL query into CONSTRUCT queries that name every gate by its content, so that the results of independent queries form one Boolean provenance circuit for all answers. The rewriting covers joins, unions, projection, filters, OPTIONAL, difference, and transitive closures. SPARQLcirc compiles the circuit and computes the exact probability of every answer by weighted model counting. For the evaluation, we draw random probabilities for the triples of WatDiv and gMark and the statements of Wikidata and evaluate the CONSTRUCT queries on GraphDB, Fuseki, and Oxigraph. The ratio of the end-to-end time of PQE with SPARQLcirc to that of PQE by compiling the provenance expressions of the SPARQL provenance rewriting NPCS decreases with the number of derivations.

papers.title: FB-MOAC: A Reinforcement Learning Algorithm for Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are effective in solving problems that can be modeled as Markov decision processes (MDPs). These algorithms primarily target forward MDPs whose dynamics evolve over time from an initial state. However, several important problems in different scenarios including stochastic control and network systems exhibit both a forward and a backward dynamics. As a consequence, they cannot be expressed as a standard MDP, thereby calling for a novel theory for RL in this context. Accordingly, this work introduces the concept of Forward-Backward Markov Decision Processes (FB-MDPs) for multi-objective problems, develops a novel theoretical framework to characterize their optimal solutions, and proposes a general forward-backward step-wise template that allows to adapt RL algorithms for FB-MDP problems. A Forward Backward Multi Objective Actor Critic (FB-MOAC) algorithm is introduced accordingly to obtain optimal policies with guaranteed convergence and a competitive rate with respect to standard approaches in RL. FB-MOAC is evaluated on diverse use cases in the context of mathematical finance and mobile resource management. papers.title: Kerkoporta: Injecting Structured-Output Backdoors in Reasoning Coding Agents
papers.summary: Existing large language model (LLM) backdoor attacks operate primarily in chat settings, where the risk is bounded by free-form text outputs. AI agents remove that bound by performing actions and executing commands on the user's machine. We introduce structured-output backdoor attacks against reasoning models in agentic coding settings. A trigger placed anywhere in the agent's context causes the model to emit an attacker-chosen tool call, which the harness executes, directly compromising the system's confidentiality, integrity, or availability. We present Kerkoporta, a methodology that constructs high-quality poison samples, injects the backdoor via supervised fine-tuning, and recovers utility loss with lightweight reinforcement learning. We evaluate on modern, heavily post-trained open-weight models across proprietary and open-source harnesses, focusing on coding for its wide adoption and long-horizon task structure. The attack reaches success rates of up to 96.2% and can be configured to generalize across harnesses or bind to a single target. The resulting models can outperform the clean baseline on standard utility benchmarks, giving victims a direct incentive to adopt them. Overall, we demonstrate that LLM backdoors can have critical security impacts in the context of modern coding agents, and we characterize the poisoning methodology required to insert backdoors that are both effective and stealthy in this setting.

papers.title: From Concepts to Actual Causes: Toward Closing the Concept-Malfunction Gap in Robot Foundation Models
papers.summary: Post-incident analysis of a robot foundation model poses a singular causal question: which internal components caused this failure, and to what degree? Mechanistic interpretability (MI), however, establishes general causal claims by decoding the concepts a policy has learned, yet knowing which concepts are encoded is insufficient for identifying the actual cause of a specific incident. In this position paper, we analyze this concept-malfunction gap by posing fault isolation in the framework of actual causality. Specifically, we formalize a fault-isolation query as a tuple of intervened internal components, counterfactual values, contingencies, and read-outs, and lay out conditions for it to be well-specified. Through this lens, we identify shortcomings of current MI approaches: they assume fixed contingencies and read out only immediate effects, letting backups obscure actual causes. We demonstrate on a toy example that these shortcomings can lead to conflicting verdicts. Lastly, based on the well-specification conditions, we outline four open research tasks toward closing the gap.

papers.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
papers.summary: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

papers.title: Spectral and Conformal: Neural Network Methods for Calibrated Trajectory Prediction and Control-Point Intervals
papers.summary: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.

papers.title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
papers.summary: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.

papers.title: DELBERT-2: Pretrained Fingerprint Language Models for DEL Protein Binder Prediction

papers.title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
papers.summary: Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols. To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.

papers.title: When AI Agents Act on Our Behalf: A Taxonomy of Human-Agent Interaction Failure
papers.summary: AI agents write and execute code, manipulate user interfaces, and transact on their users' behalf. We ask what forms failure takes in human-agent interaction, and how those forms change as agents act with greater autonomy. From 695 documented incidents in two public repositories, we developed 12 failure modes bottom-up within three interaction stages adapted from Amershi et al.'s guidelines, coding the autonomy at which each arose. What a person can do when an agent fails depends on how much the agent completes between points of user involvement--a property fixed at deployment. Therefore, the same model on the same task can fail differently under different configurations. All 12 modes appear at both low and high autonomy, and rising autonomy changes the form each failure takes. Users need controls between full delegation and full manual work, and neither incident records nor agent benchmarks reach the interaction where these failures occur.

papers.title: TADA: Technology Aware DNN Accelerator Performance and Energy Estimator
papers.summary: Deep neural network (DNN) accelerators for edge inference must meet tight energy, latency, and area (EDP) constraints, and their optimal hardware architecture and dataflow configuration is typically identified through design space exploration (DSE). However, on-chip memory technology including cell type, bank organization, and process node, is rarely treated as a first-class citizen in DSE. For example, increasing memory capacity can reduce memory accesses through greater data reuse, but at the cost of higher area and access energy, thereby limiting the compute units budget. Consequently, memory technology can fundamentally shift the optimal accelerator architecture for a given area and EDP budget. Existing machine learning (ML)-based DSE methods require repeating simulation, data generation, and model training for each new memory technology. We present TADA, a memory technology-aware DNN accelerator performance and energy estimator that predicts system latency and energy for a given workload, hardware configuration, and memory technology. TADA is trained on a synthetic dataset that generalizes across memory technologies. The dataset spans current and future technology trends while enforcing physics-based guardrails to preserve realistic area-energy trade-offs. Each memory technology is represented by a technology signature, a vector of read energy, write energy, and storage capacity across a range of areas, provided as input alongside the workload and hardware configuration. Across 21 unseen technology curves spanning SRAM, STTRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeFET, eDRAM, and CTT, TADA predicts system energy and latency with 1.5-4.4% and 0.7-1.2% mean absolute percentage error, respectively. In three pairwise case studies, it matches the simulator-selected memory technology at 98.7-100% of area budgets, with a mean EDP loss of at most 0.21%, while achieving over 10^4x higher evaluation throughput.

papers.title: A Framework for Task-Agnostic Counterfactual Fairness in Transformers through Activation Steering
papers.summary: Bias in transformer-based models is a growing concern as these architectures become more prevalent in automated decision-making systems, such as prediction models for hiring, lending, and clinical treatment recommendation. Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is a growing body of work that measures meaningful causal effects of activations on model output by identifying human-interpretable features encoded in model activations. When such features correspond to sensitive attributes, they provide a direct way to quantify the bias those attributes introduce and to causally intervene to mitigate it. However, counterfactual fairness (CF) methods have not been systematically adapted to this setting of intervening on interpretable mechanisms in transformers. We propose a framework, Mechanistic Interpretability for Counterfactual Fairness (MICF), that utilizes MI tools to reformulate CF constraints in terms of transformer activations, unifying former approaches into a single pipeline for fairness analysis in transformers. MICF does not require a prior causal model or specific transformer architecture. We evaluate MICF on real-world tabular data and show that CF can be improved across different prediction tasks.

papers.title: C3: Speech-Guided KV Retrieval for Long-Context SpeechLLM Inference
papers.summary: Speech language models encode audio at a much higher rate than text, causing the KV cache to dominate the memory, bandwidth, and decoding cost of long-form generation. KV retrieval can reduce per-step access by attending to only a query-dependent subset of the cache, but existing methods are designed primarily for text and do not account for the structure of audio attention. We first show that retrieval errors may compound autoregressively into generation drift. We then analyze full audio attention during long-form generation and identify three properties relevant to retrieval: unequal attention concentration across query heads, non-contiguous audio support, and temporal continuity across decoding steps. Guided by these observations, we propose $C^3$(Cluster-Compete-Compete), which organizes audio KVs in a hierarchical key-space index, lets query heads sharing a KV head compete for a common retrieval budget, and adaptively reallocates retrieval resolution through paired split-merge updates. Across long-form speech recognition, translation, and summarization on four SpeechLLMs, $C^3$ achieves the strongest overall performance among retrieval methods under comparable final-KV access budgets, with particularly large gains in the tight-budget regime, while improving long-context decoding efficiency and accelerator-memory scaling.
