papers.title: High-Resolution Modelling of Coronae and Winds in Solar-type Stars with Varying Rotation Rates II. Stellar Winds
papers.summary: Observations suggest a connection between steady-wind mass loss and coronal X-ray activity in low-mass main-sequence stars. Interpreting this connection is challenging because the wind is controlled mainly by the large-scale open field, whereas X-ray emission traces heating in small-scale closed fields often unresolved in global wind models. Here we use Space Weather Modelling Framework-Alfv\'{e}n-Wave Solar Model with global convective dynamo-generated magnetic maps and solar magnetograms. We model Alfv\'en-wave-heated winds for four solar-type stars plus the Sun, spanning rotation rates of $1.0$--$23.3$ times the solar rate, and magnetic field strengths of $6.0$--$1200$ G. Our models show that faster rotation yields a more tightly wound spiral, a larger Alfv\'en surface, higher terminal wind speeds, and a harsher wind-pressure environment for orbiting exoplanets, different from that of the present-day Sun. We estimate the mass- and angular-momentum-loss rates and find systematic differences from Zeeman-Doppler Imaging-based predictions. Building on the successful reproduction of X-ray coronae in our Paper~I, we obtain the first self-consistent activity--wind relation in a unified modelling framework: the mass-loss rate scales with the surface X-ray flux following a power law with an index of ${\sim}0.67$. We also re-examine magnetic braking via open-flux magnetisation, finding that the effective Alfv\'enic lever arm depends on the magnetisation parameter with a power-law index of ${\sim}0.35$. Finally, we quantify the stellar wind pressure at the orbits of several super-Earths. Together with our Paper~I, the series of results shows the distinct roles of multi-scale magnetic fields and provides physically grounded inputs for assessing habitable-zone space weather.

papers.title: Anisotropy of Satellite Galaxies-II: Spatial Segregation as the Origin of Anisotropic Satellite Quenching in Haloes and Beyond
papers.summary: Satellite galaxies in massive halos are seen to be preferentially quenched along the major axes of their central galaxies. In contrast, the AGN jet tends to point along the minor axis, which imposes interesting constraints on the role of AGN feedback in satellite galaxy quenching. Here we use the SIMBA, TNG100, EAGLE, and feedback-free SIMBA cosmological simulations at $z=0$ to show that this satellite anisotropy primarily originates from spatial segregation between quenched and unquenched populations. Quenched satellites are more centrally concentrated and more strongly aligned with the central galaxy's major axis, whereas unquenched satellites occupy larger radii and are more nearly isotropic. The persistence of this behaviour without stellar or active galactic nucleus feedback suggests that feedback is not important for satellite quenching. Beyond the halo boundary, the signal varies strongly among simulations and correlates with the excess number of galaxies along the major axis. This links large-scale anisotropic quenching to the direction-dependent distribution of groups, clusters and filamentary environments. Our results provide a unified geometrical interpretation of anisotropic satellite quenching across halo and extra-halo scales.

papers.title: A derived evolution of dark energy from cosmic inhomogeneity confronted with baryon acoustic oscillations and type Ia supernovae
papers.summary: The volume dynamics of space is a framework in which the possibility that matter can be unevenly distributed enters the expansion dynamics directly. It yields a redshift-dependent effective Hubble constant and dark-energy density parameter from the Planck parameters alone. We derive the expansion history $H(z)$ that the framework implies and show that it is flat $\Lambda$CDM with the cosmological constant replaced by a dark-energy density that grows by 31 percent toward the present, with an effective equation of state $w(0) = -1.21$ approaching $-1$ at high redshift and a present-day age of 13.52 Gyr, 0.30 Gyr younger than in the homogeneous limit. We confront it with the DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations and the Pantheon+ type Ia supernovae, with the Hubble constant, the sound horizon and the supernova absolute magnitude free, so that only the shape of $H(z)$ is tested. Relative to $\Lambda$CDM the prediction is disfavored by $\Delta\chi^2 = 65$ with one parameter fewer. A free matter density reduces this to $\Delta\chi^2 = 42$, because each probe alone accommodates the model only with incompatible matter densities (0.35 from the oscillations, 0.54 from the supernovae). Their combination bounds the heterogeneity amplitude to $\sigma_8 < 0.14$ at 95 percent confidence, against the Planck value 0.81 that enters the derivation; the best fit of the heterogeneous model is its homogeneous limit, flat $\Lambda$CDM. At the leading order in which it is currently evaluated, the heterogeneous contribution therefore cannot account for the Hubble tension, and it acts opposite to the evolution of dark energy that current distance data favor.

papers.title: Correcting stellar contamination in transmission spectroscopy with contemporaneous monitoring: Application to GJ 1214 b
papers.summary: Transmission spectroscopy is an essential tool for characterising the atmospheres of transiting exoplanets. However, stellar surface inhomogeneities contaminate transmission spectra, posing a major challenge to high-precision observations such as those from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We develop and apply methods to correct for stellar contamination, improving the accuracy of exoplanet atmospheric characterisation. We obtained coordinated multi-band photometry and high-resolution spectroscopy around JWST observations of GJ 1214 b and applied two frameworks: (i) a StarSim inversion, which infers stellar activity parameters from the monitoring data and propagates them to corrections; and (ii) UnSPOTTER, in which neural networks trained on StarSim simulations learn the mapping from monitoring data to corrections. Both frameworks agree within uncertainties and indicate that the JWST observations of GJ 1214 occurred at a favourable rotation phase with low stellar contamination. For UnSPOTTER, the inferred corrections can be constrained at approximately 10-30 ppm across the JWST wavelength range, implying post-correction residuals of the same order. If the same system were observed near activity maximum, the predicted contamination would be strongly chromatic and affect atmospheric retrievals, highlighting the importance of coordinated monitoring and robust activity correction techniques. The two approaches are complementary but serve different roles. The inversion yields physically interpretable parameters and surface maps, whereas UnSPOTTER marginalises over surface-configuration degeneracies and provides tighter predictive corrections within its validated simulation domain. Our pipeline can potentially be generalised to other active stars: with multi-band and multi-technique monitoring around JWST visits, it can provide activity forecasts for scheduling and activity corrections.

papers.title: Stacked strong and weak lensing united: Improved measurement of the stellar and dark matter distributions in massive early-type galaxies at $z\sim 0.5$
papers.summary: We present a new measurement of the stellar and dark matter distributions in massive early-type galaxies at redshift $0.4<z<0.6$ by combining stacked strong and weak lensing measurements. The stacked weak lensing measurements down to the small radius of $0.013\,\mathrm{Mpc}/h$ enabled by the Subaru Telescope Hyper Suprime-Cam data are combined with stacked enclosed projected mass measurements from 13 strong lens systems. We find that adding strong lensing constraints improves constraints on the stellar and dark matter distributions. The central dark matter profile is found to be consistent with the standard Navarro-Frenk-White density profile. The stellar initial mass function is found to be bottom-heavy. The total density profile in the inner region is described well by the power-law density profile with the slope of $-1.96\pm 0.07$, which can also explain weak lensing signals out to $1\,\mathrm{Mpc}/h$ reasonably well. The stacked weak lensing profile constrains an internal mass-sheet transformation parameter to $\lambda_{\mathrm{c}}=0.978\pm0.010$ assuming a single cored component. Our analysis demonstrates that the combination of the stacked strong and weak lensing serves as a powerful tool for studying central density profiles of galaxies.

papers.title: Raising the Optical Depth to Reionization with Dark Matter Decay
papers.summary: DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements have sharpened a discrepancy with cosmic microwave background (CMB) inferences that can be recast as a preference for $\tau_{\rm reio}\simeq0.09$, above the $\simeq0.06$ inferred from large-scale CMB polarization. We test whether electromagnetic energy injection from dark matter (DM) decaying through $\chi\to e^+e^-$ can supply this additional optical depth. Adopting an asymmetric, simulation-calibrated Gompertzian model for astrophysical reionization, we derive $\tau_{\rm reio}$ self-consistently from the free-electron history including DM decay. We jointly constrain cosmological and reionization parameters and the decay rate using ACT+Planck CMB temperature and polarization anisotropies, CMB lensing, BAO, and quasar damping-wing observations. For $m_\chi=1$ GeV, DM decay raises the marginalized mean optical depth from 0.064 to 0.072 under a flat decay-rate prior, without significantly improving the fit. Reweighting the chains with log-uniform priors lowers the mean optical depth, indicating prior dependence. The additional optical depth arises primarily from a broad ionization tail through the cosmic dark ages, rather than an earlier onset of astrophysical reionization. For DM masses from 2 MeV to 7 GeV, the 68% credible intervals remain below $\tau_{\rm reio}\simeq0.08$, a benchmark previously found sufficient to bring both the neutrino-mass tension and the exclusion of $\Lambda$CDM below $2\sigma$. The DM lifetime constraints complement photon, cosmic-ray, and gas-heating bounds and are competitive with previous CMB limits. DM decay therefore shifts the inferred optical depth upward, but the posterior-favored increase remains insufficient to substantially alleviate the CMB--BAO discrepancy.

papers.title: Extending the Pulsar radio population through Quantum Vacuum Cherenkov Emission
papers.summary: The presence of some radio pulsars within and below the so-called ``death valley'' in the $P$--$\dot{P}$ diagram challenges the standard pair-cascade models based on curvature radiation (CR) and resonant inverse Compton scattering (RICS) in neutron star polar caps. We show that Cherenkov radiation from the quantum vacuum, a strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) phenomenon enabled by vacuum polarization, constitutes a distinct pair-creation channel within the vacuum gap model. Within this model, the acceleration length scale for Cherenkov photon emission and the subsequent photon mean free path are sufficiently short to ensure rapid conversion into $e^+e^-$ pairs. This process acts as a complementary pair-creation channel, remaining viable even in regimes where classical mechanisms become heavily suppressed. This leads to a new set of death lines in the $P$--$\dot{P}$ diagram that partially overlap with and extend beyond the CR and RICS death valleys, enlarging the viable parameter space for radio-emitting neutron stars. The result provides a physical basis for coherent radio emission from long-period neutron stars previously considered inactive, and offers a new window for testing non-linear QED with next-generation radio facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array.

papers.title: A concordance model of neutron star kicks
papers.summary: Neutron stars (NSs) receive natal kicks during supernovae that affect their survival in binaries and motion through the Galaxy. The global distribution of these kick velocities across the NS population remains uncertain. Here, we combine the orbital properties and birth rates of Gaia NS and Be+NS binaries with velocity constraints from young isolated pulsars to construct a concordance model of NS natal kicks. We find that all three populations can be jointly described by a shared bimodal kick distribution. The low-velocity component follows a lognormal distribution with $\mu_{\ln v}=1.87^{+0.65}_{-0.53}$ and $\sigma_{\ln v}=0.55^{+0.85}_{-0.44}$, corresponding to a median speed of $6.5^{+5.9}_{-2.7}~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$. The high-velocity component is consistent with the distribution inferred from young pulsars, which peaks near $200~{\rm km~s^{-1}}$. The low-velocity component contributes only $\sim10\%$ of all NS births, but produces most Gaia NS binaries and roughly half of Be+NS binaries. The same model predicts systemic recoil velocities consistent with the observed kinematics of Gaia NSs, Be+NS binaries, and NS low-mass X-ray binaries. For Gaia NSs, whose formation history remains unknown, we use this kick distribution to constrain their progenitors. We favor pre-supernova binaries containing intermediate-mass stripped stars with $\sim1~{\rm M_\odot}$ companions in au-scale orbits, and predict $\sim300$ such binaries in the Milky Way today, $\sim40$ in the LMC, and $\sim30$ in the SMC. Finally, we consider the implications of these kicks for NSs in hierarchical triples. We find that 2-10$\%$ of Gaia NS triples and 3-23$\%$ of Be+NS triples retain their tertiary after the supernova. Overall, our results suggest that a shared natal kick law can account for isolated pulsars and surviving NS binaries, where most NSs receive large kicks and low kicks are common among surviving binaries.

papers.title: The variable mass-loss in low-mass red giant stars: Chromospheric motion across stellar evolution in 47 Tuc
papers.summary: Mass-Loss (ML) is a critical process that remains poorly understood despite its broad implications across astrophysics. Our current knowledge is insufficient to reproduce ML consistently across stars, particularly in cool, low-mass giants, where the time-variable nature of chromospheres (CHR) ---the region where most physical phenomena powering ML in this regime are expected to occur--- is poorly constrained. We characterize the relevant timescales of CHR variability in red giants and explore correlations with intrinsic stellar properties. We analyze the first large temporal spectroscopic monitoring of CHR variability using the H$\alpha$ line in red giants belonging to the globular cluster NGC 104 (47 Tuc) using FLAMES/GIRAFFE data. We found that after $\sim$4 days, for $\log(L/L_\odot)\gtrsim2.4$, variations in H$\alpha$ on average increase and widen their range of values with increasing luminosity, together with a systematic blueshift of the line core ---indicative of outflows--- and deeper cores ---indicating an increased chromospheric optical depth. The characteristic timescale required to observe variations in the H$\alpha$ profile is approximately one day, showing a flat trend with luminosity. While shorter-timescale variations remain consistent with statistical uncertainties, a possible increase toward dimmer stars is found. These trends appear similarly correlated with luminosity and effective temperature. No further correlation is found with different cluster sub-populations, nor are significant differences observed between AGB and RGB stars. The outflow trends closely match previous observations across a wide metallicity range. We discuss whether these observations reflect changes in H$\alpha$ sensitivity to the winds, a genuine atmospheric transition driven by changes in heating efficiency, or continued CHR expansion with geometrically dominated H$\alpha$ formation.

papers.title: A Little Red Dot emerging from a nitrogen-rich UV-luminous galaxy with Very Massive Stars
papers.summary: JWST is revealing abundant populations of high-$z$ galaxies with unforeseen properties: UV-luminous galaxies with high nitrogen enrichment, populations of very massive stars (VMSs; $>100\ M_\odot$), and early forms of massive black hole growth such as the Little Red Dots (LRDs). Here we present all these phenomena appearing simultaneously in COLA1, a luminous ($M_{\rm UV}=-21.3$) galaxy at $z=6.6$. New NIRSpec medium-resolution data reveal a blue UV continuum ($\beta_{\rm UV}=-2.5$) with strong emission lines including NIV] $\lambda1486$, stellar P Cygni profiles, and broad HeII $\lambda1640$. We fit the UV with stellar population models, and find that the models including VMSs (limited to $300\ M_\odot$) are statistically preferred. The best-fit stellar population has $M_*\approx10^8\ M_\odot$, and a young age of $2.4\pm0.8$ Myr. The rest-optical shows a redder continuum ($\beta_{\rm opt}=-1.1$) and broad Balmer lines with Balmer absorption akin to LRD spectra. By evolving the best-fit stellar population we find that the UV could dim by 1-2 mag in $\sim5$ Myr, and hence this system would be observed as a typical V-shaped LRD. We measure a supersolar $\rm log_{10}(N/O)=-0.07\pm0.05$ and subsolar $\rm log_{10}(C/O)=-0.64\pm0.11$; therefore $\rm log_{10}(N/C)=+0.58\pm0.12$. The independent density-sensitive NIV] $\lambda\lambda1483,1486$ and CIII] $\lambda\lambda1906/1909$ ratios require two zones with $n_e\gtrsim10^{6.5}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $n_e\lesssim10^{3.5}$ cm$^{-3}$, respectively. We estimate $\rm log_{10}(N/C)>1.3$ (2$\sigma$) for the dense zone, requiring extreme N/C enrichment mechanisms such as highly rotating $>100\ M_\odot$ VMSs, tidal disruption events, or supermassive stars. We speculate that runaway collisions of massive stars in a dense stellar cluster may have lead to the seeding of an intermediate-mass black hole resulting in the formation of an LRD.

papers.title: A double debris disc around a white dwarf sculpted by two planetary bodies
papers.summary: Many planetary systems survive the metamorphosis of their hosts stars into white dwarfs, as demonstrated by the detection of dusty circumstellar discs around these stellar remnants as well as chemical signatures of planetary debris in atmospheres of these stars. A small fraction of these circumstellar discs also contain gas, detected in the form of emission lines from various ionic transitions (most commonly the near-infrared Ca ii triplet). All of the 21 known gas discs exhibit double-peaked line profile characteristic of a rotating flat disc. The mechanism behind the the generation of gas is still debated, but for at least one system it has been linked with the presence of a surviving planetesimal embedded within the dust disc. Here we report the discovery of WD J132800.85-145019.95, a new gas disc system which exhibits quadruple-peaked instead of double-peaked line profiles. These emission lines originate from two separate gaseous rings extending from 0.14 Rsun to 0.34 Rsun and from 0.54 Rsun to 1.93 Rsun. We propose that this structure results from the presence of two distinct planetary bodies within these discs, ranging in size from a few km to the size of Pluto. The detection this stable double-disc presents a new challenge for the current models of debris disc formation and evolution.

papers.title: Young Planets around Young Accreting Stars: II. Circumplanetary Disk Formation and Accretion
papers.summary: We present global 3-D ideal-MHD simulations of young giant planets in a protoplanetary disk (PPD) undergoing magnetospheric accretion onto its host star. Extending our previous work, we insert three planets with planet-to-star mass ratio $q = 0.01$ ($\sim 10$ Jupiter masses) at 0.45, 0.9, and 1.8 times the magnetospheric truncation radius, $R_T$ , thereby probing the low-density cavity, disk-cavity boundary, and turbulent inner disk. The outermost two planets develop circumplanetary disks (CPDs), whereas the innermost planet forms no persistent bound structure because its high velocity relative to the magnetosphere reduces the effective Bondi radius below the planet's size. The outermost planet forms a stable, coplanar CPD whose inner region is rotationally supported and rotates at nearly the local Keplerian speed within $\sim 0.25$ Hill radii. High-latitude inflow and midplane decretion produce meridional circulation and continuous recycling between the CPD and surrounding disk. Inflow through the Hill sphere is comparable to previous Hill-based hydrodynamic estimates. The middle planet, located near $R_T$, develops a persistent polar CPD whose angular-momentum vector is parallel to the disk midplane, demonstrating that coherent circumplanetary structures can form within highly dynamic magnetospheric flows. Based on both the effective Bondi radius and thermal-mass criterion, we identify conditions under which massive giant planets form CPDs in the inner disk. Estimated planetary inflow accretion rates imply mass-doubling timescales $\gtrsim 10$ Myr due to the low disk surface density, suggesting that, in the magnetically active zone, these planets undergo only limited late-stage growth before disk dispersal.

papers.title: Nine new eclipsing accreting ultracompact white dwarf binaries from the Zwicky Transient Facility
papers.summary: Accreting ultracompact white dwarf binaries (accreting UCBs) transfer helium-rich material at orbital periods below about 65 min, and mainly divide into hydrogen-free AM CVn binaries and helium cataclysmic variables. Eclipsing systems are of particular value: they allow the component masses and radii to be measured essentially independently of stellar models, the most direct test of the proposed formation channels, and they form a sample with a simple, well-understood selection function. Only 21 eclipsing accreting white dwarf UCBs have been published. We aim to enlarge the sample of eclipsing accreting UCBs available for detailed characterisation. We searched the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) light curves of Gaia-selected candidates and of ZTF-selected dwarf novae for short-period eclipse signals using a box least-squares period search. Keck/LRIS identification spectra were obtained for nine systems. We present nine new discoveries and re-analyse the four systems first reported by Khalil et al. (2024). Eclipses are detected directly in the survey photometry of all 13 systems, which have orbital periods between 26.0 and 65.0 min and median ZTF magnitudes $g = 18.7-21.5$. Ten are consistent with being classical AM CVn binaries, and two are likely helium cataclysmic variables, of which one may host a high-state disc. The remaining system, ZTF J2116+2446, shows only hydrogen lines, making it the shortest-period UCB with hydrogen but no detected helium; it may have evolved from a white dwarf-brown dwarf binary. The nine new systems increase the number of published eclipsing accreting UCBs from 21 to 30. Because they are eclipsing, they are immediately available for the high-speed photometric modelling that yields model-independent masses and radii, to be presented in future work, including for the three hydrogen-rich systems that are key tests of the evolved cataclysmic-variable channel.

papers.title: Model-Based Retrieval of Four Years of JWST/NIRCam Wavefronts
papers.summary: The fidelity of data recovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) depends on precise monitoring of the mirror segments' surfaces and alignment. To this end, every few days the observatory takes pairs of defocused images of a reference star with its NIRCam instrument; a closed-source phase retrieval package is then employed to infer the wavefront. We here present camino (Computational Aberration Modelling and Inference for NIRCam Observations), an open-source algorithm to model NIRCam built in JAX using the differentiable Fresnel optics code dLUX and regularised maximum likelihood inference that has been conditioned on the entire archive of NIRCam wavefront sensing data. We typically improve the reduced chi-squared in fits to the defocused data from 60-65 to 12-13. We reconstruct the wavefront history of JWST from the beginning of science operations to early 2026. This open source implementation operates in parallel to the current STScI phase retrieval algorithm, allowing access by the broader scientific community to high-accuracy wavefront estimation and enabling its direct integration into science-analysis workflows. This represents a major step towards the ultimate goal of predictive calibration methods based on physics-based forward modelling, obviating the need for time-consuming observation of contemporaneous dedicated reference stars.

papers.title: The Quantum Noise Fraction and the addressable fraction in High-Frequency Gravitational Wave Detection
papers.summary: The quantum noise fraction $\beta$, the share of a detector's noise power that is quantum in origin, sets a ceiling $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{max}} = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta}$ on the sensitivity improvement that removing quantum-origin noise can yield. In the kHz--GHz band the readout degree of freedom is a bosonic mode and $\beta = 1/(2\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}+1)$, with $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}$ the Bose--Einstein occupation. Quantum noise then dominates only on the cold side of the thermal frontier $k_BT\ln 3 = \hbar\omega$ (above 229 MHz at 10 mK), which governs mechanical resonators and electromagnetic cavities alike; a real readout turns it into a joint condition on the occupation and on the excess noise of the readout chain. On a multimode acoustic antenna the frontier can be observed within one device, since the logarithmic slope of $\sqrt{S_hQ}$ along the odd-overtone comb increases by one half across it whatever the dependence of the quality factor on overtone number. On this antenna, crossing the frontier costs more in classical sensitivity than quantum enhancement returns. For a GHz mode of an existing bulk acoustic wave device at 10 mK, $\beta = 0.984$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{max}} = 7.8$. That ceiling cannot be reached with a linear readout, because with intrinsic damping the zero-point term is the force noise of the bath, fixed by the fluctuation--dissipation theorem. The addressable fraction $\beta_a$ excludes it: at the standard quantum limit the same mode has $\beta = 0.992$ but $\beta_a = 0.496$, an available improvement of 1.41 against a ceiling of 11.0. An array of $10^4$ such devices cross-correlated for one year reaches $3.6\times 10^{-24}$ Hz$^{-1/2}$ for an integration bandwidth equal to the linewidth; even granting $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{max}} = 7.8$ in full, a factor $1.0\times 10^{10}$ above the big-bang-nucleosynthesis bound remains, and it is classical.

papers.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
papers.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8\sigma$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5\sigma$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.

papers.title: How timing and mode of selection shape ancestral genetic contributions
papers.summary: We examine a population that evolves according to a biparental Moran model with two distinct types of individuals. Each individual's type is determined by the allele they carry at one biallelic locus, which is transmitted in a Mendelian way. This type influences the individual's mating preferences. We investigate two specific mating patterns: (i) where the type determines the level of attractiveness, and (ii) where the type dictates the level of homogamous choosiness. In both scenarios, one type has an advantage over the other. Assuming an initial proportion b of individuals are of the advantaged type, we give an explicit formula for the asymptotic proportion of the population's genome that originates from these advantaged ancestors under an infinite population size approximation. Our results enable a comparison of the relative strengths of homogamous choosiness, attractiveness, and viability selection in terms of genome transmission, and prove notably that viability selection is always more efficient than both forms of reproductive selection.

papers.title: Sharp transitions between optimal therapy regimes reveal robust dosing strategies against drug-induced persistence
papers.summary: Anti-cancer drug treatment can induce tumor cells to adopt reversible drug-tolerant persister states, facilitating resistance evolution and eventual treatment failure. Although low-dose and intermittent therapies have been proposed as alternatives to maximum tolerated dose (MTD) therapy in this setting, it remains unclear when and why these strategies are optimal. To address this question, we develop a mathematical model of drug-induced persistence where the drug can promote switching to a drug-tolerant state or inhibit reversions to sensitivity in a dose-dependent manner. We uncover sharp transitions between qualitatively distinct therapy regimes, including intermittent high-dose and continuous low-dose therapy, driven by the relative dose sensitivities of cell death and phenotypic switching. In particular, intermittent treatment is optimal when the drug inhibits reversions at doses too low to effectively kill the sensitive cells. We finally exploit the simple regime structure of optimal therapies to show that robust alternatives to MTD therapy can be identified under incomplete knowledge of the underlying dynamics

papers.title: Recurrence in Sequence Space: How Epistasis Mimics Shared Ancestry
papers.summary: Sequences in a protein family do not explore the sequence space freely: folding, packing, and binding couple residues, so the set of viable sequences is irreducibly correlated, a phenomenon referred to as epistasis. We show that such correlations lower the \emph{intrinsic dimension} $d_{\rm IN}$ of sequence space, counteracting the concentration of measure and broadening the distribution of pairwise distances. Consequentially, they make it likely that independently evolving lineages \emph{recur}, approaching one another by chance long after they last shared an ancestor. Using Kac's lemma we show that the logarithmic mean recurrence time grows linearly with the intrinsic dimension, $\log \tau_{\rm rec} \propto {d_{\rm IN}}$ for typical sequences, so strongly constrained (low-dimensional) families recur often and generate sequence similarity that carries no genealogical signal. We establish this first in a solvable Ising-like model with tunable correlation, then in a real protein family using Potts models and Markov chain Monte Carlo, where $d_{\rm IN}$ remains predictive of recurrence even in multi-basins landscapes. Because recurrence is a property of the evolutionary process rather than of any estimator, it bounds the recoverability of deep history for distance-based and likelihood methods alike.

papers.title: Mathematical modeling to study combination strategies for neural stem cell therapy in glioblastoma
papers.summary: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are a promising treatment platform due to their ability to cross the restrictive blood-brain barrier and migrate toward damaged regions of the brain. These properties can be leveraged to target brain tumors, as NSCs can infiltrate tumor lesions and deliver therapeutic agents such as drugs, oncolytic viruses, and genetic materials. Despite the advantages of NSCs, translational challenges remain, including patient-specific chemotactic signaling and immune responses, variability in migration and localization at tumor sites, and optimization of delivery strategies. In this work, we focus on intranasal delivery of NSCs and combination strategies for the treatment of brain cancer. To investigate strategies for improving NSC arrival at the tumor site, we developed a hybrid mathematical model of NSC migration that couples an agent-based model with a partial differential equation, where cell motion is guided by the spatial dynamics of chemoattractants. Using data collected from a murine model and our mathematical model, we {investigate treatment-motivated downstream effects associated with three combination strategies:} (1) IL-10 pretreatment, (2) CXCL12 pretreatment, and (3) radiotherapy. We find that IL-10 pretreatment improves NSC arrival numbers at tumor only under the Gaussian chemoattractant profile, whereas CXCL12 pretreatment moderately improves arrival numbers when the tumor is located in the anterior brain. Radiotherapy significantly enhances the tumor arrival under uniform profiles. These simulation studies suggest that both treatment strategies and chemoattractant distribution influence intranasal NSC delivery, and the proposed model can be used to predict how targeted modulation of chemotactic signaling and tissue-guided migration may improve delivery outcomes.

papers.title: A resident-traveller model for global aspects of vaccination

papers.title: Cell lines that share a well are not independent observations in the Tahoe-100M drug screen
papers.summary: Pooled drug screens treat and sequence dozens of cancer cell lines together in one well. Tahoe-100M, the largest, is used to train and benchmark models that predict how unmeasured cell lines respond to drugs, and its benchmarks, reproducibility ceilings and statistical tests treat the cell lines of a well, and random halves of a well's cells, as independent observations of a drug's effect. Because the drug is applied to the well, this is harmless only if the lines of a well share nothing beyond the drug's reproducible effect. We tested this with pairs of untreated control wells on 13 plates, with replicate wells whose labels we checked, and with two plates that repeat each other well by well. In each test the cell lines of a well share a component of expression that a replicate well does not reproduce, also when the two wells occupy the same inferred position; where drugs are present, it cannot be told apart from an interaction of plate and drug, but in untreated wells it can. In replicate wells at different positions whose labels pass the check, about a third of what two halves of a well have in common (35%, 95% interval 22-58%, 9 compounds) is not reproduced by the replicate well. The well effect inflates results that take something from a well and judge it in the same well: retrained versions of two published models that take a measured response as input lose about a quarter to a third of their score when the input comes from a replicate well instead of the predicted well (22-43% under the control-well reference), halves of a well overstate how well the experiment reproduces, and a test across the lines of a well calls 5 of 13 plates significant when two untreated wells are compared. Many labels of strongly responding replicate wells, those of plate 13 above all, fail the label check. Evaluations, ceilings and tests on such data should treat the well as the experimental unit.

papers.title: A Planar Switching Neuron Shares Logarithmic First-Spike Latency with Its Three-Dimensional Parent But Not Its Onset Mechanism
papers.summary: Can a reduced neuron model reproduce first-spike latency scaling while changing how a stimulus initiates sustained firing? We compare a piecewise-linear planar Neurosimilator with its three-dimensional parent. Both exhibit logarithmic latency dependence over the investigated input intervals, with different fitted coefficients. The mechanisms differ. In the parent, sustained spiking and a stable resting focus coexist in a spiking--rest bistability regime. An abrupt step accesses spiking, while slow stimulation can retain rest at the same final input. Its step-induced firing threshold is therefore an operational basin-access threshold below the saddle-node limit point, not a loss of equilibrium stability. In the planar model, the resting equilibrium instead reaches a switching boundary while its subthreshold eigenvalues remain negative. We derive the planar latency law from this boundary approach. The model generates repetitive excursions without an imposed reset and admits exact trajectories within six switching regions. Similar measured latency scaling thus coexists with different mechanisms of access to firing. Validating a reduced model's mechanism of excitability requires examination of stimulus protocol and attractor access alongside equilibrium structure and spike timing.

papers.title: The Kinetic Basis of the Genetic Code
papers.summary: The origin of the genetic code is an enigma, requiring explanations for the emergence of degeneracy, the organizational structure of the code, and the correspondence between codons and amino acids. Here, we use the asymmetric cooperativity model to show that these features arise from asymmetric cooperativity in codon-anticodon association process. We first provide mechanistic and evolutionary accounts of wobble base pair degeneracy, without providing any preferential treatment to the third position. The model, with four tunable parameters, reproduces the organizational structure of the genetic code, and provides theoretical codon-anticodon association times. Although ribosomal kinetic data are not used in parameter estimation, these theoretical association times correlate with experimentally determined ribosomal residence times (r=0.73). The resulting timescales, extending over four decades, also exhibit correlations with diverse physicochemical properties of amino acids, at multiple timescales, motivating a nonequilibrium picture in which energy released during codon-anticodon association is transferred to its cognate amino acid to be dissipated into water. Finally, without incorporating information about aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases or further parameter adjustment, the model recovers the division of amino acids associated with the two aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase classes, with a combined segregation score of 0.92 ( p~10^{-8}). These results suggest that wobble degeneracy, genetic-code organization, translation kinetics, amino-acid physicochemistry, and the two-class organization of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases may reflect a common underlying kinetic constraint. We propose that non-equilibrium, asymmetrically cooperative kinetics, that possibly underlie DNA/RNA replication process, also provided a physical basis upon which the genetic code and its subsequent translation machinery evolved.

papers.title: Evolutionary characterization of whole-genome doubling across human cancers
papers.summary: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) is common across human cancers and is associated with tumour progression and adverse clinical outcomes. However, how genome-doubled tumours evolve across diverse cancer types remains poorly understood. Here we characterize WGD-associated tumour evolution by integrating genomic analyses of 41,332 tumours from 12 cancer types with evolutionary timing and multi-omic data. Several canonical driver mutations generally preceded WGD when both occurred, as did the onset of homologous recombination deficiency-associated mutagenesis. Notably, post-WGD chromosome-arm losses showed substantially weaker cancer-type dependence than pre-WGD losses, with 61-75% less variance explained by cancer type. Beyond chromosomal evolution, WGD+ tumours showed reduced interferon-response and HLA antigen-presentation programmes linked to epigenetic remodelling, without disproportionate enrichment of genetic immune-escape alterations. Our findings highlight WGD as a recurrent evolutionary transition associated with altered chromosomal evolution and epigenetically linked immune adaptation across cancers.

papers.title: Pin and Replay, or Refuse: Conditional Exactness and Probabilistic Validation Across Reference Releases
papers.summary: Biologists annotate genomes by searching proteins against reference databases such as Pfam, which publish new releases every few weeks to months. Each release forces a full re-search, though most of the database is unchanged: 86.6% of Pfam entries matched between releases 38.1 and 38.2 after excluding build metadata and comments. Reusing old results is hard because search programs are fixed binaries whose printed statistics depend on whole-database size. We present TARE (Tool Annotation Replay with Evidence), a wrapper that reruns an unmodified program only on entries that can matter, pinning the program's database-size setting to the new release so it prints the numbers a full run would print. TARE then tests the replay by adding back omitted entries and refuses with a failure status if any line changes, dumping a full stock body when the tool still runs. Two claims stay separate: conditional exactness under a stated contract (tested each update, not proved), and runtime assurance as probabilistic validation at a stated prevalence---not a guarantee against shipping incorrect output. In the all-record timing, TARE audits 299 records from all queries, so a hidden dependency affecting at least 1% of that population ships with probability at most 5% (valid oracle); rarer faults are outside that bound. On Pfam 38.1->38.2, TARE is 3.47x faster than a full rerun under that audit (median over 8 genomes after excluding 1 flagged genome; 95% CI 3.30-3.81). Historical candidate-population timings on the same nine genomes were 4.24x (Bernoulli; 95% CI 4.17-4.68) and 3.49x (bounded s=299; 95% CI 3.32-4.10). Cost of checking versus unchecked replay is 1.58x (C/B). Across 715,704 HMMER and Infernal output lines, none differed from a full run. TARE refused DIAMOND, whose first filter reads neighboring database bytes, and BLAST+, whose unpinned probe rows fit none of TARE's column rules.

papers.title: Do agents need to sleep?
papers.summary: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

papers.title: Keep on growing or change direction? Dependence of clonal plant survival on the probability of side-branching
papers.summary: In clonal organisms, the genetic individual (genet) may consist of several physiological individuals (ramets). Clonal plants typically grow horizontally by means of stolons or other clonal growth organs. Some species grow linearly for several ramet generations, while others produce side branches frequently. We hypothesize that the probability of side-branching ($b$) affects genet survival ($G$) depending on the ramets' ratio of birth to death rates ($\lambda$). We used a spatially explicit model of ramet population dynamics to compare three growth strategies. In the neutral case, growing forward and side-branching were equally probable, whereas forward-growing and side-branching plants had lower and higher $b$, respectively. We found that the genet's survival threshold (the critical $\lambda_c$) strongly depended on the branching probability. The lowest threshold, and hence the broadest range of survival, occurred in moderately forward-growing plants, in which the average length of linear (non-branching) intervals was $1.89$ units. Above the threshold, the $G(b)$ relationship strongly depended on $\lambda$. Genet survival was promoted by forward growth in sparse ramet populations (low $\lambda$). However, this advantage gradually disappeared as $\lambda$ increased, and branching probability became effectively neutral across a broad parameter range encompassing both forward-growing and side-branching plants. This suggests strong selection for low branching intensity in unfavorable habitats, but weak or negligible selection in favorable habitats.

papers.title: Coupling cellular trajectories and RNA kinetics on continuous expression manifolds with ManifoldVelo
papers.summary: Jointly recovering pseudotime and RNA velocity from static single-cell transcriptomes requires reconciling global trajectory structure with local expression changes, particularly in complex cycles and branching differentiation. Here we introduce ManifoldVelo, a topology-conditioned framework that jointly learns cellular coordinates, continuous RNA trajectories and regulatory kinetics. Derivatives of unspliced and spliced RNA trajectories are matched to transcription-splicing-degradation dynamics, including between observed cells, allowing expression reconstruction, cellular ordering and kinetic estimation to inform one another. ManifoldVelo recovers pseudotime across all evaluated single-cell trajectory types, including cyclic, multibranch and smooth non-branching trajectories. ManifoldVelo achieves the best pseudotime recovery among compared methods in multipeak cyclic simulations and the highest directional agreement for spliced RNA velocity in both multipeak cyclic and branching simulations. Real-data analyses support phase prediction across experimental plates and differentiation trajectories consistent with pancreatic developmental stages and marker expression. Its central advantage is the joint recovery of temporal position and local dynamics across distinct trajectory structures within a reusable dynamic reference. New cells are assigned pseudotime and velocity predictions from spliced RNA alone, without refitting the reference model. ManifoldVelo provides a foundation for dynamic cell atlases that transfer learned temporal and kinetic information to new samples.

papers.title: Intrinsic network dynamics catalyze switching in functional connectivity states of the brain
papers.summary: Dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) reflects ongoing reconfiguration of large-scale brain networks, but the temporal organization and network processes underlying spontaneous state transitions remain poorly understood. We developed functional connectivity state switching (FCSS), a phase-coherence-based framework that tracks multiscale changes in dominant whole-brain connectivity configurations. In Human Connectome Project fMRI, FCSS was strongly evoked by cognitive state and condition switches, and distinct transition dynamics differentially predicted working-memory performance. During rest, spontaneous FCSS was characterized by progressive changes in network segregation, integration, and cross-network communication as connectivity approached a switching event. Critically, event-related analysis time-locked to spontaneous FCSS revealed opposing pre-switch dynamics: salience-network contribution increased while default-mode-network contribution decreased, suggesting coordinated engagement and disengagement of these networks before switching. This reciprocal reweighting may provide a network-level mechanism for spontaneous FC reconfiguration. Together, these findings identify both global reorganization and network-specific processes underlying spontaneous and task-evoked brain-state transitions in the human brain.

papers.title: Automatic Generation of Novel Highly-Functional Molecular Sequences
papers.summary: While multiple methods now exist to generate functional sequence variants from existing annotated examples, it is unclear how well such methods can be used to generate sequences that exceed the functionality of those contained in the example set. Using two complete fitness landscapes, we quantify how effectively generative tools can search sequence space and find rare, novel, highly functional sequences, focusing on variational auto-encoders and information-theoretic methods. We find that an information-theoretic method that does not require training and runs significantly faster than standard Machine-Learning/Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) methods also is significantly more effective in finding rare highly-functional sequences. We discuss the application of this novel method to discover rare polypeptides with anti-bacterial properties that are specific to bacterial, but not eukaryotic, cell membranes.

papers.title: CogBattery: Human-Referenced Evaluation of Cognitive Task Behavior and Structure in Language Models
papers.summary: Human cognitive tasks let us compare language models with humans under controlled conditions. Yet a model can reproduce the direction of a human effect while making different errors. CogBattery evaluates 54 open-weight language models on text adaptations of 13 cognitive paradigms, comparing each with human data from its source study. Like humans, models respond more to n-back lures than to controls, yet they make far more false alarms on ordinary non-targets. Most models' reported confidence separates correct from incorrect answers less well than humans' does, and most always choose the same wager, including models that classify accurately. These patterns span many model families. Across tasks, model scores share two dimensions. The first is closely tied to scale, yet larger models are not consistently closer to humans. Predefined cognitive groupings show no reliable predictive advantage over random groupings of the same size. These results show that matching human effect directions does not establish human-like behavior. CogBattery provides condition-level human references for testing errors and confidence reports in new models.

papers.title: Identifying unknown time delay and spatially varying coefficients in a reaction-diffusion equation from boundary measurements
papers.summary: This work investigates an inverse problem for a general class of linear reaction-diffusion systems incorporating multiple delayed contributions, namely retarded diffusion, retarded time derivatives, and retarded source terms. The objective is to simultaneously recover the unknown time lag $\tau>0$ and spatially heterogeneous coefficients from boundary flux measurements alone. The recovery strategy exploits the singular temporal behavior generated by an incompatibility between the prescribed initial history and the boundary data. In contrast to prior inverse problems for delay equations, which assume $\tau$ known and are confined to ODE or abstract settings, our approach operates in a parabolic PDE framework with spatially varying coefficients. Once $\tau$ is identified, we establish a Lipschitz stability estimate via a Carleman inequality, in the case of time-independent coefficients $p=p(x)$, $q=q(x)$. This is the first result to simultaneously recover an unknown delay and spatially dependent coefficients in a delayed parabolic PDE from boundary data.

papers.title: Substrate hypergraph cycles: unique steady states and persistence for every enzyme assignment; oscillations enabled by enzyme sharing
papers.summary: We associate a directed substrate hypergraph with an enzymatic reaction system. The hypergraph records which substrates each composite reaction consumes and produces, and each composite reaction is realized by a Henri--Michaelis--Menten (HMM) module whose enzyme may be distinct, shared with other reactions, or absent. We call the hypergraph a cycle when it is strongly connected and every substrate is produced by exactly one reaction and consumed by exactly one reaction, each time with coefficient one; equivalently, its dual is a strongly connected ordinary directed graph. For a cycle, every HMM realization, under every enzyme assignment and for all positive rate constants, has exactly one positive steady state in each stoichiometric compatibility class that contains a strictly positive point, and no steady state on the boundary of such a class, and every trajectory in such a class is persistent. The interior dynamics, in contrast, depend on how enzymes are shared. When each enzyme catalyzes at most one reaction, every trajectory in such a class converges to its unique steady state. With enzyme sharing, convergence can fail even for the three-substrate transformation cycle $X_1\to X_2\to X_3\to X_1$: if two transformations share an enzyme and the third has its own enzyme or none, the steady state can undergo a supercritical Hopf bifurcation that produces a stable limit cycle. Thus the substrate structure controls existence, uniqueness, and persistence, while the pattern of enzyme sharing controls the interior dynamics. The results extend to weighted cycles, which allow higher stoichiometric coefficients, and to longer chains of intermediates.

papers.title: In-depth data movement characterization of DNA read mapping algorithms
papers.summary: Read mapping algorithms represent a critical bottleneck in genomic analysis pipelines due to the resources required; a problem that is becoming more pronounced as sequencing technologies advance and datasets expand. We present an extensive workload characterization of leading read mapping algorithms across diverse sequencing technologies to identify hardware acceleration and optimization opportunities. We analyzed the following implementations: MashMap, wfmash, and Minimap2 for whole-genome alignment (WGA); NGMLR, Minimap2, and LRA for long reads; and Bowtie2, BWA-MEM, StrobeAlign, and minibwa for short reads. We used the Intel VTune Profiler for detailed memory analysis to identify memory- bound functions, cache usage patterns, and data transfer bottlenecks. We further analyzed a selected subset of alignment tools using the DAMOV-SIM simulator to obtain a more granular view of data movement characteristics for two different cache structures. Based on our results, Minimap2 emerges as the fastest alignment tool for long read scenarios, but falls behind in whole-genome alignment due to poor multithreading. Across all three categories, some programs (e.g., LRA, BWA-MEM) are highly memory-bound. More in-depth analysis via DAMOV-SIM revealed that some memory-bound tools, in particular, do not fully utilize the multi-level cache hierarchy in modern multi-core CPU architectures. Our results show that while some tools require algorithmic redesign for performance gains, some others can benefit from running on PIM architectures.

papers.title: Static and Dynamic Functional Brain Networks Reveal Distinct Connectivity Alterations Across the Alzheimer's Disease Spectrum
papers.summary: Brain network analysis using functional MRI has advanced our understanding of cortical activity and its disruption in neurodegenerative disorders underlying dementia. Dynamic (time-varying) brain networks, which capture spatial and temporal patterns of regional cortical co-activity, remain relatively unexplored across the Alzheimer's disease (AD) spectrum. We analysed age- and sex-matched static and dynamic functional brain networks from resting-state fMRI in 315 individuals with AD, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and cognitively normal healthy controls (HC) from ADNI-3. Networks were constructed using the Juelich brain atlas, with static connectivity estimated from full time series and dynamic connectivity via a sliding-window approach. Group differences were assessed at link and node levels using non-parametric statistics and bootstrap resampling. Time series from regions identified in these analyses were then used in Random Forest classification to test whether the alterations carried discriminative information at the individual level. HC and MCI showed largely similar node-level static and dynamic connectivity, whereas AD exhibited pronounced alterations in network organisation and temporal variability. Stable (stationary) differences emerged in connectivity between white matter regions and parietal and somatosensory cortices, whereas temporally varying differences consistently involved the amygdala and hippocampal formation. Node centrality analysis suggested that white matter connectivity differences are predominantly local. Our results highlight shared and unique connectivity patterns in static and dynamic networks, emphasising the importance of incorporating dynamic information into brain network analyses of the Alzheimer's spectrum.

papers.title: AMRScan 2: provenance-recorded detection of antimicrobial resistance determinants in bacterial assemblies, with archived susceptibility data from NCBI Pathogen Detection
papers.summary: Studies that relate bacterial genomes to antimicrobial susceptibility test (AST) results need determinant calls and phenotypes that can be traced to the exact genome, software, database and source export they came from. AMRScan 2 is a rewrite of the AMRScan toolkit for this purpose. Its Nextflow workflow runs NCBI AMRFinderPlus on genome assemblies in a pinned container, writes a provenance record for every sample with the command, the software version and the SHA-256 hashes of the input, of every database file and of the report, and converts each report into a table with a fixed schema that keeps every original column. The conversion step stops if a report no longer matches its provenance record. A second tool archives AST and isolate tables exported from NCBI Pathogen Detection, checks each export against an independent count, and builds isolate and endpoint tables offline that can be rebuilt and compared byte for byte. AMRScan does not infer phenotype from determinants; calls and phenotypes are kept as separate layers and joined by assembly accession. The caller wrapper was used to call 10,521 public Escherichia coli assemblies on a workstation without a failed call, and a run of 1,000 of these assemblies through the workflow on an HPC system gave byte-identical reports. The workflow follows nf-core conventions and is tested with unit tests, nf-test and continuous integration. This version replaces the 2025 description of AMRScan 1, a BLAST search against CARD, which is kept unchanged in the repository.

papers.title: Analyzing Memory Effects in Large Language Models through the lens of Cognitive Psychology
papers.summary: Memory, a fundamental component of human cognition, exhibits adaptive yet fallible characteristics as illustrated by Schacter's memory "sins".These cognitive phenomena have been studied extensively in psychology and neuroscience, but the extent to which artificial systems, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), emulate these cognitive phenomena remains underexplored. This study uses human memory research as a lens for understanding LLMs and systematically investigates human memory effects in state-of-the-art LLMs using paradigms drawn from psychological research. We evaluate seven key memory phenomena, comparing human behavior to LLM performance. Both people and models remember less when overloaded with information (list length effect) and remember better with repeated exposure (list strength effect). They also show similar difficulties when retrieving overlapping information, where storing too many similar facts leads to confusion (fan effect). Like humans, LLMs are susceptible to falsely "remembering" words that were never shown but are related to others (false memories), and they can apply prior learning to new, related situations (cross-domain generalization). However, LLMs differ in two key ways: they are less influenced by the order in which information is presented (positional bias) and more robust when processing random or meaningless material (nonsense effect). These results reveal both alignments and divergences in how LLMs and humans reconstruct memory. The findings help clarify how memory-like behavior in LLMs echoes core features of human cognition, while also highlighting the architectural differences that lead to distinct patterns of error and success.

papers.title: A phenotype-structured reaction-diffusion model of avascular glioma growth
papers.summary: We consider a phenotype-structured reaction-diffusion model of avascular glioma growth. The model describes the interaction dynamics between tumour cells and oxygen, and takes into account anisotropic cell movement and oxygen diffusion related to structural anisotropy of the brain's extracellular environment. In this model, phenotypic heterogeneity of tumour cells is captured by a continuous phenotype-structuring variable, the value of which evolves due to phenotypic changes. We first analyse a one-dimensional version of the model and formally show, through a Hopf-Cole transformation, that it admits, in appropriate asymptotic regimes, phenotypically heterogeneous travelling wave solutions, wherein the locally prevailing cell phenotype varies across the wave due to the presence of oxygen gradients. This provides a mathematical formalisation for the emergence of intratumour phenotypic heterogeneity driven by differences in oxygen availability across the tumour. We then report on the results of both 1D simulations, which corroborate the results of formal asymptotic analyses, and 2D simulations, which also demonstrate the impact of anisotropy in cell movement and oxygen diffusion on tumour growth and on the phenotypic composition of the tumour edge. These results are complemented with additional results of 3D simulations, which are carried out on the geometry of the brain by using a hybrid finite difference-finite element method and integrating patient-specific magnetic resonance imaging data with diffusion tensor imaging data.

papers.title: Neuromodulation-inspired gated associative memory networks: extended memory retrieval and emergent multistability
papers.summary: Classical autoassociative memory models have been central to understanding emergent computations in recurrent neural circuits across diverse biological contexts. However, they typically neglect neuromodulatory agents that are known to strongly shape memory capacity and stability. Here we introduce a minimal, biophysically motivated associative memory network in which neuromodulator-like signals are modeled by a self-adaptive, activity-dependent gating mechanism. Using many-body simulations and dynamical mean-field theory, we show that such gating fundamentally reorganizes the attractor structure: the network bypasses the classical spin-glass transition, maintaining robust, high-overlap retrieval far beyond the standard critical capacity. Mechanistically, when the gates act as fully open or fully closed switches, the gate stabilizes transient "ghost" remnants of stored patterns even far above the Hopfield limit, converting a single memory fixed point attractor into a cluster of fixed points. The retrieved state is set by the initial overlap rather than quantized to the stored pattern. This graded dependence may be exploited for input-driven computation with persistent activity. These results establish that neuromodulation-like gating alone, without modifying synaptic weights or introducing explicit higher-order couplings, can dramatically expand memory capacity, eliminate catastrophic breakdown, and reshape a discrete attractor landscape into a rich continuum, suggesting a general and biologically accessible route to enhanced computational capabilities in neural circuits and neuromorphic architectures.

papers.title: Behavioral patterns and mean-field games in epidemiological models
papers.summary: We introduce a new type of Mean Field Game epidemiological models, in which subpopulations have different behavioral patterns: some people exhibit a type of ``rational'' self interested behavior by choosing Nash-equilibrium long-term strategies while others follow pre-specified ``non-rational'' patterns (e.g., either sticking to their usual habits or trying to mimic those around them). Our new B-MFG models allow for occasional behavioral switches, which rational individuals also take into account when formulating their Nash-equilibrium strategies. Although this modeling approach is general, here we develop it for individuals choosing their ``contact rates'' within a particular Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible-Dead (SIRSD) epidemic model. The latter is based on a frequency-based force of infection with proportionate mixing and the mortality rate that rapidly increases once the proportion of infected individuals exceeds some prescribed threshold, resulting in a strain on medical resources. Numerical tests illustrate the properties of our model and highlight the ways in which additional/non-rational behavioral patterns and behavioral switching increase the impact of infectious diseases. The paper aims to build a bridge between two distinct communities of epidemiological modelers and to promote the consideration of behavioral patterns in broader Mean Field Games literature.

papers.title: Differential Dynamic Causal Nets: Model Construction, Identification and Group Comparisons
papers.summary: Pathophysiological modelling of brain systems from microscale to macroscale remains difficult in group comparisons partly because of the infeasibility of modelling the interactions of thousands of neurons at the scales involved. Here, to address the challenge, we present a novel approach to construct differential causal networks directly from grouped electroencephalogram (EEG) data. In the proposed modular network, each node represents a locally averaged regional neural system via a canonical Jansen-Rit model while directed edges stand for node-wise input-output connections. The network is hierarchically structured in the sense that node and edge parameters are random, varying in subjects, but follow a mixed-effects model. We show that unlike the classical Jansen-Rit models, the proposed node models are locally structurally identifiable. An evolutionary optimisation algorithm for parameter inference in the proposed method is developed using a loss function derived from Chen-Fliess expansions of stochastic differential equations. The method is demonstrated by fitting the proposed modular network to grouped epileptic EEG data in both sensor- and source- levels. We identify significant changes in the parameters that characterise dynamic networks within and between brain regions. We reveal network disruptions, due to imbalance of excitatory-inhibitory interneurons and other altered epileptic brain connectivities, before and during seizure periods, and contrast them between case and control groups. The performance of the proposed method is also evaluated on synthetic data.

papers.title: Oxygenation and spatial heterogeneity shape radiotherapy protocol ranking through phenotypic adaptation
papers.summary: Tumor response to radiotherapy is strongly influenced by oxygen availability and phenotypic heterogeneity, yet their combined impact on the relative performance of fractionation schedules remains unclear. Here, we develop a mathematical model that integrates spatial oxygen dynamics with continuous phenotypic adaptation to hypoxia and radiation, and use it to systematically compare radiotherapy protocols under a common normal-tissue toxicity constraint. Under spatially uniform oxygenation, we find that alternative fractionation schedules provide little improvement over standard-of-care protocols in normoxic conditions. Under moderate hypoxia, however, a distinct class of protracted schedules with longer inter-fraction intervals substantially increases time-to-progression, in some cases by up to twofold. This regime-dependent benefit is consistent with a shift in the balance between reoxygenation and selection for resistant phenotypes. When oxygen delivery is spatially heterogeneous, treatment outcomes depend strongly on the geometric organization of oxygen sources. Even with identical total oxygen supply, different spatial configurations lead to large variability in time-to-progression and can alter the relative ranking of radiotherapy protocols. These results show that radiotherapy effectiveness is not an intrinsic property of a treatment schedule alone, but emerges from its interaction with tumor microenvironmental structure and evolutionary dynamics. Incorporating both spatial heterogeneity and phenotypic adaptation may therefore be important for the consistent evaluation and design of fractionation strategies in heterogeneous tumors.

papers.title: Synergy and Complementarity: The Generative Basis of Chemical Organizations
papers.summary: Identifying structural features ensuring the persistence of a reaction network is fundamental for understanding the evolution and complexification of biological entities. By defining organizations as subsets of species that are closed and self-maintaining, Chemical Organization Theory (COT) shows that organizations enable filtering out the regions of the phase space where attractors can exist. Despite various theoretical explorations current methods to compute the organizations face unclear combinatorial challenges. In this article, we first perform a systematic study of such combinatorial challenges and identify a criteria of productive novelty and irreducibility that separate relevant from redundant combinations. Second, we identify the minimal building blocks that shall be combined to build organizations, called elementary reaction closures (ERC), and characterize them as a hierarchy. Third, we show that all persistent modules can be generated as combination of ERCs only, and operationalize two properties among ERCs, synergy and complementarity, that define a sufficient criteria to build such generators in a minimal way. Fourth we show that every relevant persistent module can be built from such minimal sequences of ERCs. We next show that the synergies and complementarities we use to generate persistent modules not only scale radically slower than usual combinatorial methods. We quantify these structures across $438$ biological reaction networks from the BioModels and BiGG databases. The proportion of fundamental synergies and complementarities among all ERC pairs shrinks as networks grow even as raw counts increase, confirming that larger biological networks achieve persistence through a progressively smaller and more selective sets. We do not prescribe algorithms to compute organizations, discuss how algorithms based on our results could permit applying COT.

papers.title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
papers.summary: Comprehensively characterizing cellular landscapes to elucidate cell diversity is a central goal in biology. Recent advances in single-cell profiling have created unprecedented opportunities for this endeavor by capturing diverse transcriptomes with remarkable breadth. However, current foundation models generally struggle to leverage such holistic and valuable information to represent a cell. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression into a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million image-based cell profiles across 40 species and covering over one million genes, CellNet improves the recognition of rare and condition-associated cellular states, enables the study of genes beyond experimentally measured panels, and uncovers associations between poorly characterized non-coding RNAs and known biological programmes. CellNet paves the way for AI-enabled cell-biology discovery at the whole-transcriptome scale. The CellNet website is available at https://www.cellnet.top.

papers.title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
papers.summary: Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

papers.title: A stochastic epidemic model with memory of the last infection and waning immunity
papers.summary: We adapt the article of Forien, Pang, Pardoux and Zotsa, on epidemic models with varying infectivity and waning immunity, to incorporate the memory of the last infection. To this end, we introduce a parametric approach and consider a piecewise deterministic Markov process modeling both the evolution of the parameter, also called the trait, and the age of infection of individuals over time. At each new infection, a new trait is randomly chosen for the infected individual according to a Markov kernel, and their age is reset to zero. In the large population limit, we derive a partial differential equation (PDE) that describes the density of traits and ages. The main goal is to study the conditions under which endemic equilibria exist for the deterministic PDE model and to establish an endemicity threshold that depends on the model parameters. The local stability of these equilibria is also analyzed. The endemicity threshold is computed for several examples, including models that incorporate a vaccination policy, and a local stability result is obtained for a memory-free SIS-type model.

papers.title: Quantifying structural uncertainty in chemical reaction network inference
papers.summary: Dynamical systems in biology are complex, and one often does not have comprehensive knowledge about the interactions involved. Chemical reaction network (CRN) inference aims to identify, from observing species concentrations over time, the unknown reactions between the species. Existing approaches such as sparse regularisation largely focus on identifying a single, most likely CRN, without addressing uncertainty about the network structure. However, it is important to quantify structural uncertainty to have confidence in our inference and predictions. In this work, we explore how effective sparse regularisation methods are for quantifying structural uncertainty. Locally optimal solutions to sparse regularisation are mapped to CRN structures; however, it is unclear whether this approach encompasses all plausible CRNs. We find that inducing sparsity with nonconvex penalty functions results in better coverage of the plausible CRNs compared to the popular lasso regularisation. To validate our approach, we apply our methods to real-world data examples, and are able to simultaneously recover reactions proposed across multiple literature sources for a reaction system. Our emphasis on network-level probabilities enables a novel, hierarchical representation of structural ambiguities in the space of CRNs. This representation translates into alternative reaction pathways suggested by the available data, thus guiding the efforts of future experimental design.

papers.title: Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves: from tents to houses
papers.summary: One of the classical results of mathematical population genetics states that the frequency of a beneficial mutant's offspring, on its way to fixation in a large population, looks like a logistic curve. A logarithmic scaling (both in height and time) of these selective sweep curves leads (in the case of strong selection) to a tent-like shape in the large population limit: First the logarithmic frequency of the mutant increases linearly from 0 to 1, then that of the former resident decreases from 1 to 0. For moderate selection the logarithmic frequencies develop (in the large population limit) a jump at the beginning/the end of the sweep, which takes the shape of the tent into that of a house. Our main result (proved for the Moran model) assesses the regularity of this convergence in the large population limit: It is uniform in the house's roof (phases of linear growth and decline) and "Skorokhod $M_1$" in the house's walls (closely around the jumps). Apart from interest in its own right, we anticipate that this result and the proof techniques will be instrumental for extending the description of clonal interference by Poissonian interacting trajectories (as it was done in Hermann et al. (2024) for strong selection) also to moderate selection.
