papers.title: A Cross-Entropy Audit (CEA) for Consciousness Tests Moved from Brain to Large Language Model
papers.summary: Brain tests of consciousness are often applied to large language models (LLMs). Here consciousness means access: whether information, such as a heard sound, becomes available for report and use. A brain recording is in microvolts and an LLM's internal activations are arbitrary numbers, so the two share no common measurement unit. A brain test of this kind compares competing statistical models of how responses vary over repeated trials. The test's decision names the best-fitting model. The decision is wrong when the test names two states for responses that vary smoothly, or the reverse. No method we reviewed measures how often a transferred test is wrong. We call such a method a transfer audit and propose one, the cross-entropy audit (CEA). First, our audit holds back part of the trials and fits each model to the remaining trials. It then scores how well each fitted model predicts the held-back responses. Comparing two models gives a score difference in nats per trial. That difference does not depend on whether the recording is in microvolts or in activations, so brain and machine are scored on one scale. Second, the audit writes down five choices that such tests make for brain data: the competing models, their fitting, what counts as one independent sample, what the uncertainty interval describes, and the decision rule. Each may need to change on a machine. Third, the audit runs the test on simulated data built to follow one model, so the right decision is known, and counts wrong decisions. In our example, the two models of a two-state test, carried over unchanged to an LLM, found two states in 989 of 12,000 smoothly varying simulated datasets. The audited version of the test found two states in none of them. It detected 599 of 600 two-state datasets. The audited version's uncertainty interval, however, was too narrow at six of the twelve smoothly varying settings and is being repaired.

papers.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
papers.summary: Taxonomic classifiers based on exact matches differ in which matches they use and in how each match splits its credit among the taxa containing it: Kraken~2 gives a $k$-mer's credit to the lowest common ancestor of those taxa, SPUMONI~2 labels each position of the read, Tagger gives each maximal exact match (MEM) one label, and Cliffy splits a match's credit evenly over a roughly logarithmic sample of the taxa. We compare these schemes on the same long MEMs, mainly on short 16S rRNA reads classified to genera with SILVA, where credit proportional to the number of occurrences of the MEM in each taxon is the most accurate, by 1.0 to 6.8 percentage points. We compute long MEMs with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, and count their occurrences in each taxon with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, in time proportional to the number of tag runs in the MEM's BWT interval, without locating any occurrence. We bound the number of tag runs in terms of the BWT runs and of how often suffixes with long common prefixes have different tags, and show that tags constant on $d$ blocks of the text have a macro scheme with at most $r + 2d$ phrases. On SILVA our index takes 1.44\,GB and classifies a read in 66\,$\mu$s with one thread at 93.8\% accuracy; on the same reads and server, it is 14 times smaller than Cliffy's undigested index, and 4.4 times faster and 8 percentage points more accurate than Cliffy's LCA query on it. Over minimizer digests it takes 0.49\,GB and reaches 92.5\%; on the server, 92.1\% against 84.2\% for Cliffy's LCA query on its digested index. On nanopore reads from whole genomes, where almost every long MEM occurs in one species, we instead use each read's longest MEMs, found in one pass of a variant of Boyer--Moore--Li with a $k$-mer filter, which assigns 99.6\% of the reads to their species with no length threshold.

papers.title: A five-species counterexample to the Hofbauer--Kon--Saito conjecture on qualitative permanence
papers.summary: Hofbauer, Kon and Saito showed that a Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix $A$ with negative diagonal can be qualitatively permanent only if (C1) every cycle of length $\ge 2$ of $A$ is nonpositive and (C2) every negative cycle contains exactly one negative entry. They conjectured that these conditions are also sufficient, and proved this for $n\le 3$. We give a $5\times 5$ integer matrix with seven nonzero off-diagonal entries that satisfies (C1) and (C2) but is not qualitatively permanent. For an explicit integer growth vector, in which one species is an obligate consumer as the definition allows, the system has an interior equilibrium, and an asymptotically stable heteroclinic cycle on the boundary of the orthant attracts an open set of interior orbits. Adding non-interacting species gives counterexamples for every $n\ge 5$. The interactions form a one-way feedback loop together with a predator of two prey. The verification is elementary except for one heteroclinic connection, which lies in a face that is not Volterra-Lyapunov stable. For it we prove a connection lemma based on invasion graphs, which reduces the question to a smaller, stable face. The failure is robust. It persists under small perturbations, including weak additional interactions, so every sign pattern that satisfies (C1) and (C2) and contains ours is a counterexample, and it occurs for an open cone of growth vectors. For $n\ge 6$ there are also counterexamples in which every species grows when alone. Finally, we announce that the conjecture holds for $n=4$ and that, for $n=5$, four minimal sign patterns characterise its failure.

papers.title: R\'enyi-2 entanglement of purification of the symmetric Werner state
papers.summary: This paper determines exactly the R\'enyi-2 entanglement of purification of the normalized symmetric Werner state in every local dimension $d\ge2$ \begin{equation*} \mathrm{EoP}_2(W_{+,d})=\log_2\frac{4d(d+1)}{d^2+3d+4}. \end{equation*} We establish additivity for tensor power and, more generally, additivity for finite products of symmetric Werner states with different local dimensions. A canonical purification and its products achieve these values globally, even when arbitrary joint purifications with unrestricted finite dimensional auxiliary systems are allowed. We further examine perturbations away from the symmetric endpoint, and prove the continuity of the optimal value at this endpoint; moreover, we show a sharp square root order of variation in the optimal purity, while the canonical purification remains asymptotically optimal in the achieved entropy as this weight goes to zero.

papers.title: Exhaustive Construction of Generalized Parent Hamiltonians for Matrix Product States
papers.summary: Characterizing local Hamiltonians that host interesting many-body states as eigenstates has been an important problem in quantum many-body physics. For matrix product states (MPS), there is a well-known construction of parent Hamiltonians that have the MPS as the frustration-free ground state. However, recent results on quantum many-body scars have shown that such a construction does not exhaust all possible Hamiltonians that have the MPS as an eigenstate. In this work, we develop an exhaustive construction of generalized parent Hamiltonians that have a given translation-invariant MPS as an eigenstate. These go beyond the conventional projector-based construction of frustration-free parent Hamiltonians, where each local Hermitian term has the MPS as an eigenstate, by allowing non-Hermitian telescoping terms that cancel out with periodic boundary conditions (PBC). We derive a local tensor equation that establishes a correspondence between inequivalent classes of generalized parent Hamiltonians, i.e., those that cannot be related using linear combinations with frustration-free Hamiltonians, and the MPS transfer matrix spectrum. We illustrate the connection to intrinsic physical properties, including non-Abelian symmetries and zero correlation length, and further extend this construction to block-injective MPS. Our framework hence provides a systematic bridge between generalized parent Hamiltonians and the local structure of quantum states.

papers.title: Benchmarking Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks and their classical surrogates on long-range strongly correlated models
papers.summary: We benchmark quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) and their classical surrogates for phase differentiation in one-dimensional strongly correlated systems with beyond-nearest-neighbour terms. Using an anisotropic Heisenberg spin chain and an extended $t$-$t'$ Fermi-Hubbard model as representative spin and fermionic testbeds, we train QCNN classifiers on labelled ground-state datasets and map out finite-size phase diagrams. In hybrid setups, we employ Pauli backpropagation to express the QCNN measurement as a weighted sum of Pauli-string expectation values to be evaluated directly on input states, and study how truncation parameters control the trade-off between approximation accuracy and the size of the resulting Pauli expansion. Robust convergence is achieved for the Heisenberg model under aggressive truncation, whereas the Fermi-Hubbard model requires substantially looser thresholds, resulting in a sharp growth in retained Pauli strings and evaluation cost. Our results contribute to charting where hybrid quantum-classical training is viable for learning strongly correlated quantum states, and provide practical guidance for choosing truncation regimes in Pauli backpropagation-based surrogates.

papers.title: Triple descent in quantum linear regression
papers.summary: Quantum linear regression models, such as quantum extreme learning machines and quantum fidelity kernels, are trained on features that can only be estimated from finitely many measurement shots. Sampling noise is usually treated as a nuisance that more shots suppress; we show instead that it can fundamentally reshape the instabilities of the learning problem. As the number of measurement outcomes grows, the prediction error displays a triple-descent profile, with two peaks of fundamentally different origins. The first, classical, peak occurs when the measurement first becomes informationally complete, is a direct analogue of double descent in classical linear regression, and is caused by ill-conditioning of the measurement itself. This peak affects predictions only through their variance, and is thus suppressed by increasing the number of shots at inference. The second, quantum, peak occurs beyond informational completeness when the number of outcomes matches the number of training states: shot noise populates unphysical outcome combinations and the regression fits these pure-noise features with large weights, corrupting the learned model itself. More training or test shots cannot remove this quantum peak, which disappears only in the ideal limit of exact training features. Using random-matrix theory, we derive the shape of both peaks analytically, accounting also for ridge regularization. Our results show that treating quantum features as exactly known overestimates classical instabilities while missing genuinely quantum ones.

papers.title: Application a quantum machine learning algorithm to the applied problem of modeling the thermal regime of a servers

We trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters. We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning. Furthermore, using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.

papers.title: Early Fault-Tolerant Magic State Synthesis and Spacetime Efficient Analog Rotations with Color Code on a Superconducting Quantum Processor
papers.summary: With recent improvements to syndrome extraction scheduling and decoding, and the availability of complete transversal Clifford operations and lattice surgery, color code is an especially promising platform for quantum processors with local connectivity. The key ingredient for universal computation is thus generating useful magic states with limited resources. Space-Time Efficient Analog Rotations (STAR) and Fault-tolerant magic state synthesis (MSS) are two such methods for magic state generation, targeted for near-term and long-term quantum computing, respectively. In this work, we perform the first implementations of both magic state paradigms on a superconducting quantum processor. We present a STAR-type injection protocol on the color code, with favorable error rate and spacetime costs versus prior protocols on both the color and surface codes. We then implement a MSS factory by performing multi-patch magic state cultivations, interleaved with transversal Clifford operations, and lattice-surgery magic state teleportation. Under post-selection, we achieve a kickback tomography correct sign probability of $99.9859\%$ on cultivated $T_L$ states, $96\%$ tomographic fidelity on logical analog rotation states, and $91\%$ fidelity on synthesized logical magic states consuming 3 cultivated $T_L$ states, 3 transversal Hadamard operations, and real-time feed-forward $S_L$ corrections during magic state teleportation. We compare the efficacy of post-selection, Most-Likely-Error (MLE) decoding, and concatenated-matching decoding throughout, highlighting the potential of end-to-end color code computation.

papers.title: Measurement-angle control of a continuously monitored quantum oscillator: purification limits and optimal protocols
papers.summary: We study the dynamic purification of a continuously monitored quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a thermal bath, where the control is the quadrature measurement angle of up to two detectors with prescribed strengths and efficiencies. Within the Gaussian regime, the conditional state covariance obeys a deterministic Riccati equation, and we ask what purity can be reached and sustained by manipulating the angle in time, in analogy with rapid-purification protocols for qubits. We propose, analyze, and compare constant-rate, greedy, vibrational, and variational monitoring strategies on the basis of sustained purity starting from the thermal bath state, and quantify to what extent they are able to maintain higher purity levels compared to lab-fixed or phase-locked detectors. We highlight structural features, operational limits, and optimal protocols from each strategy and study how model parameters shape control performance. We observe that in the absence of measurement-frame anisotropy, the time-dependent strategies achieve higher but similar performance. Once this symmetry is broken, their performances diverge, either improving or worsening depending on the relative timescales of oscillator dynamics, thermalization, and measurement.

papers.title: Detector Placement Relaxes Efficiency Requirements for Detecting a Weak Coherent Link
papers.summary: A weak coherent link can produce unusually early arrivals without changing stationary count rates. Missed jumps along routes available without the link can produce similar records, obscuring its presence. On an eight-site ring, relocating the same detector losses exposes one more crossing on the easiest background route to hide, without changing the dynamics or leading link signal. At fixed error and a common observation-time scaling, the tolerated missed fraction and time-bin width follow fourth-root rather than square-root scaling with link strength. These requirements hold for every decision using the counting record and are met using three event counts per bin, with all elapsed time included. At the same stationary collected flux, where jumps are monitored can therefore determine the time resolution needed for weak-link sensing.

papers.title: Optimal Estimation in Weak Value Amplification with a Position Pointer
papers.summary: We experimentally evaluate five estimators for weak-value amplification (WVA) using a position pointer to measure birefringence time delays. Two general approaches are considered: measuring the position shift $\Delta x$ and measuring the probability change $\Delta P_w$ of successful postselection. Specifically, five estimators are investigated: CCD-detected fringe shift $\Delta x$, quadrant photodiode (PDQ) transversal voltage difference (XDIFF), and lock-in amplifier output phase $\eta$ (for $\Delta x$ measurement), as well as PDQ total output voltage (SUM) and CCD-detected average photon number $N_r$ (for $\Delta P_w$ measurement). The measurement precision is characterized by the Allan deviation over a range of input laser powers $P_0$. Generally, measuring the position shift $\Delta x$ yields higher precision than measuring the probability change $\Delta P_w$. At $P_0=0.5$~mW, corresponding to a laser-power-limited regime, direct measurement of the fringe displacement with the CCD achieves a minimum Allan deviation of $(5.30\pm0.10)\times10^{-3}$~as, approaching the corresponding photon-statistical Cram\'er--Rao bound (CRB). At $P_0=50$~mW, corresponding to a detector-limited regime, PDQ detection combined with lock-in demodulation provides the best precision, reaching $(1.80\pm0.06)\times10^{-3}$~as and remaining close to the corresponding CRB. These results demonstrate that the optimal readout depends on the available optical power, detector dynamic range, and technical noise, providing practical guidance for selecting readout strategies in high-precision WVA-based metrology.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Parameter Setting in Digitized Counterdiabatic QAOA
papers.summary: Optimizing parameters separately for each problem instance limits the reuse of variational quantum algorithms. We develop empirical scaling laws for parameter setting in the digitized counterdiabatic quantum approximate optimization algorithm (DC-QAOA) for weighted MaxCut. The prescription combines exact covariance under uniform edge-weight rescaling with power laws in mean degree fitted separately to offline-optimized cost and counterdiabatic angles. After the weight and degree scales are removed, the optimized angles of different training graphs cluster around common amplitudes, so a small coefficient table suffices. Frozen coefficients assign angles from a target graph's mean degree and root-mean-square edge weight without target-instance variational optimization. In ideal-circuit simulations across 1050 test graphs spanning ten graph families and five positive edge-weight distributions, mean optimal-solution probability is higher than that of the fixed-angle quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) at each depth from one to four layers, reaching 19.36% versus 13.11% at four layers. A six-layer extension on 600 graphs also shows a mean probability advantage. Hardware execution on the IBM Quantum processor ibm_fez for 21 unit-weight 3-regular graphs shows a mean probability advantage at one layer, while the ordering reverses at two layers. In separate energy-based experiments, direct assignment gives a higher mean approximation ratio than random-start optimization reaches within 500 evaluations, and refinement started from the formula angles improves it further. These results show how a scaling-based representation of optimized angles can guide parameter reuse across graph instances, enabling direct parameter assignment without target-instance variational optimization and providing initial angles for local refinement.

papers.title: The exact information cost of randomized measurements in quantum metrology
papers.summary: Randomized measurements provide state-independent readout for multiparameter quantum sensing. Although 3-designs retain a constant fraction of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for every pure state, we show that 2-designs need not. In dimension \(d\), complete mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) retain exactly \(1/(d+1)\) of the QFI in the worst state and direction, attaining the universal lower bound for 2-designs built from orthonormal bases; symmetric informationally complete (SIC) measurements retain exactly \((1-1/\sqrt{d+1})/d\). The loss comes from aligned blind spots. Relative to a basis, pure-state changes split into population and phase parts of equal dimension, but probabilities respond only to the former. Mutual unbiasedness turns a population change for one basis into a phase change for every other. The worst case already occurs for a qubit encoded in two levels. Independent random bases instead scatter their blind spots. In sufficiently large dimensions, five Haar-random bases retain, with high probability, a dimension-independent QFI fraction for every pure state and direction. Random Clifford measurements on any number of qubits retain exactly one third. Thus blind-spot geometry, not second-order symmetry alone, controls worst-case metrological performance.

papers.title: Enhanced shortcuts to adiabaticity in an interacting giant-atom-atomic-waveguide system
papers.summary: In realistic quantum systems, isolated few-level models usually provide only an approximate description, since the controlled subsystem is generally coupled to additional degrees of freedom. As a result, a quantum control scheme designed for an isolated system may lose its original performance in a more complex coupled setting. Here, we consider a giant atom coupled to an interacting atomic waveguide and investigate enhanced shortcuts to adiabaticity (eSTA) in such a structured system. As a first step, a weak-coupling perturbative analysis identifies how changes in the initial and target states, together with dynamical transitions, contribute to the fidelity loss. Starting from a shortcut to adiabaticity control scheme for the uncoupled system, the enhanced STA correction improves the final fidelity by modifying only the giant-atom control fields. This improvement is found for both periodic and open boundary conditions of the atomic waveguide. The results demonstrate a way to design an eSTA protocol for an interacting composite system.

papers.title: Implications of the PXP ground-state sign structure for neural-network variational Monte Carlo
papers.summary: Positive-definite neural-network quantum states cannot directly represent the ground state of the PXP Hamiltonian, since the ground-state wavefunction carries a nontrivial relative-sign structure. Building on the chiral symmetry of the PXP Hamiltonian, we show that this sign structure is fixed exactly by the parity of the total up-spin number: a diagonal unitary transformation that assigns a sign to each spin configuration according to this parity maps the PXP Hamiltonian to its negative, rendering the transformed Hamiltonian stoquastic on the Rydberg-blockaded Hilbert space. Since the configuration graph of allowed configurations is connected, the Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees a unique, strictly positive ground state of the transformed Hamiltonian, yielding an exact sign rule for the ground state of the original Hamiltonian in terms of the parity of the up-spin number. Variational Monte Carlo performed directly on the transformed Hamiltonian with a positive-definite ansatz therefore requires no architecture-specific modification to represent the true ground state. We evaluate the performance of this formulation using five representative neural-network quantum state architectures, SineKAN, reflection-symmetrized SineKAN, RBM, MLP, and LSTM, for different chain lengths.

papers.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
papers.summary: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = \Omega(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=\Omega(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.

papers.title: Iterative Quantum Optimization: From Greedy Reductions to Branch-and-Bound
papers.summary: Iterative quantum optimization (IQO) uses quantum-generated information to select a sequence of classical problem reductions. We introduce Bound-Aware Tree-IQO which combines this iterative structure with bounds and reversible search. Feasible measured samples update a shared incumbent, while valid classical bounds prune branches that cannot improve it. Incorporating backtracking yields an anytime method that returns the best feasible solution found when interrupted, or can be run as a complete search to return and certify the optimum. For suitable single-variable or pairwise reductions, an initial IQO path can determine the branching schedule without further quantum calls, though certifying the optimum may take superpolynomial classical time. To motivate our framework, we prove two limitations of irreversible IQO reductions based on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). We show an infinite family of unweighted MaxCut instances on which globally optimized level-1 QAOA makes standard Recursive QAOA strictly prefer a first reduction that excludes every optimal solution, and limits that branch to an approximation ratio of at most $2/3+o(1)$. In contrast, a single backtrack recovers an optimal solution using the same quantum information. Causal cone arguments give a complementary obstruction at every fixed depth of standard QAOA: a weighted MaxCut instance is shown to contain two edges with identical two-qubit reduced states, even though every optimum requires opposite edge parities. MaxCut experiments show that QAOA-guided ordering is nonrandom in exact-certification tests through $n=28$, while demonstrating that quantum samples can strengthen the incumbent and enable further pruning. Our results suggest that quantum data could provide useful guidance toward solving hard combinatorial optimization problems more effectively than either quantum or classical algorithms alone.

papers.title: Photon-loss tolerance of the surface-GKP code with anti-photon-loss decoding
papers.summary: Photon loss somewhat limits fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing. We investigate its effect on finite-energy Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) states by modeling the pure-loss channel directly. We obtain photon-loss threshold estimates for the surface-GKP code using nearest-lattice-point inner GKP decoding and minimum-weight perfect matching for the outer surface code. For GKP states with $\epsilon=0.01$ and $\epsilon=0.05$, corresponding to GKP squeezing of $20$ and $13\,\mathrm{dB}$, the estimated thresholds are $\gamma^\ast=5.5\%$ ($0.24\,\mathrm{dB}$) and $\gamma^\ast=5.9\%$ ($0.26\,\mathrm{dB}$), respectively. We then introduce an anti-photon-loss inner decoder that compensates for the contraction of the measured quadrature. It increases the corresponding threshold estimates to $\gamma^\ast=9.8\%$ ($0.45\,\mathrm{dB}$) and $\gamma^\ast=6.3\%$ ($0.28\,\mathrm{dB}$). Our results highlight the importance of accounting for loss-induced lattice contraction in inner decoding and demonstrate that quadrature compensation enhances the photon-loss tolerance of surface-GKP codes for both high- and moderate-quality GKP states, providing a route toward more photon-loss-robust optical quantum computing.

papers.title: Leaving Quantum Bias on the Table: Pushforwards as a Path to Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization
papers.summary: Constrained quantum samplers often produce infeasible outputs that retain information about good feasible solutions. We develop a post-measurement framework that constructs problem-dependent classical feasibility maps from constraint-violation statistics and pushes the raw quantum sampling law forward onto the feasible set. The probability of each repaired solution is the total raw mass of its repair preimage, enlarging the successful sampling event from a target feasible set to its full repair preimage. We derive exact identities for repaired success and expected cost, and separate repair-basin geometry from sampler-dependent probability concentration. For noisy implementations, we distinguish leakage from the encoded subspace from concentration loss within it. For permutation constraints, Hungarian maximum-overlap repair provides an O(n^3) implementation, which we study on traveling-salesman problems (TSP). We derive conditional repaired-success bounds and quantify how basin aggregation reduces the absolute-transfer budget required by these bounds. Noiseless simulations show that optimal repair basins contain selectively overweighted infeasible contributors. For an n=10 TSP instance, pushforward repair recovered the optimum using approximately 10^3 shots, compared with 10^6 shots in the original CE-QAOA workflow without repair. On a 127-qubit IBM processor, using encodings of up to 100 qubits, repaired candidates match reference tours on smaller benchmarks and improve them on larger instances. These results establish concentration of quantum probability on useful repair preimages as a design principle for constrained quantum optimization.

papers.title: Coherence controls the visibility of frozen disorder in an open quantum chain
papers.summary: A Gaussian position distribution need not imply that frozen disorder is irrelevant. We study a resonant quantum chain where neighboring sites couple with opposite signs to auxiliary states that decay with frozen, random return probabilities. Lowering dephasing spreads the effect of each local return bias over more sites. We take dephasing to zero at a fixed, sufficiently weak disorder amplitude. On the scale of a coherent wave packet, the position distribution approaches the same Gaussian for almost every frozen sample. At larger distances and later times, it remains sample dependent and is described by diffusion in a random potential with Brownian spatial statistics. The covariance of bounded, direction-sensitive position readouts from independent trials in the same field distinguishes these regimes. Simulations resolve their separation at finite dephasing. Taking weak disorder before vanishing dephasing also reveals a different packet-scale response from a memoryless random-force model matched in clean diffusion and leading potential strength. The coherent response develops an integrable logarithmic peak near the initial site, where the reference response stays finite. It reflects the correlated duration and displacement of motion between jumps, together with the unfinished packet at measurement.

papers.title: Multicopy teleportation and quantum program retrieval on superconducting quantum hardware
papers.summary: Correction-free teleportation protocols offer a probabilistic route around the limits imposed by the quantum no-programming theorem, but have remained largely theoretical. Here, we experimentally implement and benchmark correction-free multicopy teleportation on noisy superconducting quantum hardware. Key to this is an efficient circuit implementation: by suitably decomposing the unitary that maps the multicopy measurement basis onto the computational basis, we substantially reduce circuit depth and gate count. For one- and two-qubit input states, using $k=2$ and $3$ copies, we observe success probabilities substantially exceeding the single-copy bound with fidelities above 0.85. We further explore applications to probabilistic programmable quantum processors, in particular the storage and retrieval of unitary operations encoded in quantum program states. Our results establish the practical feasibility of multicopy teleportation and highlight its potential for near-term quantum processors and distributed quantum computing.

papers.title: Experimental Realization of a Nonreciprocal Quantum Battery
papers.summary: Quantum batteries promise faster and more efficient energy storage and extraction by harnessing quantum mechanics, serving as essential building blocks for future quantum devices. A key practical requirement-unidirectional energy flow during charging-is straightforward in classical batteries via potential difference, yet remains a major challenge in the quantum regime due to the inherent reciprocity of coherent coupling. Here, we realize the first backflow-free, nonreciprocal quantum battery in the few-quantum regime, implemented in a highly controlled trapped-ion system via a qubit-reservoir engineering technique. By subtly tailoring quantum interference between coherent and dissipative couplings of two laser-cooled motional modes, we achieve strictly unidirectional energy flow from the charger to the battery. We observe maximum charging power at an exceptional point and demonstrate a complete charge-discharge cycle with unitary work extraction. This work establishes the foundation for directional energy transfer and storage in micro- and nanoscale quantum devices, with broad implications for nonreciprocal energy harvesting, precision metrology, information processing, and quantum thermodynamics.

papers.title: Where Does a Variational Quantum Classifier Lose Accuracy? Angle Encoding, Readout and the Fidelity-Kernel Reference in Cyberattack Detection
papers.summary: When a variational quantum classifier performs poorly at detecting network attacks, it is hard to tell which part is to blame: the encoding, the trained circuit or the readout, which turns measurements into a class. In this work, we build upon a recent amplitude-encoded classifier, and we try to separate their contributions to the NSL-KDD benchmark in noiseless simulation. We compare angle and amplitude encoding, vary one component at a time, and measure each circuit against a classical yardstick: a support-vector machine on the encoded states, whose accuracy estimates what a well-trained circuit can reach. Most of the shortfall lies in the readout. Reading one qubit, or the parity of all qubits, leaves several percentage points unused, while a readout trained together with the circuit recovers most of them from the same measurements. This also explains why some classifiers stop improving as further layers are added. The encodings suit different needs. Angle encoding gives the more accurate detector on traffic like the training data and, from eight features up, shallower circuits; amplitude encoding needs far fewer qubits and catches more attacks of types never seen in training. Finally, we report that classical models, given the same inputs, are about as accurate as the best circuits, thus, registering no quantum advantage.

papers.title: Quantum Mpemba effect of Z2 symmetry restoration in the Dicke model
papers.summary: We study a symmetry-restoration quantum Mpemba effect in the dissipative Dicke model as an example of a weakly $\mathbb Z_2$-symmetric open quantum system, where the full Liouvillian is parity covariant although individual quantum jumps connect the two Hilbert-space parity sectors. Using the entanglement-asymmetry (EA) diagnostic to monitor parity restoration, we compare coherent-product and cat-product initial states. Coherent-product states show conventional relaxation, with larger initial asymmetry decaying more slowly and no Mpemba crossing observed. Cat-product states, by contrast, can reverse this hierarchy over a finite region of initial-state space. This reversal is enabled by initial-state mode filtering: the cat-product superposition suppresses the contributions of the leading slow Liouvillian modes, allowing a more asymmetric state to restore parity through faster decay channels. Our results reveal that symmetry-restoration QME can arise even when parity is preserved only as a weak Liouvillian symmetry, with quantum jumps mixing the Hilbert-space parity sectors. The anomalous relaxation is governed by initial-state-dependent filtering of the leading slow Liouvillian modes, providing a mechanism for symmetry-restoration QME beyond strongly conserved symmetry sectors.

papers.title: Binary Quantum Hypothesis Testing with a Rejection Option: The Exact Error-Exponent Trade-off
papers.summary: We characterize the exact error-exponent trade-off in binary quantum hypothesis testing with a rejection option for faithful states on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. The probabilities of rejection under the two hypotheses are required to vanish exponentially, with exponents at least $K$ and $L$. We show that a quadruple $(a,b,K,L)$ of positive error and rejection exponents is achievable if and only if it satisfies three single-letter conditions: two conditions involve Petz--R\'enyi quantities and coincide with the converse bound conjectured to be tight by Ji and Regula; the third involves the $\alpha$--$z$ R\'enyi quantities on the triangle $\max\{\alpha,1-\alpha\}\le z\le1$. The proof combines a sector decomposition inside Schur--Weyl blocks, an explicit one-shot measurement construction, and an exact minimax argument.

papers.title: Single-Mode Squeezing Using Degenerate Four-Wave Mixing in a Dual-Pump TWPA
papers.summary: Single-mode squeezing of the electromagnetic vacuum is a key resource for mode-selective noise reduction in quantum measurements. At microwave frequencies, single-mode squeezing is typically obtained by using Josephson and Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers designed for three-wave mixing operation. In single-pump degenerate four-wave mixing, the coincidence of pump, signal, and idler frequencies complicates separation of the squeezed field from the strong pump. A dual-pump configuration enables degenerate operation while keeping both pumps spectrally separated from the squeezed mode. Here, we demonstrate single-mode squeezing in a flux-tunable, dual-pump Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier, employing reversed-Kerr phase matching. By independently calibrating the single-pump gains, we find that the strongest squeezing occurs along approximately balanced-gain trajectories, while the optimal squeezing does not necessarily correspond to the highest dual-pump gain. At flux biases $\Phi_\mathrm{ext}/\Phi_0 = 0.0$ and $0.5$, the minimum quadrature noise levels reach $-2.48 \pm 0.18~\mathrm{dB}$ and $-1.62 \pm 0.20~\mathrm{dB}$ relative to vacuum, respectively. These results establish the proposed architecture as a platform for single-mode squeezing in microwave continuous-variable quantum technologies.

papers.title: Normal Factor Graph Representations of Stabilizer Quantum Codes with Applications
papers.summary: We develop normal factor graph (NFG) representations of stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes and entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes. We introduce two complementary representations. Quantum-code NFGs describe stabilizer and normalizer label codes and provide a graphical framework for establishing self-orthogonality, constructing codes from component codes, and identifying encoding and decoding circuits. Quantum-probability NFGs represent the quantum-mechanical probabilities associated with encoding, noise, and measurement. We also introduce a doubleedge formulation that makes the relationship between these two representations explicit. We apply the framework to convolutional and tail-biting convolutional stabilizer codes, as well as to two classes of low-density parity-check stabilizer codes. Finally, we extend the quantum-probability representation to entanglementassisted codes.

papers.title: Multiparameter quantum metrology for general and adaptive strategies
papers.summary: We develop a conic-programming framework for multiparameter estimation of quantum processes under different classes of sensing strategies. Estimation precision depends on the choice of input probe state and measurement and, when a channel is used multiple times, on the arrangement of channel uses and intermediate controls. We specify different strategy classes through linear normalization constraints on generalized measurements, and formulate the local estimation problem using linear constraints and a linear objective function. We show that the separable-cone program gives the exact precision limit under the local estimation conditions considered here, while cone relaxations yield Cram\'er-Rao-type lower bounds. For $N$ uses of an identical quantum channel, we prove an exact $1/N$ scaling law for an RLD-based positive-cone lower bound, even for general process-matrix testers that allow indefinite causal order. Under the stated conditions on the channel and its parameter dependence, the minimum weighted mean-square error also scales as $1/N$. This extends an RLD-based restriction on Heisenberg scaling from adaptive strategies to this broader class. For fixed-order adaptive strategies, we show that each process-side conic bound equals the corresponding state-estimation bound optimized over sensor combs. We establish this equality by constructing a sensor comb from the process-side normalization operator. A noisy three-parameter field-sensing model illustrates the framework.

papers.title: All-to-All Connectivity in Superconducting Qubits via Metamaterial-Mediated Interactions
papers.summary: We show that encoding superconducting qubits as dual-rail or spin-locked transmons lets a metamaterial waveguide couple them all-to-all while suppressing the spurious entanglement that burdens shared-mode architectures, a step toward the non-local connectivity that quantum low-density parity-check codes require. In a bare-transmon architecture, the dispersive coupling between each populated mode and every idle qubit attached to it entangles spectators with the gate, and cancelling it by dynamical decoupling lengthens every gate. The encoding suppresses this coupling at the hardware level, from second to fourth order in the inverse qubit--mode detuning. A two-tone cross-resonance drive then generates a M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen interaction between encoded qubits, which we use for an entangling gate and a joint parity measurement, both selective and parallelizable through different modes. Simulating two dual-rail transmons sharing three resonators with a mode lifetime of $30\,\mu$s, we find that heralding transmon relaxation as erasure leaves a gate infidelity of $1.4\times10^{-3}$ at $152$~ns, dominated by photon loss. Photon loss and mode crowding together bound the array size. The gate duration must exceed the inverse mode spacing, which shrinks as the array lengthens, while photon loss grows with gate duration. This bound grows linearly with the mode lifetime and with the inter-resonator coupling; at a lifetime of $150\,\mu$s, five times the simulated value, and a coupling of $80$~MHz, a $10^{-3}$ error budget admits $13$ qubits on $25$ resonators.

papers.title: Cooling-path-selected self-assembly of telecom InAsP quantum dots

These results establish cooling as an active epitaxial step for telecom InAsP quantum-dot formation and wavelength control.

papers.title: Persistence of Fractal Structures in Iterated Quantum Protocols: Robustness to Preparation and Gate Errors
papers.summary: Repeatedly combining entangling gates on an ensemble of qubits with measurement and postselection on a part of them induces a nonlinear evolution of the unmeasured qubits' state, whose fractal convergence boundaries make the outcome sensitive to the initial state. We study a family of iterated protocols in which $n$ identical qubits are coupled by CNOT gates, $n-1$ of them are postselected, and a parametrized single-qubit unitary acts on the survivor. For orders $n=2$ to $5$, we map the box-counting dimension of the pure-state Julia sets over the complex parameter plane and identify the symmetries that constrain it. Allowing mixed initial states, we find that moderate preparation noise preserves the main parameter-dependent trends of the boundary dimension over much of the studied range, and that the three-dimensional quasi-Julia boundary in the Bloch ball has a dimension that is approximately equal to the dimension of the pure-state Julia set plus one. We further model gate imperfections by an effective depolarizing channel and by fixed coherent interactions. Weak errors leave the estimated dimensions consistent with their ideal values even where the convergence regions visibly deform, and $ZZ$ errors are shown to be exactly conjugate to the ideal protocol at a rotated parameter. Finally, we analyze the postselection and storage cost of an implementation and propose a diagnostic test combining conditional fidelity with acceptance statistics, which we demonstrate on IQM Emerald and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q.

papers.title: Chaos, Fractals, and Ergodicity in Nonlinear Quantum Protocols
papers.summary: Iterated nonlinear quantum protocols provide a straightforward way of realizing nonlinear dynamics in quantum systems through measurement and postselection. We further characterize the associated chaotic behavior through the distribution of Lyapunov exponents. Our results show that ergodic-like dynamics persists beyond the quadratic case, while the geometry of the corresponding parameter regions and the typical degree of chaoticity depend strongly on the order of the nonlinear transformation.

papers.title: Maximum purity of absolutely separable and absolutely PPT states in qutrit--qudit systems
papers.summary: A bipartite state is absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT) if it remains PPT under every global unitary transformation, and absolutely separable if it remains separable. For every qutrit--qudit system $\mathbb{C}^3\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$, $n\ge3$, we prove that the maximum purity is the same for absolutely separable and APPT states and equals $\max\{(3n+8)/(3n+2)^2,\,3/(8n)\}$. The maximizing ordered spectrum is unique and contains exactly two distinct eigenvalues: the larger one has multiplicity one for $3\le n\le8$ and multiplicity $n$ for $n\ge9$. We also derive, in terms of the purity, an upper bound on the minimum partial-transpose eigenvalue achievable by global unitary transformations, and characterize all states for which the bound is attained. These results confirm the inscribed-polytope purity conjecture of Ahiable, Kothakonda, and Winter for all qutrit--qudit systems. They also give a lower bound, sharp over explicit purity ranges, on the global depolarizing noise needed for absolute separability or APPT.

papers.title: Floquet engineering of quantum relaxation
papers.summary: Dynamical decoupling suppresses decoherence by averaging selected interactions between a quantum system and its environment. Here, we extend this notion through a general Floquet formalism that maps periodic control onto relaxation and dephasing channels. Environmental fluctuations are decomposed into Floquet components that sample the noise spectrum at distinct frequencies, with coupling strengths determined by control-induced Floquet coefficients. We experimentally investigate this approach using a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under multi-pulse control. By tuning the drive and detuning, we reshape the coupling to environmental fluctuations and create isolated operating points where the dominant decoherence channel vanishes, strongly suppressing Floquet dephasing. The resulting coherence enhancement follows the predicted Floquet coupling coefficients and can be shifted by modifying the control sequence. These results establish Floquet driving as a general framework for engineering transverse and longitudinal relaxation through the design of quantum control protocols.

papers.summary: Hybrid quantum-classical workloads, particularly Potential Energy Surface (PES) scans in quantum chemistry using batched VQE and QAOA, involve many structurally similar Hamiltonians differing only in coefficients. Existing warm-start and meta-optimization strategies reuse parameters between instances but still consume fixed quantum-classical resources, ignoring cross-instance structural similarities. We present OptiPESS, a GPU-accelerated runtime system for adaptive resource allocation in hybrid quantum-classical execution. OptiPESS introduces the Locality-Occupancy-Variance (LOV) metric, a lightweight, geometry-aware measure of Hamiltonian similarity, coupled with efficient alignment and Pauli-classification passes. Using LOV, OptiPESS performs distance-aware scheduling of iteration and shot budgets, predicting which instances can be skipped, quick-solved, or fully optimized. Implemented atop CUDA-Q with persistent multi-GPU execution and near-linear scaling, OptiPESS reduces classical and quantum evaluations by up to 78.3\% and wall-time by up to 74.8\% while maintaining baseline accuracy. This demonstrates how lightweight static analysis and adaptive scheduling can transform quantum-classical co-execution from fixed-budget loops into a predictive, resource-aware runtime.

papers.title: Boson sampling is fragile to loss
papers.summary: Boson sampling experiments aim to demonstrate quantum computational advantage with increasing numbers of interfering photons. A central question is whether their computational hardness survives under photon loss. We show that even an arbitrarily small nonzero uniform loss rate permits efficient classical sampling in the average case when the rate remains fixed as the system grows. We exploit how loss suppresses correlations involving many photons to approximate the full output distribution using low correlation orders. The resulting samplers run in time polynomial in system size and inverse total variation error, with the error averaged over Haar random interferometers. The results apply to Fock state boson sampling with single-photon states in distinct input modes and arbitrary additional vacuum inputs, and to Gaussian boson sampling with equal squeezing of bounded strength in every input mode. Classical sampling is efficient even when the mean detected photon number grows linearly with system size, showing that large photon counts alone do not ensure computational hardness.

papers.title: Purity maxima, absolute separability, and spectral volumes of absolutely PPT states
papers.summary: For $m\otimes n$ systems with $n\ge m\ge3$, we determine the exact maximum purity of absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT) states and the unique maximizing ordered spectrum when $n\ge2m^2-4$ for even $m$ or $n\ge2m^2-m-4$ for odd $m$. Under these dimension assumptions, absolutely separable states have the same maximum purity, attained at the same unique ordered spectrum. The proof uses an outer polytope defined by two linear head--tail inequalities, each comparing a sum of the largest eigenvalues with a sum of the smallest. Under explicit multiplicity assumptions, we derive an exact matrix criterion for APPT membership of full-rank spectra with three distinct eigenvalues. For every $m\ge10$, this criterion gives explicit APPT boundary spectra at $n=4m-2$ and $n=4m$ that disprove both cases of the maximum purity conjecture of Ahiable, Kothakonda, and Winter. We also determine the exact completely absolutely separable (CAS) purity maximum and its unique maximizing ordered spectrum in every bipartite dimension. We prove that the inner APPT polytope consists entirely of absolutely separable spectra. The resulting linear sufficient condition for absolute separability strictly improves the reduction-map and eigenvalue-ratio tests. Finally, we compute the exact relative volumes of the CAS set and an outer polytope defined by a single head--tail inequality. Under the uniform measure on spectra, the CAS, absolutely separable, and APPT volumes have the same asymptotic order $\sqrt n\,e^{-\kappa_m n}$ for every fixed $m\ge2$, with explicit $\kappa_m>0$.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Learning of Quantum Many-Body Systems from Gibbs and Thermal Metastable States via the Stationarity Test
papers.summary: We study the problem of learning a finite-range quantum Hamiltonian on an $n$-qubit $D$-dimensional lattice from copies of its Gibbs states at a known inverse temperature $\beta$ or its thermal metastable states. Existing efficient algorithms at arbitrary temperature have sample guarantees with an $e^{\poly(\beta)}$ dependence, leaving open whether the exponent can be made linear in $\beta$. We achieve this improvement: for $\beta\ge1$, our algorithm learns all Hamiltonian coefficients to $\ell_\infty$-error $\epsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ using $\tO\bigl(e^{O(\beta)}\epsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta)\bigr)$ copies and total time $\tO\bigl(n e^{O(\beta)}\epsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta)\bigr)$. The measurements act on individual copies and are supported on balls of radius $O\bigl(\beta^2+\beta\log(1/\epsilon)\bigr)$. Our sample complexity achieves the optimal exponential order in $\beta$, with optimal $\epsilon^{-2}$ dependence up to logarithmic factors. Building on the stationarity-test framework \citep{Bergamaschi2026Stationarity}, we prove a unified Fisher-information coercivity bound showing that errors in the candidate Hamiltonian produce a detectable signal with only an $e^{-O(\beta)}$ loss in sensitivity. The key is a smooth frequency filter whose bandwidth remains independent of temperature, together with sharper estimates relating this signal to the Hamiltonian coefficients. For thermal metastable states, the guarantee holds under local drift $\zeta\le e^{-C\beta^{2D+1}}$, for a geometry-dependent constant $C>0$, and above an accuracy floor $\tO(e^{O(\beta)}\zeta)$. The argument applies to both Gibbs and thermal metastable states and, combined with local measurements and projected stochastic gradient descent (SGD), yields both learning guarantees.

papers.title: From Ghost SICs to SIC-POVMs: A Galois Reduction of Zauner's Conjecture
papers.summary: Symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (SIC-POVMs, or SICs) are optimal minimal measurements for quantum state tomography. Problem~1 of Horodecki, Rudnicki and \.Zyczkowski's open problems in quantum information asks for SICs in infinitely many dimensions. By work of Appleby--Flammia--Kopp and Radchenko--Wheeler, ghost SICs, which satisfy the SIC equations with Hermiticity up to parity, exist unconditionally for $d\ge4$. We study the passage from ghosts to SICs. We compute all isolated points of the complexified SIC variety for $d=4,5,6$; exactly half are SICs. We prove that no symmetry of the SIC equations maps a ghost to a SIC, so the step is purely arithmetic, and that a SIC exists in dimension $d$ whenever the ghost overlap units satisfy a place law: each Galois conjugate is real or unimodular according to the infinite place of the real quadratic field $F$ below it. If the unit field is abelian over $F$, the place law is the Stark relation $c_-=\kappa$; equivalently, a Galois conjugate of an associated near-group fusion category is unitary exactly when it is pseudo-unitary. For $d$ a power of a prime $p\equiv5\pmod 6$ or of $3$, an infinite family, we prove that under the algebraic part of Stark's conjecture $c_-=\kappa$ is equivalent to the triviality of $\kappa$ on the Hilbert-class-field part of the unit field. That condition involves no complex conjugation, and it follows from a sign-free multiplet hypothesis. We state an explicit $GL_2$ reciprocity law for the squared ghost overlaps that implies $c_-=\kappa$, and we prove it for the computed algebraic overlaps in $d=5,7,11,15$ by Artin reciprocity and a check in every ray class. Zauner's conjecture remains open: the algebraic part of Stark's conjecture and the multiplet hypothesis are not proved here.

papers.title: Access Resources and Stability of Error-Correction Capabilities in Continuous Strategic Codes
papers.summary: Continuous quantum error correction depends on which parts of a measurement record remain available to the controller at recovery. We study this temporal access using continuous strategic codes, formulated as open continuous process tensors contracted with causal instruments and conditional recovery. For monitored stabilizer codes, a common-optimal-correction criterion identifies when records can be merged without loss and yields a factorization for separated CSS inference. Terminal decision labels and causal persistent memory carry different costs: five persistent classical states reach the complete-record optimum in a finite-strength counting model, whereas its two-window diffusive counterpart has nine terminal decision labels and requires unbounded memory for exact causal recovery. Uniform lower and constructive upper bounds establish an optimal fidelity deficit of order $m^{-2}$ for $m$ persistent states in the diffusive model. Counting and diffusive stability bounds translate open-process approximation into guarantees for deployed-controller performance and retained access advantages, quantified by explicit quantizers and model-mismatch curves. The same process--instrument framework connects storage with persistent environments and irreversible noise to spacetime interrogation and record-selected paths for a logical $T$ gate. These results specify which record distinctions recovery needs, the memory cost of approximating them, and the logical protection retained under model error.

papers.title: Bounds and sufficient conditions in quantum Zeno effect
papers.summary: When a quantum system undergoes a series of repeated measurements during its time evolution to check whether it remains in the initial state, the resulting state lifetime can decrease (the quantum Zeno effect) or increase (the quantum inverse Zeno effect) as the inter-measurement period increases. Several transitions between these two regimes may occur within the same system. A carefully chosen measurement period $\tau_\ast$ (or rate $r_\ast$ in the case of a stochastic measurement protocol) brings the state lifetime to its global minimum. Here, we describe the upper and lower bounds on the optimized state lifetime, which are expressed in terms of characteristic time scales encoded in the state survival probability $P(T)$, which is assumed to decrease monotonically to zero at large $T$. In addition, we analyze the bounds on the optimal measurement periods/rates and formulate sufficient conditions for observing the inverse Zeno effect. The analysis is also extended to states with non-monotonic survival functions. The results are illustrated numerically with an example of a system of optically trapped ultra-cold atoms.

papers.title: Decoherence suppression in quantum dense coding
papers.summary: By harnessing entanglement to transmit information beyond the limits of classical communication, quantum dense coding serves as a key component in various quantum technologies. However, in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum era, noise-induced decoherence poses inevitable challenges to its practical implementation. By investigating the non-Markovian decoherence dynamics of the two categories of quantum dense coding protocols realized in discrete- and continuous-variable systems, we demonstrate a physical mechanism to suppress the decoherence in quantum dense coding. It is found that the formation of a bound state in the energy spectrum of the entire system consisting of each subsystem and its local environment of the quantum channel restores the quantum advantage of dense coding in the presence of decoherence. Refreshing our understanding on the noisy effect on quantum dense coding, our finding offers a guide toward the practical realization of noise-tolerant quantum dense coding.

papers.title: Mitigating sloppiness with intermediate controls in sequential multiparameter spin interferometry
papers.summary: Multiparameter quantum sensing requires different parameters to produce distinguishable probe responses while allowing their information to be extracted simultaneously. In sequential sensing without intermediate control, two phases encoded through the same generator are locally indistinguishable. Here we show that parameter-independent intermediate controls overcome this limitation in a collective-spin interferometer by separating the corresponding effective generators in the probe covariance geometry. Specifically, a transverse collective rotation provides an analytically tractable realization, and intermediate one-axis twisting (OAT) generates additional nonlinear operator directions and a broad regime of enhanced joint estimation. For fixed total particle number $N$ and matched twisting resource, both marginal precision bounds lie below those of a separated-OAT strategy while measurement incompatibility remains weak. For intermediate OAT, conditional optimization of an upper bound on the Holevo cost yields asymptotic $N^{-2}$ scaling. For this protocol, a fixed rotated-Dicke measurement retains simultaneous two-parameter enhancement over a broad phase region. These results show that nonlinear intermediate control can mitigate sloppiness while preserving quantum-enhanced precision with a common readout.

papers.title: An Observable-Algebra Approach to Quantum Coherence in Anyonic Systems
papers.summary: Physical restrictions on operations can make quantum coherence inaccessible. Quantifying off-diagonal density matrix elements in a chosen basis alone does not reveal which information is hidden by each restriction. To distinguish their effects, we describe physical restrictions through subalgebras of accessible observables. The associated trace-preserving conditional expectations unify two reconstruction principles: each gives both the maximum-entropy state compatible with the accessible data and the closest state in the corresponding subalgebra in relative entropy. We apply this framework to anyonic systems to separate the contributions from local-charge superselection and non-Abelian fusion rules. We prove that the charge-line severing map is the conditional expectation onto the local-product subalgebra. It is completely positive and quantum-trace-preserving, and uniquely reconstructs a state in this space from all local-product expectation values. The hierarchy of measurement restrictions then separates total bipartite coherence into three nonnegative contributions: coherence between local charges, inaccessible fusion information, and conventional coherence. The first two decompose the anyonic charge entanglement and distinguish the effects of local-charge superselection from the remaining fusion information. Finally, we relate basis-independent measures of anyonic coherence to entanglement. For pure anyonic states with vacuum total charge, the optimized total and correlated coherence equal the total and conventional relative-entropy entanglement, respectively.

papers.title: Quantum Lower Bounds for Collision Problems
papers.summary: We establish tight lower bounds on the adaptive and non-adaptive quantum query complexities of Promised $k$-to-one Finding on an exactly $k$-to-one input string $x\in\mathbb Z_q^n$, for every fixed $k\ge2$ and every feasible alphabet size $q\ge n/k$. The lower bounds are $\Omega_k(n^{1/2-1/(2(2^k-1))})$ for unrestricted adaptive algorithms and $\Omega_k(n^{1-1/k})$ for one-round non-adaptive algorithms. The former matches the adaptive quantum algorithm of Liu and Zhandry [LZ19], whereas the latter matches classical birthday sampling even when the parallel queries are arbitrarily entangled. We also establish the non-adaptive lower bound $\Omega_k(\sqrt{n/k})$ for $k$-to-one Testing when $q\ge n$, resolving an open question posed by Koiran, Landes, Portier, and Yao [KLPY10]. Our proofs generate the balanced input from a uniformly random permutation and use compressed permutation oracles to describe the information learned by the algorithm. The adaptive proof bounds the growth of partial collisions through successive queries. The one-round proof instead analyzes the state after the parallel queries directly, bounding the probability that the compressed database contains a full collision. In both proofs, a short verification step accounts for correct outputs that include unrecorded positions. For the decision problem, we also compare one-round states with independent and distinct output labels.

papers.title: Long-term yields of short-rate models as Feynman-Kac ground states: a variational quantum eigensolver with single-setting energy estimation on two NISQ platforms
papers.summary: We show that the long-term yield of a short-rate model is the ground-state energy of a Schrodinger operator obtained from the Feynman-Kac bond-pricing equation, so that it can be computed by a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We treat the Vasicek, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Black-Karasinski models; the last has no closed form. Calibrated monthly to the U.S. Treasury curve from 1985 to 2026, the long-term yield follows the 30-year yield with an in-sample correlation of 0.98. The Hamiltonian is stoquastic, so its ground state is positive and the energy can be estimated from computational-basis samples with a single measurement setting. On ibm_cleveland, gate noise appears mainly as bit flips of the high-order qubits. A bit-flip deconvolution with a tail set fixed by a WKB criterion, combined with readout mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation, gives four-qubit estimates within 33-125 bp of the grid ground-state energies for all three models, and within 23-67 bp for Treasury-calibrated parameters. On IonQ Forte Enterprise the same analysis reduces the error in the same proportions. On the same circuits, a Pauli-measurement VQE deviates by 791-1,129 bp, so the single-setting estimator gives about ten times smaller errors with one setting instead of nine. An on-device VQE converges from 4,939 bp to 130 bp.

papers.title: Tensor Contraction with ZX Calculus, a Graph-Theoretic Approach
papers.summary: Tensors are higher dimensional generalisations of vectors and matrices. Tensor networks are a diagrammatic representation of complicated relations between tensors, and tensor contraction is the evaluation of a tensor network analogous to matrix multiplication. Tensor networks and tensor contraction are ubiquitous in computer science, physics, and applied mathematics. Most existing tensor contraction algorithms are focused on finding an optimal contraction order of the tensors' bonds. However, finding the optimal order is an NP-hard problem. It is equivalent to another possibly more straightforward but still NP-hard problem of finding the treewidth of the line graph of the tensor network. While in general finding the optimal bond-by-bond contraction order is hard, in many practical cases there is no need to find an optimal order. This observation leads to the core innovation of this thesis, which is a new tensor contraction paradigm that uses graph theoretic operations to produce an equivalent tensor network whose line graph has lower treewidth than the original tensor network, before applying the bond-by-bond contraction algorithm. We call these graph theoretical operations \textit{rewrite preprocessing}, and we name the algorithms that apply rewrite preprocessing before regular bond-by-bond contraction \textit{Tensor Contraction with Graph Operation}. There are many possible ways to perform rewrite preprocessing; in this thesis, we focus on the graph operations of ZX calculus, a diagrammatic language for quantum circuits. Ample numerical simulations have been performed to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

papers.title: Quantum Path Finder: Navigating Constraint Space via Non-Abelian Gauge Dynamics
papers.summary: Quantum algorithms are commonly designed within the circuit paradigm or through adiabatic evolution. Here we introduce \emph{Quantum Path Finder} (QPF), a distinct algorithm-design paradigm based on non-Abelian gauge dynamics in a constraint-protected degenerate manifold. Each Boolean variable is promoted to a qutrit whose additional state represents an unassigned variable. The problem Hamiltonian then defines a connected manifold of feasible partial assignments, and time-dependent local qutrit rotations generate coherent transport on this manifold. Unlike conventional adiabatic quantum computation, QPF does not require the state to follow an instantaneous eigenstate along a prescribed interpolation: adiabaticity with respect to the constraint gap protects the feasible manifold, while adiabatic following within that manifold is optional. The algorithmic task is therefore to design paths and interference in constraint space rather than only to engineer a sequence of gates or a ground-state interpolation. We illustrate the framework with three applications. For unstructured search, a two-level analysis and numerical evolution recover Grover-type scaling under explicitly stated assumptions. For complete $3$-XORSAT, the accessible gauge sector has a size-independent gap, in contrast to the exponentially closing gap of a conventional transverse-field adiabatic path. For satisfiable $3$-SAT instances, finite-size benchmarks demonstrate high satisfied-clause fractions at short classical comparison budgets, without claiming an equal-cost quantum advantage. We also outline a superconducting-qutrit implementation and discuss the conceptual relationship between QPF and nondeterministic Turing machine.

papers.title: Rule-based hardware-configurable static analysis for quantum programs
papers.summary: The rapid evolution of quantum hardware necessitates an adaptable static analysis framework for validating quantum programs. In this work, we introduce SHARP, a rule-based static analysis framework designed for OpenQASM that decouples hardware-specific constraints from the validation engine. By employing a rule-based approach, SHARP allows quantum computing services to validate programs against evolving instruction set architectures (ISAs) without having to modify the core analysis engine. SHARP achieves this by ingesting ISA descriptions as standalone data, making the validation engine resilient to hardware updates. Furthermore, the framework employs an analysis-driven validation mechanism that enables multi-stage validation, simplifying rule construction and enhancing extensibility. We demonstrate how SHARP supports hardware-specific validation tasks and discuss its impact on quantum software development, including language decoupling, program-level constraint validation, and feature access control. Our findings suggest that SHARP provides a path toward a scalable and maintainable programming interface for quantum computing.

papers.title: Interaction order sets the onset cost of steady-state quantum magic
papers.summary: Maintaining quantum magic under continuous noise requires coherent control and a supply of purity. We determine the cost of local stabilizer replacement resets sustaining any positive stationary magic in autonomous qubit networks with depolarization rate $\gamma$, interactions on at most $k$ sites, and Hamiltonian strength $J$ per site. An exact global stabilizer decomposition and a matching finite construction give the optimal onset scaling $\gamma(\gamma/J)^{1/(k-1)}$, uniformly over network size and noisy ancillas. For two-body interactions, the leading maximal-reset-rate coefficient is $1/(2\sqrt2)$ for every fixed finite size $N\ge2$, allowing mixed reset targets and heterogeneous rates. The same coefficient holds uniformly over growing networks with pure Pauli targets and equal reset rates. The converse combines hafnian stabilizer geometry with a positive random-order forest expansion.

papers.title: Classical and Quantum Dynamics in State Space: Projective Hilbert Space, Measurement, and Classical Emergence
papers.summary: We develop a geometric formulation of classical and quantum dynamics in which projective Hilbert space is taken as the primary state space and classical configuration and phase spaces arise as submanifolds of localized quantum states. The Fubini-Study metric induces the Euclidean metric on these submanifolds, while the tangential component of Schr\"odinger evolution reproduces Hamiltonian and Newtonian dynamics. We then extend the construction to stochastic motion. Brownian dynamics on the localized classical manifold is lifted to a common stochastic unitary evolution in projective Hilbert space; under homogeneity, isotropy, and independence assumptions, the corresponding Hermitian increments have Gaussian Unitary Ensemble statistics. This yields a random-matrix Schr\"odinger dynamics whose transition probabilities depend only on Fubini-Study distance. Through the embedding of localized states, the classical Gaussian transition law becomes the Born rule in projective state space. Measurement outcomes are identified with first arrival at detector-defined finite-resolution equivalence classes, while each realized state-space evolution remains linear and unitary. The framework is applied to classical emergence, macroscopic stabilization, double-slit experiments, composite systems, and entangled states. A spatially local Caldeira-Leggett-type system-environment model is also shown, under explicit thermal, symmetry, Ohmic, and coarse-graining assumptions, to generate the Brownian family required by the stochastic lift. The remaining open problem is to establish the range and universality of this mechanism for realistic many-body measuring environments.

papers.title: Sound-wave interference reveals the symmetry of a quantum transition
papers.summary: A single sound quantum emitted from two places interferes with itself, like a particle passing through two slits. The fringe position reveals whether the sources emit with the same sign (symmetric) or opposite signs (antisymmetric). Knowing this symmetry is important because qubits in solids lose energy by emitting such sound quanta, phonons. For a qubit shared between two sites, antisymmetric emission cancels at long wavelengths, suppressing energy loss, whereas symmetric emission does not. Lifetime measurements give only the total loss and cannot distinguish them. Such fringes appear in double quantum dots, but their position has not been analysed. Here we measure it for single phonons emitted as one hole tunnels between two gallium arsenide quantum dots. Using a quantitative model of sound focusing in the crystal, we find that the two dots emit antisymmetrically, as expected for a moving charge, with only a small symmetric part. Spin-flip transitions in a magnetic field weaken the fringes without shifting them. For double-dot charge qubits, antisymmetric emission is predicted to reduce phonon losses strongly at the frequencies where qubits operate, and phonon interferometry gives a direct way to measure how qubits release energy and to design longer-lived qubits.

papers.title: From Fabrication Disorder to Quantum-Protocol Yield in Inverse-Designed Silicon Photonic Beam Splitters
papers.summary: Telecom-band silicon spin-photon qubits offer a promising platform for scalable quantum networks and distributed information processing, but their fixed emission wavelengths require compact, low-loss beam splitters with precise splitting and fabrication robustness. Conventional designs can face trade-offs between footprint, optical performance, and wavelength-specific operation. Here, we employ adjoint-based inverse design to optimize photonic geometries beyond conventional layouts, developing 1*2 Y-splitters and 2*2 directional couplers for the silicon T (1326 nm) and Al1 (1482.44 nm) spin-photon qubits. The devices achieve footprints of 2.9 and 26 um^2, respectively, with excess losses of 0.14-0.44 dB and back-reflection below 5*10^-4. We assess fabrication tolerance using 100-realization Monte Carlo simulations incorporating etch bias, line-edge roughness, thickness, and refractive-index variations. Mirror symmetry reduces the splitting-ratio spread of the Y-splitter by a factor of seven to nine relative to the directional coupler. We translate these variations into dual-rail fidelity, ideal splitting-ratio-limited Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility, and random-number min-entropy. All realizations satisfy a protocol-performance threshold of 0.95. At 0.99, the tolerated splitting-ratio deviation shrinks from 0.035 for visibility to 0.0035 for min-entropy, and the simulated yields are 68% (T) and 91% (Al1) for coupler visibility and 90% (T) and 66% (Al1) for Y-splitter min-entropy. The tolerance of the target protocol, rather than the device alone, therefore sets the fabrication requirement for silicon spin-photon beam splitters.

papers.title: What is the connection between quantum relationality and symmetry-based relationality?
papers.summary: Although it has often been noted that both quantum mechanics and relativistic physics involve significant forms of relationality, the nature of the connection remains unclear. In addressing such a question it makes sense to start from the simplest possibility, so in this article I set out to consider the viability of the hypothesis that the two types of relationality are ultimately the same: that is, quantum states always characterize degrees of freedom which can be changed by a symmetry transformation, so they are relativized for exactly the same reason as partial observables in general relativity. I use the idea that we only measure partial observables to argue that this suggestion is compatible with all existing empirical evidence for quantum mechanics, and then I consider the consequences for ongoing debates about the nature of measurement in quantum mechanics.
