papers.title: Amortized Stabilizer R\'enyi Entropy of Quantum Dynamics
papers.summary: Magic states are essential resources for fault-tolerant quantum computation. We introduce the amortized stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (SRE), which quantifies the largest SRE increase generated by a unitary, including arbitrary pure inputs and reference systems. Initial nonstabilizerness can enhance this increase, whereas analogous amortized logarithmic robustness and extent collapse to stabilizer-input optimizations. We establish structural properties and exact amortized 2-SRE values for the $T$ and $CCZ$ gates. We then derive explicit lower bounds on approximate $T$-state cost, with diamond-distance error, allowing stabilizer ancillary states, Pauli measurements, and classical feedforward. A Choi-state witness gives computable bounds for quantum Fourier transforms, controlled rotations, fractional controlled-SWAP gates, and finite Heisenberg-chain evolutions. We distinguish the unrestricted optimization from its Choi witness and specify the access and precision requirements for estimating Pauli moments. An odd-moment variant yields a confidence-qualified cost witness from ordinary copies.

papers.title: Models of liquid-sample confinement for nanoscale NMR
papers.summary: Diffusion is a prominent source of noise affecting nuclear magnetic resonance at the nanometer scale (nano-NMR), preventing high-resolution studies of unpolarized liquid samples and hindering the development of nanofluid devices. Actively managing diffusion noise through sample confinement is likely to unveil alternative noise sources that have so far been disregarded, as they occur in longer timescales and consequently are masked by diffusion. These secondary noise sources could diminish the advantages provided by sample confinement, but they may also yield valuable information about the behavior of the fluid sample and its interactions with the confinement device. In this article, we study in detail two previously unaccounted noise models for confined nano-NMR, namely, surface interactions and porosity, and discuss their implications for typical nano-NMR experiments.

papers.title: Hardware-Efficient Entanglement Distillation Using Bosonic Systems
papers.summary: High-fidelity entanglement shared between distant quantum systems is an essential resource for quantum communication and computation. Entanglement distillation addresses this need by converting multiple noisy Bell pairs into fewer higher-fidelity pairs, using only local quantum operations and classical communication. However, this approach typically requires a substantial overhead in the number of qubits. To bypass this hurdle, we propose to leverage the high-dimensional Hilbert space of a single pair of bosonic systems to store a large amount of entanglement, replacing the need for multi-qubit systems. To distill entanglement in such a setup, we devise a new entanglement distillation protocol, tailored for bosonic systems. The protocol converts a highly-entangled noisy state between two bosonic systems into a lower-dimensional but high-fidelity entangled state, using only local bosonic operations. We show that our protocol significantly enhances the fidelity of the entangled state in the presence of naturally occurring loss and dephasing errors. Compared to methods relying on multiple Bell pairs, our scheme offers a more hardware-efficient strategy, providing a practical route toward the realization of entanglement distillation.

papers.title: Chirally frustrated superradiant phases in a Jaynes-Cummings trimer
papers.summary: We investigate the emergence of frustrated quantum phases in a Jaynes-Cummings (JC) trimer with complex hopping amplitudes between the cavities, which represents the smallest frustrated unit in light-matter systems. The complex hopping amplitudes that can be engineered via synthetic gauge fields introduce chiral effects and geometric frustration to the system. We obtain analytic solutions in the semiclassical limit and map out the phase diagram of this model, featuring one normal and three distinct superradiant phases. Among these phases, a chirally frustrated superradiant phase emerges, characterized by broken chiral and translational symmetries and unidirectional photon flow. These results reveal how frustration and symmetry breaking can arise in JC systems with synthetic gauge fields and strong light-matter coupling.

papers.title: Directional Codes for Quantum LDPC Error Correction on Square and Hexagonal Grid Architectures
papers.summary: Utility-scale quantum computing requires quantum error correction (QEC) to protect quantum information against noise. Currently, superconducting hardware is a promising candidate for achieving fault tolerance due to its fast gate times and feasible scalability. However, it is often restricted to two-dimensional nearest-neighbour connectivity, and therefore the variety of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes that can be implemented on it without sacrificing QEC performance is believed to be greatly restricted. In this paper we construct a new family of qLDPC codes, which we call ``directional codes'', that outperforms the rotated toric code (RTC) while satisfying the connectivity requirements of the widely adopted square-grid, and some even the sparser hexagonal-grid, on a torus. The key idea is to utilise the iSWAP gate -- a native gate demonstrated on superconducting qubits -- to construct circuits that measure the stabilisers of these qLDPC codes without the need for additional connections. We numerically evaluate the performance of directional codes, encoding four, six, twelve and eighteen logical qubits, using a common superconducting-inspired circuit-level Pauli noise model. We also compare them to the RTC and to the bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, currently the two most popular quantum LDPC code families. As a concrete example, when evaluated with the Tesseract decoder with short beam setting, the best directional code family investigated achieves the same logical error rate as the RTC at physical error rate $p=10^{-3}$ but requires only a quarter to a third of the number of physical qubits to encode a given number of logical qubits. Our discovery opens a novel direction in QEC code design, suggesting that complex high-connectivity hardware may not be necessary for low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation.

papers.title: Hierarchy of entanglement detection criteria for random high-dimensional states
papers.summary: Entanglement is a cornerstone in quantum information science, yet detecting it efficiently remains a challenging task. Focusing on states with nonpositive partial transpose (NPT), we establish a hierarchy among entropy-based, majorization, realignment, and reduction criteria for Haar uniformly generated random states in finite dimensions, analyzing their performance based on rank and subsystem dimension. We prove lower bounds on the rank of mixed quantum states beyond which the realignment and entropic criteria fail to detect entanglement. We evaluate the relative effectiveness of the considered detection methods using three key indicators -- fraction of detected states, mean detectable entanglement, and minimum required entanglement. Our results provide insights into the entanglement thresholds needed for reliable detection, showing that, beyond a certain level of entanglement, all criteria become equally powerful for low-rank states, while a hierarchy emerges among the various criteria for moderate to high ranks. Intriguingly, the proposed ordering among the considered criteria in qubit-qudit systems is different from that in higher dimensions. Additionally, we establish that the detection efficiency is influenced by the asymmetry in the subsystem dimensions, by illustrating how the realignment criterion behaves more efficiently than other detection methods when the difference between the subsystem dimensions is small.

papers.title: Work extraction from long-lived quantum coherence of a three-level system
papers.summary: We analyze work-extraction protocols using the long-lived quantum coherence of a three-level quantum system coupled to a thermal bath. Specifically, we propose an optimized protocol to extract the maximum extractable work (MEW), measured by the free energy difference (FED), from quantum coherence in a single-shot thermodynamic cycle. Our results highlight the thermodynamic advantages of long-lived coherence in a three-level quantum system and could influence future designs of coherence-driven quantum thermal machines.

papers.title: Lower-depth local encoding circuits for the surface code
papers.summary: The surface code is the most studied error-correcting code thanks to its high threshold, simple decoding, and locality in two dimensions (2D). This paper presents depth $d$ encoding circuits for the rotated surface code. Our circuit is constructed inductively from circuits that grow the code from $d$ to $(d+2)$. We prove that depth $d+O(1)$ is optimal for inductively constructed circuits.

papers.title: Low Overhead Universal Quantum Computation with Triorthogonal Codes
papers.summary: We study the use of triorthogonal codes for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation and propose two methods to circumvent the Eastin-Knill theorem, which prohibits any single quantum error-correcting code from supporting both universality and a transversal gate set. We show that our methods reduce the resource overhead compared with existing fault-tolerant protocols. We develop a simple fault-tolerant implementation of the logical Hadamard gate for triorthogonal codes by exploiting the fact that they have transversal controlled-Z (CZ) gates, resulting in a circuit with reduced overhead. We also introduce a procedure for generating a symmetric Calderbank-Shor-Steane code paired with a triorthogonal code, which allows CNOT and CZ gate transversality across the pair of codes. In addition, we present logical state teleportation circuits that transfer encoded states between the two codes, allowing all logical operations to be performed transversally. Our methods can be integrated into the Steane error correction framework without incurring additional resource cost. Finally, using the 15-qubit code as an example, we demonstrate that our protocols significantly reduce the gate overhead compared with other existing methods. These results highlight the potential of combining distinct code structures to achieve low-overhead, universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.

papers.title: Hyperfine spectroscopy and nuclear spin control of dark defects in diamond
papers.summary: Spin defects in diamond serve as powerful building blocks for quantum technologies, especially for quantum sensing and networking. Electron-nuclear defects formed near optically active spins such as the nitrogen-vacancy center provide a resource for multi-qubit quantum registers. Here, we identify the hyperfine components, including their relative sign, and nuclear spin species of two unknown dark spin defects using zero-field double electron-electron resonance spectroscopy and a protocol based on electron-nuclear double resonance. New ab initio calculations assign one defect to a known nitrogen interstitial, while the hydrogen-related defect matches no calculated or previously reported structure. We further use this protocol to demonstrate initialization, unitary control, and long-lived coherence of the hydrogen nuclear spin qubit, with a coherence time of 1.0(3) ms. These characterization and control tools establish a framework for harnessing unknown electron-nuclear defects for quantum registers.

papers.title: Sequential realization of Quantum Instruments
papers.summary: In adaptive quantum circuits classical results of mid-circuit measurements determine the upcoming gates. This allows POVMs, quantum channels or more generally quantum instruments to be implemented sequentially, so that fewer qubits need to be used at each of the $N$ measurement steps. In this paper, we mathematically describe these problems via adaptive sequence of instruments (ASI) and show how any instrument can be decomposed into it. Number of steps $N$ and number of ancillary qubits $n_A$ needed for actual implementation are crucial parameters of any such ASI. We show an achievable lower bound on the product $N.n_A$ and we determine in which situations this tradeoff is likely to be optimal. Contrary to common intuition we show that for quantum instruments which transform $n$ to $m(>n)$ qubits, there exist $N$-step ASI implementing them just with $(m-n)$ ancillary qubits, which are remeasured $(N-1)$ times and finally used as output qubits.

papers.title: Pervasive Vulnerability Analysis and Defense for QKD-based Quantum Private Query
papers.summary: Quantum Private Query (QPQ) based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is among the most practically viable quantum communication protocols, with application value second only to QKD itself. However, prevalent security vulnerabilities in the post-processing stages of most existing QKD-based QPQ protocols have been severely overlooked. This study focuses on hidden information extraction under undetermined signal bits, revealing that most such QPQ protocols face severe security threats even without complex quantum resources. Specifically, direct observation attack causes incremental information leakage, while the minimum error discrimination attack efficiently steals additional database inforamtion. To address these critical flaws, the proposed multi-encryption defense scheme is compatible with existing QPQ protocols. The study demonstrates the necessity of the multi-encryption strategy for the security of databases in QPQ, providing key theoretical and technical support for constructing practical QPQ protocols resistant to real-world attacks.

papers.title: Madelung hydrodynamics of spin-orbit coupling: action principles, currents, and correlations
papers.summary: We exploit the variational and Hamiltonian structures of quantum hydrodynamics with spin to unfold the correlation and torque mechanisms accompanying spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in electronic motion. Using Hamilton's action principle for the Pauli equation, we isolate SOC-induced quantum forces that act on the orbital Madelung--Bohm trajectories and complement the usual force terms known to appear in quantum hydrodynamics with spin. While the latter spin-hydrodynamic forces relate to the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), SOC-induced orbital forces originate from a particular current operator that contributes prominently to the spin current. This distinction between force terms reveals two fundamentally different mechanisms generating quantum spin-orbit correlations. Leveraging the Hamiltonian structure of the hydrodynamic system, we also elucidate spin transport features such as the correlation-induced quantum torques and the current shift in the spin Hall effect. This Hall shift leads to a new definition of the transport spin current thereby addressing an open question in spintronics. Finally, we illustrate the framework via the Madelung--Rashba equations for planar SOC configurations and propose a particle closure for possible numerical implementations.

papers.title: A Stochastic Reconstruction of Entangled States: from Quantum Foundations to Machine Learning and Decision Making
papers.summary: This article presents a concrete mathematical framework for the generation of entangled quantum states from classical stochastic processes. We demonstrate that any density operator $\rho_{AB}$ of a composite system can be derived from the correlations between two underlying stochastic processes, $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$, representing the random fluctuations of its subsystems. This construction utilizes a two-scale temporal scheme - micro and macro time - where quantum correlations emerge as macro-correlations derived from underlying micro-correlations. We propose the Double Covariance Model (DCM), which reproduces the some properties of quantum theory by treating quantum states as the fourth-order moment structure of an underlying classical probability space. DCM may also have potential implications for applications, particularly in quantum-inspired simulation and technology, and quantum-like modeling of cognition and decision making, as a tool for generation of density matrices with classical stochastic processes.

papers.title: Entanglement in quantum spin chains is strictly finite at any temperature
papers.summary: Entanglement is the hallmark of quantum physics, yet its characterization in interacting many-body systems at thermal equilibrium remains one of the most important challenges in quantum statistical physics. We prove that the Gibbs state of any quantum spin chain can be exactly decomposed into a mixture of matrix product states with a bond dimension that is independent of the system size, at any nonzero temperature. As a consequence, the Schmidt number, arguably the most stringent measure of bipartite entanglement, is strictly finite for thermal states, even in the thermodynamic limit. Our decomposition is explicit and is accompanied by an efficient classical algorithm to sample the resulting matrix product states.

papers.title: High-fidelity non-adiabatic dark state gates for neutral atoms
papers.summary: Rydberg blockade gates are the most experimentally mature entangling operations in neutral-atom quantum processors, combining fast gate times with simple control, but their performance degrades at larger interatomic separations and remains sensitive to motional and technical noise. Non-blockade gate schemes, such as dark state and geometric protocols, offer complementary robustness but typically rely on complex and experimentally demanding control. Here we show that quantum optimal control enables non-blockade gate schemes to be implemented using the experimentally established pulse-shaping techniques developed for blockade-based gates. Focusing on the dark state gate, we construct non-adiabatic implementations that preserve the intrinsic robustness of adiabatic dark state protocols while achieving gate times comparable to time-optimal blockade gates using only smooth, experimentally feasible pulses. The resulting gates exhibit enhanced resilience to motional coupling, laser noise, and interaction inhomogeneity, particularly near and beyond the blockade radius. This work establishes a practical route to fast, robust non-blockade-based two-qubit gates without increased experimental complexity.

papers.title: Quantum tomography for non-iid sources
papers.summary: Quantum state and process tomography are typically analyzed under the assumption that devices emit independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) states or channels. In realistic experiments, however, noise, drift, feedback, or adaptive behavior can violate this assumption. We show that projected least-squares tomography remains statistically optimal even under fully adaptive state and channel preparation. Specifically, we prove that the sample complexity for reconstructing the time-averaged state or channel matches the optimal i.i.d. scaling up to logarithmic factors for non-adaptive, single-copy measurements. For average states of rank $r$, the sample complexity is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d r^2/\epsilon^2)$ to achieve trace-norm accuracy $\epsilon$, while for process tomography it is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^6/\epsilon^2)$ to achieve diamond-norm accuracy $\epsilon$. Thus, dropping the i.i.d.\ assumption does not increase the fundamental sample complexity of quantum tomography, but only changes the interpretation of the reconstructed object. Finally, by tracking the drift of the source using only past outcomes, we certify high average preparation purity and entanglement even when the time-averaged state is mixed or separable.

papers.title: Unified Probe of Quantum Chaos and Ergodicity from Hamiltonian Learning
papers.summary: Developing measures of quantum ergodicity and chaos stands as a foundational task in the study of quantum many-body systems. We analytically and numerically show that our metrics not only distinguish between integrable and ergodic regimes in various spin chains but also quantify chaos and ergodicity, allowing us to locate regions of parameter space displaying maximal ergodicity and maximal sensitivity to local perturbations. Our approach not only provides conceptual ways to study quantum chaos and ergodicity but also presents viable experimental methods for quantum simulators.

papers.title: Testing the 3D QRNG by Undoing
papers.summary: We propose a method to test whether a photonic 3D QRNG operates according to the underlying theory by realizing the proposed measurement with the correct output probabilities and value-indefiniteness conditions, thereby generating strongly incomputable and maximally unpredictable sequences of random digits. The test relies on undoing the unitary evolution realized by the 3D QRNG. The test verifies the unitarity of the realized transformation, quantifies the magnitude of the residual noise, and detects those fabrication errors that are not common to the device and the undoing procedure; photon loss and dark counts are removed beforehand by heralding and are therefore outside its scope. By testing the validity of the implementation, the test can corroborate the theoretically proven features of the 3D QRNG, such as strong incomputability and unpredictability, or indicate how the implementation should be corrected, if necessary. The test can be easily incorporated into the QRNG and used as a means of experimental certification. The test module is fabricated identically to the QRNG.

papers.title: Quantum algorithm for solving high-dimensional linear stochastic differential equations via amplitude encoding of the noise term
papers.summary: This work studies quantum algorithms to solve high-dimensional stochastic differential equations (SDEs) $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{X}_t = A(t) \mathbf{X}_t \mathrm{d} t + B(t) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{W}_t$. Aiming for a speed-up in the dimension $N$ of $\mathbf{X}_t$, we generate quantum states that encode $\mathbf{X}_t$ in the amplitudes, while most of the existing quantum methods for SDEs employ binary encoding. A key challenge is the amplitude encoding of the noise term, and we address this by utilizing the quantum circuit implementation of a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG). We propose two methods: the Dyson series-based method and the Euler-Maruyama (EM)-based method. In the former, we express the noise term via the Dyson series approximation of the time evolution operator, while in the latter, it is approximated using the EM time discretization. Both methods use the quantum linear systems solver to generate the amplitude-encoding state of $\mathbf{X}_t$, making only ${\rm polylog}(N)$ queries to the PRNG circuit and the block-encodings of $A$ and $B$. Additionally, going beyond state preparation, we present methods to estimate expectations of functions of $\mathbf{X}_t$ using the state.

papers.title: Quantum circuit design via dynamic Pauli constraints
papers.summary: We introduce the Motte model, a software-oriented model of quantum computation motivated by the practical constraints of near-term quantum hardware. In this model, gates are specified by constraints expressed in terms of Pauli observables, with each disjoint layer of gates accompanied by a pairwise or k-local quantum state tomography of the device. We prove that the model is equivalent to the coupling-graph-restricted circuit model, and hence universal for BQP, with only polynomial overhead: emulating a depth-D circuit on N qubits requires O(D^2 N log N) elementary operations. Because the gate applied at each step is fixed exactly by the tomographic report, this emulation is robust to both the sampling and readout noise of the tomography. The model formalizes an idiom shared by existing work that ranges from quantum imaginary time evolution for the study of quantum systems to the use of quantum computers for procedural generation in games. It therefore provides a natural interface for designing quantum software entirely in terms of physically observable quantities, relevant for the NISQ era and into fault-tolerance, with gate and decoherence noise lying outside the present scope.

papers.title: How to make quantum cheese: efficient geometry oracles for exponentially many pseudorandom microstructures
papers.summary: Quantum algorithms for partial differential equations often assume oracle access to the geometry of the material being simulated. As explicitly specifying a geometry pixel by pixel on an exponentially large grid automatically yields an exponential cost, a central question is when such oracles can effectively be implemented by polynomially sized quantum circuits. We give explicit polynomial-size circuits for a family of geometries with exponentially many pseudorandom microscopic features. The geometry is generated by a pseudorandom procedure and a convolution with a local kernel to shape the texture. This proves to be a versatile framework, that includes materials with fixed-shape holes, spatially correlated textures, and activation--inhibition patterns. For a fixed kernel with bounded integer coefficients, the oracle cost is polynomial in the number of qubits, even when the number of microfeatures is exponential. We implement the circuit constructions in PsiQuantum Construct and verify their behaviour through numerical simulation. We also discuss why efficient access does not follow from an arbitrary description of the material, by proving worst-case query lower bounds for amplitude-encoded formation fields and databases of holes.

papers.title: Context-Verified, Error-Budget-Aware Decomposition Selection for Toffoli Networks
papers.summary: The cheapest Toffoli (CCX) decompositions (relative-phase and control-reduced Toffolis) save two-qubit gates, which dominate the error budget of near-term hardware, but they are correct only in context, since a relative phase is observable only when superposed branches interfere. We propose quantum chip performance tuning (QCPT), a compiler that selects the cheapest decomposition for each Toffoli (stage 1) and admits it only if a per-instance check shows that it equals the exact gate, up to one phase, on every state that can enter it; a whole-circuit certificate gates the output. The output acts as the exact circuit on every valid input, superposed ones included, up to a reported global phase, which per-state checks do not guarantee. Substituting relative-phase Toffolis wherever they fit changes the unitary of six of twelve benchmark circuits used as subroutines, whereas stage 1 changes none and removes 31.0% of the two-qubit gates. A certified resynthesis of classical circuits of up to ten qubits raises the saving to 43.1% on the primary suite and to 57.5% on 20 small RevLib circuits (in-sample). A bound on the compilation error plus the per-gate device error separates what the compiler adds from what a depolarizing two-qubit model of the device adds. In mirror tests on ibm_aachen, QCPT (best of four candidates, one of them the Qiskit circuit) returns more often than Qiskit on all nine circuits; in simulation with the calibration that drives its selection, on 29 of 33 circuits and worse on none by more than 0.01. An iterative language-model search with our certificate obtains no fewer gates on any of nine circuits and needs about 45 times longer (one run each). QCPT gives no gain without Toffoli structure. Certified context-dependent selection can thus let near-term devices run larger Toffoli circuits at a given success probability, with a gain that varies by family.

papers.title: A Single Physical Principle Determines Quantum Relative Entropy
papers.summary: Why does quantum relative entropy occupy such a privileged role among measures of distinguishability? We show that a single operational principle determines it. If one pair of states can be distinguished at least as successfully as another for every prior, when both are assisted by the same auxiliary pair, acting as a catalyst, a distinguishability measure should assign it no smaller value. Remarkably, for a normalized measure, this requirement singles out Umegaki relative entropy under mild classical continuity and expansibility on uniform distributions: adding impossible outcomes leaves their associated entropy unchanged. Qubit catalysts already suffice. No additivity or quantum continuity is assumed. We also prove that, without auxiliary assistance, respecting binary discrimination dominance uniquely determines the quantum extension of every regular classical divergence, including the Hirche--Tomamichel extensions of classical $f$-divergences. For additive classical divergences, these extensions respect classical catalysis; allowing noncommuting qubit catalysts is what singles out Umegaki relative entropy.

papers.summary: We define a two-particle quantum walk of identical particles on a graph $G$ via the one-particle Grover walk on the Kronecker product $G \otimes G$, and call it the two-particle Grover walk. In systems of identical particles, quantum mechanics requires that quantum states have a certain invariance with respect to the exchange of particles. Focusing on the symmetry of the Kronecker product $G \otimes G$ as a graph, we show that the time evolution operator of this walk commutes with the swap operator, which ensures that this requirement is satisfied. Furthermore, we study the entanglement entropy of quantum states evolved by this walk. For the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$, we completely determine the values of $n$ for which the quantum states evolved from specific initial states attain the upper bound of the entropy at some time, and prove that they are exactly $1$ and $2$.

papers.title: Geometric Mode Steering of the Quantum Mpemba Effect
papers.summary: The slowest Liouvillian mode often bottlenecks the relaxation of an open quantum system to its steady state. Standard strategies circumvent this bottleneck by selecting special initial states or engineering the dissipator. Here we investigate this problem when the input and the subsequent dissipative generator are prescribed. We introduce a predissipative geometric steering protocol that reshapes a prescribed pure or mixed state before relaxation begins---coherent rotations interleaved with nonselective projective measurements---at a fixed Lindblad generator. By steering the state's Bloch direction along geodesic paths, the protocol suppresses its overlap with the slowest Liouvillian modes. The prepared state can then start farther from equilibrium yet relax faster, realizing the quantum Mpemba effect, as diagnosed by reduced slow-mode overlap and a larger initial distance to stationarity, with distance crossings for complex slow modes verified from the full dynamics. Our framework treats real and complex spectral gaps within a common mode-overlap description. We also quantify the state-side cost of this preparation through cumulative measurement-induced mixing and illustrate its tradeoff with fidelity for a mixed target. We demonstrate Mpemba acceleration in driven qubit and multiqubit systems and discuss the required operations in trapped-ion and superconducting platforms.

papers.title: Quantum error-correcting codes from aperiodic monotiles: the Hat and the Spectre
papers.summary: Li and Boyle showed that the Penrose tiling defines a quantum error-correcting code: superpositions of tilings over isometry orbits protect quantum information against erasure of any bounded region. We extend the construction to the aperiodic monotiles discovered by Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss. For the Hat, we prove strong local indistinguishability for all Hat tilings, and we prove local recoverability unconditionally for all nonsingular Hat tilings via the torus parametrization of the underlying cut-and-project scheme. The remaining singular case reduces to one sharply posed geometric question -- can a region that is a union of hats be retiled a second way? -- which we verify computationally has no counterexample up to a substantial scale: a certified $2490$-tile patch admits precisely one tiling by hats, so all $2^{2490}$ of its tile-subregions retile uniquely. Unlike the Penrose, Ammann-Beenker and Fibonacci tilings, both monotiles form two local-indistinguishability classes, so their code spaces split into two erasure-correcting sectors carrying a superselected classical label. Whether the label survives depends on which isometries are gauged: the Spectre's classes are exchanged by a $30^{\circ}$ rotation and merge once all proper isometries are gauged, whereas the Hat's are exchanged only by reflections. Under the physically natural gauge group $SE(2)$, the Hat code therefore stores one robust classical bit -- the handedness of its long-range order, readable in any bounded window with separation $\Delta = |K|\sqrt{5}/3$ -- alongside its protected quantum sectors. It is the reflexible monotile, not the chiral one, that carries the chirality bit. We give the exact Perron-Frobenius data of both codes, including the per-class reflected-Hat frequencies $(3\mp\sqrt{5})/6$ and the Spectre orientation-class frequencies $(5\pm\sqrt{15})/10$.

papers.title: Random unitary circuits with constant spectral gap
papers.summary: We prove constant lower bounds for the spectral gap of the following random walks on unitary groups $\mathsf{SU}(2^n)$ on $n$ qubits. (i) Random Pauli Rotation: choose an $n$-qubit Pauli operator $P$ and an angle $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$, both uniformly at random, and apply $e^{\mathrm i \theta P}$. (ii) Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit: choose $n-1$ unitaries $U_{i}$ uniformly at random from $\mathsf{SU}(4)$ (including central phases of the parent group) independently, and apply $U_{2j-1}$ on two qubits $2j-1, 2j$ and then $U_{2j}$ on two qubits $2j, 2j+1$. Importantly, the gap bounds are independent of $n$ and apply for all finite dimensional unitary representations of $\mathsf{SU}(2^n)$ uniformly. Our results immediately imply that the Random Pauli Rotation and Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit converge to approximate unitary $t$-designs after $\mathcal{O}(nt)$ steps. As a consequence, we improve implications for the complexity growth of random unitary circuits as a function of the depth. The existing argument can be applied almost verbatim, but previously the depth had to be $\mathcal{O}(2^{cn})$ for some $c < 1$. Our unconditional constant spectral gap removes this restriction. We prove analogous constant-gap results for orthogonal and Clifford groups; the latter is indispensable for our result on the Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit. The former implies convergence to approximate orthogonal $t$-designs. In this case, the implied mixing time with respect to a constant additive and multiplicative error is optimal (up to an absolute constant factor) for $t=2$.

papers.title: Noise-robust discrimination of incoherent point sources with spatial-mode demultiplexing
papers.summary: We theoretically predict and experimentally demonstrate that a reduced spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) measurement using only the two lowest-order Hermite-Gaussian modes exhibits remarkable robustness against background noise in discriminating between a single source and two incoherent point sources. We establish a theoretical framework incorporating uniform background noise and derive an analytical Chernoff exponent expression, showing that SPADE consistently outperforms direct imaging (DI) across all source separations. Experimental results confirm that SPADE-based hypothesis testing approaches the quantum limit even when the background-to-signal photon ratio per pixel is 0.11. This advantage stems from SPADE's ability to concentrate source information into minimal detection modes, reducing the cumulative background noise impact. Our findings provide a practical detection scheme for applications where background noise is inevitable, such as astronomical observations and quantum sensing.

papers.title: Is the Quantum-Entangled Universe a Small World?
papers.summary: Partial entanglement may provide enough connections in the universe to satisfy the definition of a small world. To investigate this possibility, we define a network of particles on a given space-like hyper-surface with a long-range link between any two particles that are connected by a chain of exchanged particles involving a limited number of interactions. Considering the mean free paths of particles in different regions of space and the resulting probability distributions of entanglement connections vs. distance, we find evidence of small-world or random network structure on all but the smallest scales - corresponding to stars and planets - on which other types of connections would need to be added to complete the small world picture.

papers.title: Non-local Magic: closed-form solution and equivalence with magic of purification
papers.summary: Non-local magic quantifies the non-stabilizerness beyond the local choice of basis. Its evaluation is a hard problem requiring optimization over local unitaries. Here, we show that for the log-stabilizer fidelity this optimization admits an exact closed-form analytic solution depending only on the Schmidt spectrum. We then address the open problem of non-stabilizerness of mixed states by introducing the magic of purification and show that it naturally induces a resource theory whose free states are the states with zero stabilizer entropy. For the log-stabilizer fidelity, the magic of purification admits a distance-based formulation in terms of the Uhlmann fidelity. We prove that non-local magic coincides with the minimum magic of purification along the unitary orbit of the reduced density operator. This framework introduces non-local magic as the relevant resource for non-trivial steering and the characterization of entangling and non-stabilizer resources in measurements. These results provide both an efficient analytical characterization and a mixed-state resource-theoretic interpretation of non-local magic.

papers.title: Photonic Time-Delayed Quantum Extreme Learning Machine
papers.summary: We propose and numerically simulate a photonic quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) based on non-linear interactions in a time-delay non-linear interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection. We theoretically demonstrate the QELM's computational capability by binary classification of the non-linear two moons benchmark. Analysis of the learned output weights and alternative quantum readouts shows that compact feature sets based on photon-number correlations preserve classification accuracy while potentially reducing measurement complexity. We further show that the QELM maintains its classification performance under the effect of losses by naturally redistributing the learned weights across a larger set of available features. These results highlight the potential of time-delay photonic implementation as an experimentally accessible QELM platform.

papers.title: Predictive Structure Behind Rare Outcomes in Random Quantum Circuits
papers.summary: Local random quantum circuits can occasionally produce unusually large output probabilities. However, the final output distribution containing such a peak does not by itself reveal how the peak formed during circuit evolution. We investigate whether states formed during circuit evolution carry structural signatures that predict subsequent peak formation. In numerical experiments, circuits selected for large terminal peaks exhibit stronger pairwise correlations and probability redistribution, together with lower bipartite entanglement and output entropy, than controls generated by the same random-circuit model. Their intermediate states retain higher fresh-peak event probability when the remaining gates are independently regenerated. Within an unconditioned ensemble, a fixed structural score computed from the initial circuit segment predicts new-peak probability. Averaged equally across n=8-16, a replay with equal numbers of remaining-circuit evaluations shows that score-based allocation yields 1.80 times as many peaks as uniform allocation and about 18% more than a fixed baseline based on probability concentration and redistribution. Randomizing relative phases while preserving computational-basis probabilities strongly attenuates the selected-state advantage, demonstrating a functional contribution from relative-phase organization. Controlled gate-selection tests further show that the identified structure can guide circuit construction to promote peak formation. Together, these results connect rare output events to intermediate-state structure with predictive and constructive value under finite-depth local dynamics.

papers.title: Quantum Generative Modeling with a Coherent Memory, Exact Training and a Memory-Dimension Advantage
papers.summary: We introduce the coherent memory Born machine (CoMB), an algorithm for quantum generative modeling on a register whose size does not depend on the dimension of the data. CoMB generates a sample one component per round. In each round, a work register is entangled with a memory register and measured, and the outcome gives one component. The memory is never measured and carries correlations between rounds. We show that the characteristic function of the generated distribution is a product of small matrices, one per round. This gives exact training, with maximum mean discrepancy losses and gradients costing time linear in the data dimension, without sampling or likelihood. We also compile every round onto one work qubit and evaluate device noise exactly. To isolate coherence, each CoMB is compared with its dephased twin and with equally trained classical hidden Markov models. We benchmark it on continuous data, $368$-cell calorimeter showers from five qubits, and on sequential data, handwritten digits from three qubits. The coherent memory provides a memory-dimension advantage. Four coherent levels do the work of about six classical states on both benchmarks, and of at least five with $95\%$ confidence on showers at every training budget, including convergence. On showers, removing their coherence raises the loss by $23$ to $31\%$. With eight levels, where all models approach a common floor, coherent and classical memories become indistinguishable with longer training. On an IBM Heron processor, the memory carries two thirds of the inter-round correlation through twelve mid-circuit measurements.

papers.title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Testing Fourier Dimensionality
papers.summary: A boolean function $f$ has Fourier dimension $k$ if its strings with nonzero Fourier coefficients span a subspace of dimension $k$. We first consider the property testing task of determining whether a function has Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. We show that there is an $O(k/\sqrt{\epsilon})$-query quantum property tester for this problem, which we show to be almost optimal. Combined with Gopalan \etal's classical lower bound of $\Omega(2^{k/2})$, this demonstrates an exponential quantum advantage for this task. We complement this result with a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester, giving a quadratic improvement over the previous best tester, and essentially settling the classical query complexity. We then introduce and study the tolerant version of this problem. That is, determining whether a function is $\alpha\epsilon$-close to having Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this tolerant version of the problem is essentially just as hard as the standard version of the problem. That is, we show this problem has a $\tilde{O}(k/\epsilon)$ quantum tester, and a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester.

papers.title: Universal Inductive Inference of Quantum States
papers.summary: Solomonoff's universal inductive inference [Inf. Control. 1964] is one of the most general frameworks for learning from sequential data and predicting future observations. It provides prediction guarantees for any computable stochastic source. We ask whether an analogous universal theory of induction can be developed for quantum systems. To this end, we introduce universal quantum inductive inference, a framework for learning and predicting quantum sources that may exhibit arbitrary correlations and entanglement across time. Given the outcomes of past measurements and the corresponding post-measurement quantum systems, the learner produces a joint state that predicts the next measurement outcome and post-measurement system while preserving correlations with the past systems. We model a quantum source as a multipartite quantum state whose description is generated by an unknown $s$-bit program within a given time bound. The learner is required to produce a state that is $\epsilon$-close in trace distance to the target with probability at least $1-\delta$. We establish an information-theoretic inference algorithm with round complexity $O(s\epsilon^{-2}\delta^{-1})$. We further prove a matching lower bound in the relevant parameter regime, even for classical sources. As a second result, we construct a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm that outputs a classical description of the conditional state of the next system given past measurement outcomes. Our information-theoretic tomography algorithm achieves round complexity $O(sn^2\epsilon^{-4}\delta^{-2})$, where $n$ is the number of qubits received in each round. Finally, we investigate the computational hardness of universal quantum inductive inference under quantum cryptographic assumptions.

papers.title: A Tale of Two Walks: From Kac to KMP and Back
papers.summary: We reveal an unexpected connection between two interacting particle systems: Kac's walk and the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) process. We first establish a mixing-time analogue of Aldous's conjecture for the KMP process on general graphs: the mixing time of the $t$-particle process on any connected $d$-vertex graph is at most $O(\log d)$ times the corresponding single-particle mixing time, uniformly in $t$. As an application, we improve the mixing-time bound for coordinate hit-and-run on the $n$-dimensional standard simplex from $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ [KV26] to $O(n\log n)$, while removing the dependence on the initial distribution. We then show that the twirling channel induced by the parallel Kac's walk on the symmetric subspace can be exactly encoded by a Markov chain on partitions, which naturally lifts to a parallel KMP chain on the complete graph. We prove that $O(\log d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ repetitions of the parallel Kac's walk suffice to approximate Haar twirling on the symmetric subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}$ to error $\varepsilon$, uniformly in all $t$. Our main technical contribution is a new structural property of KMP-type dynamics: conditional product structure, which holds for both the standard KMP processes on general graphs and the parallel KMP processes on complete graphs. Conditioned on suitable auxiliary randomness, the evolution of the labeled KMP process factorizes into independent single-particle updates. Combining this structure with an exact coupling inspired by the analysis of Kac's walk, we remove the dependence on the number of particles from the mixing bounds for both unlabeled KMP models. This bypasses the $\log(\pi_{\min}^{-1})$ dependency from spectral-gap arguments, which is often prohibitively large for many-particle systems. Using this framework, we prove mixing bounds that are sharp up to logarithmic factors for both unlabeled KMP models.

papers.title: Single-shot state preparation thresholds in quantum LDPC codes: soundness, confinement, and statistical mechanics
papers.summary: Single-shot error correction does not by itself establish equally direct and robust logical-state initialization. We study preparation of CSS quantum low-density parity-check code states using one noisy round of the code's checks. We prove that linear confinement over a weight range growing at least logarithmically, together with at least logarithmic distance, suffices for a nonzero threshold under independent local-stochastic readout and data noise in the relevant CSS sector. The threshold is certified by ideal recovery of a decoder-defined logical channel. The key is a correction rule that preserves the logical class under local syndrome changes, allowing the proof to proceed without a local-stochastic bound on the preparation residual. This gives a single-block guarantee for quantum expander codes without dimension jumps or batching. Under the stronger linear-soundness hypothesis, we establish local-stochastic residual noise, enabling composition with compatible fault-tolerant gadgets. For a retained-record formulation, we also derive an exact statistical-mechanical representation of optimal final recovery at fixed preparation decoder. A decoder-dependent logical-sector order parameter characterizes asymptotically successful block decoding. Monte Carlo results for the three-dimensional toric code provide finite-size evidence for a threshold beyond both linear sufficient conditions. These results distinguish logical robustness from local-stochastic residual-noise control and identify decoder consistency as a route to single-shot initialization.

papers.title: Computational Bounds for $f$-Routing
papers.summary: The $f$-routing protocol is a leading candidate for quantum position verification (Kent, Munro, and Spiller, Physical Review A, 2011), but security guarantees for explicit functions remain limited. We prove unconditional resource lower bounds for uniform attackers. Our techniques bypass communication-complexity bounds central to previous works, which are inherently at most linear in the input length. We show that, for input length $n$ and a sufficiently small constant $\epsilon>0$, a uniform strategy running in time $T$ and succeeding with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ on every input implies the following computational bounds on $f$. 1. If the strategies are arbitrary quantum channels, then $f\in \mathrm{QSZK}(\mathrm{poly}(T))$, where $\mathrm{QSZK}(T)$ is the class of languages having quantum statistical zero-knowledge proofs in which the verifier runs in time $T$ and the simulator in time $\mathrm{poly}(T)$. 2. If the strategies are Clifford+T circuits using at most $t$ magic gates, then $f\in \mathrm{DTIME}(\mathrm{poly}(T2^t))$. 3. If the strategies are explicit Pauli-sparse unitaries acting on at most $T$ qubits and having at most $s$ nonzero Pauli coefficients, then $f\in \mathrm{DTIME}(\mathrm{poly}(Ts))$. Time and space hierarchies then yield explicit functions secure against superlinear and even all polynomial-time adversaries under our computational restrictions. These bounds exceed the bounded-storage qubit bound $q\leq\log n$ of Bluhm, Christandl, and Speelman (Nature Physics, 2022) for the inner product function $f=\mathrm{IP}$, at the cost of restricting adversarial computation and increasing honest evaluation complexity.

papers.title: Random Quantum Circuits Beyond Moment Matching
papers.summary: Random quantum circuits aim to efficiently reproduce the statistical properties of ideal random quantum evolution. One approach is to construct approximate unitary designs, which match the moments of Haar-random unitaries up to a prescribed order with controlled error. We establish quantitative guarantees for how accurately these designs reproduce the distribution of each output probability. We show that, for every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design on $n$ qubits, the distribution of each output probability is within $O(k^{-1/2}(1+k/2^n)^{-1/2}+\varepsilon)$ in Kolmogorov distance of the Porter-Thomas distribution, a beta distribution with parameters $1$ and $2^n-1$. This bound is optimal up to constant factors, implying that a substantially better uniform bound requires additional structure. We then show that a mild form of local invariance suffices. We prove that any such design that is invariant under unitary translations acting on a single qubit approximates Porter-Thomas to total variation distance $O(k^{-1/2}+\varepsilon)$. Every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design invariant on $\log k+O(1)$ qubits achieves error $2^{-\Omega(k)}+O(\varepsilon)$ in Kolmogorov distance and $2^{-\Omega(k)}+O(\varepsilon\log(2/\varepsilon))$ in total variation distance. These results identify the distributional accuracy guaranteed by moment matching and the structure that improves it. As an application, we show that the Shannon entropy of the output distribution of a strong $\varepsilon$-approximate $k$-design is concentrated around its Haar value $n-\Theta(1)$: its mean differs from the Haar mean by $O(k^{-1/4}+\varepsilon^{1/2})$ and its standard deviation is $O(2^{-n/2}+k^{-1/8}+\varepsilon^{1/4})$. Consequently, a trusted device sampling such circuits generates $n-O(1)$ bits of entropy per sample, which makes them useful for random number generation.

papers.title: Beyond light cones: State preparation complexity in quantum spin glasses
papers.summary: We introduce a technique for studying state preparation complexity in the quantum $p$-spin model on $n$ qubits, a disordered quantum spin system with random interactions on every set of $p$ qubits. We reduce the task of proving state preparation lower bounds to bounding the local profile complexity of the class, a quantity derived from the metric entropy of the set of vectors recording each state's expectation values against all weight-$p$ Pauli strings. We show that, for sufficiently large fixed $p$, any class with local profile complexity $O(n^2)$ remains separated from the ground-state energy by $\Omega(\sqrt n)$, a gap on the leading energy scale. When the profile complexity is $o(n^2)$, we prove the stronger conclusion that the class cannot outperform a benchmark class of simpler states at leading order. Product states always provide such a benchmark. Our framework strengthens known bounds and covers classes beyond the reach of previous methods. These include examples where circuit lightcones extend across the entire system, preventing an application of standard arguments. We obtain an $\Omega(n^2/\log n)$ gate lower bound for preparing near-ground states and depth--width tradeoffs, allowing arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates and arbitrarily many discardable ancillas. We also derive lower bounds on entanglement depth and matrix product state bond dimension, and energy obstructions for forward and reverse magic at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966). For Clifford circuits doped with $T$-gates, we obtain sharper energy comparisons using product stabilizer states as a more restrictive benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem (arXiv:1810.12197) with metric-entropy bounds for the Gaussian process indexed by the local profiles of states in the class.

papers.title: Complete Classification of Reversible Entanglement Transformations of Two Qutrits
papers.summary: We study single-copy exact deterministic transformations of bipartite quantum states under local operations and classical communication (LOCC), and give a complete classification of the states in two three-level systems that can be transformed into each other. This classification applies to finite protocols and to the countable protocols specified in this paper. If two entangled states can be transformed into each other but do not satisfy local unitary equivalence, then both can be decomposed into an entangled block and a separable part, and the two parts can be distinguished by local measurements. The two entangled blocks have the same probability weight and satisfy local unitary equivalence, while the separable parts may differ. We further prove that every entangled state has a unique least retained block; after retaining its probability weight, the local unitary equivalence class of this block completely determines the reversible equivalence class of the original state. For negative partial transpose states, one only needs to compute the negative spectral subspace of the partial transpose and perform at most three matrix zero tests to determine this retained block.

papers.title: Emergent SSH physics and localization in a cavity--atom system beyond the rotating-wave approximation
papers.summary: We investigate a cavity--atom system beyond the rotating-wave approximation and recast its dynamics as an effective tight-binding problem in the excitation-number basis. The same experimentally relevant light--matter platform exhibits two distinct regimes controlled by the photon number. In the large-photon-number regime, the hopping amplitudes become nearly uniform and the effective lattice reduces to a dimerized SSH-type chain subject to a linear energy gradient. The spectrum then organizes into one or two Wannier--Stark ladders, giving rise to controllable Bloch and Bloch--Zener oscillations and quantitatively explaining the observed revival patterns. In the small-photon-number regime, the intrinsic $\sqrt{\bar n+(\cdots)}$ dependence produces a pronounced hopping deformation, namely dimerized couplings that increase along the excitation-number lattice. This deformation reshapes the density of states, enhances collective localization, and generates an energy-resolved spatial bias of the eigenstates. The corresponding real-time dynamics displays direction-dependent anomalous diffusion together with Bloch-like revivals and beat phenomena in selected parameter windows. Our results show that the same cavity--atom platform can realize both emergent ladder spectra and hopping-induced localization in excitation-number space.

papers.title: Hamiltonian-Dependent Compressibility and Physical Preservation in Approximate Quantum Compilation using Tensor Networks
papers.summary: Approximate quantum compilation (AQC) using tensor networks provides a promising route to reducing the circuit resources required for quantum simulation. However, the factors governing the compressibility of many-body dynamics and the extent to which compressed circuits retain physically relevant information on quantum hardware remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions using AQCtensor for an 80-qubit one-dimensional anisotropic XYZ Heisenberg chain initialized in a N'eel state. By varying the exchange anisotropy and external magnetic field, we find that compression performance changes systematically with the anisotropic coupling configuration and field orientation. These variations are strongly associated with a nested-commutator measure related to second-order Trotter error, with corresponding directional trends also reflected in the target-state MPS bond dimension. For an 80-qubit quantum-hardware evaluation, AQCtensor compresses a 10-repetition target evolution to 5 repetitions while retaining a target-state fidelity of 0.995474, reducing the total circuit depth by 45.9% and the two-qubit gate count by 47.6%. The compressed circuit exhibits comparable behavior across magnetization, nearest-neighbor correlation, and Hamiltonian expectation measurements, while process-level diagnostics and local reduced-state tomography provide complementary characterization beyond these observables. Together, these results link AQCtensor compressibility to Hamiltonian commutator structure and target-state complexity and demonstrate substantial circuit reduction while retaining physically relevant features in an 80-qubit quantum-hardware experiment.

papers.title: V-type Atomic Variance Squeezing
papers.summary: Variance squeezing of a V-type atom interacting with a dissipative cavity is investigated. First, the influence of atomic initial state parameters on the variance squeezing is explored. The results show that the atomic variance squeezing switches alternately between Sx and Sy as the initial state parameter alpha sweeps from -pi to pi. The two squeezing intervals are symmetric about alpha = pi/4, each with a width of pi/2. For alpha = pi/14, only the Sx component can generate variance squeezing and will eventually disappear with time evolution due to unavoidable environmental noise. Then, the influence of system parameters on the variance squeezing is also studied. It is found that, the optical variance squeezing depth of Sx is determined solely by the atomic initial parameters and is independent of the system parameters. Both weak cavity-environment coupling and atom-cavity detuning can significantly enhance the robustness of the Sx variance squeezing. The SGI parameter has an extremely weak influence on variance squeezing. These results are beneficial for high-precision quantum communication applications.

papers.title: Constrained dissipation and the lifetime of quantum many-body scars
papers.summary: We investigate the fate of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model subject to Markovian dissipation. We show that when local jump operators respect the same symmetries of the Hamiltonian the full Liouvillian spectrum displays a tower of states with properties analogous to standard quantum scars: large overlaps with N\'eel states and equally spaced gaps in the imaginary part of the eigenvalues, set by a single frequency. Whether the long-time dynamics is dominated by scars is determined by the real parts of the eigenvalues, which are set by the ratio between the two relaxation rates $\gamma_{\pm}$ describing spin flips down-to-up or up-to-down respectively. For asymmetric dissipation ($\gamma_+ > \gamma_-$) the scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts: the resulting enhanced fidelity oscillations are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. In contrast, replacing the full projection operator in the dissipators with a partial one breaks the symmetries of the problem and is seen to destroy dissipative scars altogether.

papers.title: Quantum algorithms for optimal control: large-scale finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulation
papers.summary: We develop quantum algorithms for optimal control over a prescribed finite time interval (finite horizon), focusing on continuous-time linear-quadratic regulation (LQR). This foundational control problem often requires solving a nonlinear matrix Riccati equation, which can be costly for large systems and long control durations on conventional classical solvers. We instead work directly with the state-costate optimality equations, reformulating the LQR problem as a multiple-shooting linear system. Importantly, we prove a condition-number bound for the system that is independent of the horizon, under stabilizability and detectability assumptions. By incorporating the initial and final conditions into a single linear system, we can solve the subsequent linear system more efficiently with a quantum linear systems subroutine. For a given initial state, our quantum algorithms return classical estimates of the optimal cost and the optimal control inputs at a selected time, without constructing a Riccati solution operator. Given sparse-matrix block-encodings, an initial-state preparation oracle and a fixed number of control inputs, the query and gate complexities scale polylogarithmically with system size and control duration, provided that sparsity, relevant norms, and stability parameters are bounded. The dependence on the target error is inverse-linear up to logarithmic factors. We establish the required bounds uniformly in system size and duration for a family of damped mass-spring chains with two endpoint controls. Numerical experiments support the analysis.

papers.title: Cooling more while dissipating less: anomalous tradeoffs from thermodynamic geometry
papers.summary: We show that, starting from the same state, optimal driving can sometimes reach a colder (or hotter) target in the same amount of time while dissipating less energy, or equivalently dissipate the same amount of energy in a shorter time. We study this counterintuitive phenomenon in the slow-driving regime of an open quantum system, where we name it Near-Equilibrium Anomalous Tradeoff (NEAT). We establish necessary conditions for its occurrence and show its underlying geometric origin. While NEAT is reminiscent of the well-known Mpemba effect, the two phenomena are distinct in general. We demonstrate NEAT in an exactly solvable qutrit model, as well as for d-dimensional birth-death dynamics with independently controlled energy levels. Finally, we show how NEAT can improve the performance of Carnot engines.

papers.title: Quantum f-divergences from retrodictive tests: a unifying classical variational principle
papers.summary: A single classical f-divergence has several inequivalent quantum versions, but what distinguishes them operationally is less clear. Matsumoto's reverse tests characterize the maximal quantum f-divergence as the least classical distinguishability needed to prepare two quantum states with one device. Here we introduce retrodictive tests, in which two reverse tests sharing a reference state are coupled via Bayesian retrodiction to define a forward and a reverse stochastic process. In the forward process, the system is prepared by the first device and measured by the Petz transpose of the second; the reverse process interchanges their roles. We seek the least classical distinguishability between these two processes, as measured by the f-divergence between their joint laws, for fixed prescribed states and reference. For full-rank states in finite dimension, we prove that the canonical spectral implementations attain this minimum simultaneously for every operator-convex f. The reference then determines which quantum f-divergence is obtained: a flat reference gives the standard divergences, with the Nussbaum--Szko{\l}a distributions as optimal joint laws; either prescribed state as reference recovers Matsumoto's reverse tests and the maximal divergences; and power references give the geodesic family. In particular, the Umegaki and Belavkin--Staszewski relative entropies arise from the same classical variational principle under different choices of reference. Spectral optimality extends to processes containing a quantum channel; for channels with full-rank Choi operator, the minimum of the forward relative entropy agrees with a known average entropy production.

papers.title: Classification of the Karlsson-Szollosi Intersection
papers.summary: We show that $K_6^{(2)} \cap X_6^{(2)} = D_6^{(1)} \cup C_6^{(1)}$ up to standard Hadamard equivalence, where $C_6^{(1)}$ is a non-affine one-parameter family of complex Hadamard matrices. This demonstrates that the intersection of the two-parameter Hadamard families of Karlsson and Sz\"oll\H{o}si is strictly larger than the affine Di\c{t}\u{a} curve $D_6^{(1)}$. Our new parametrisation of the Sz\"oll\H{o}si family $X_6^{(2)}$ in Karlsson coordinates and our constructive classification of the Karlsson-Sz\"oll\H{o}si intersection shed light on the intersection of block-reducible forms and hypocycloid constraints. This may support the search for mutually unbiased bases in composite dimensions.

papers.title: Suppressing microwave crosstalk in superconducting quantum processors by designing parasitic drive capacitances
papers.summary: As superconducting quantum processors scale to large qubit counts, unwanted microwave drive crosstalk becomes an important source of coherent errors. Here, we investigate the role of parasitic coupling paths in the suppression of drive crosstalk in a processor with two fixed-frequency transmon qubits and a tunable coupler. To account for the many different coupling paths, we develop a detailed circuit model to capture the dependence of crosstalk on the coupler frequency. We experimentally demonstrate suppression of crosstalk, finding that the suppression does not originate solely from cancellation of the effective qubit-qubit coupling, but also is a result of interference between other coupling paths. Building on these insights, we show that drive crosstalk can be suppressed with the right choice of parasitic capacitances, which otherwise often are treated as unwanted design imperfections. Our results provide practical guidance for low-crosstalk device design of superconducting quantum processors and point toward a broader strategy in which parasitic coupling paths are engineered rather than simply minimized.

papers.title: Defining 2-group symmetries on lattices and extracting their anomalies
papers.summary: Ordinary $0$-form symmetries $G$ can mix with $1$-form symmetries $\Pi_2$ to form a $2$-group $\mathcal{G}$. We give a concrete lattice definition for a class of finite $2$-group symmetries in terms of local relations among symmetry operators. These relations identify the Postnikov class $[\rho]\in H^3(BG,\Pi_2)$ that characterizes the mixing. We develop a method to extract anomalies of these symmetries in one spatial dimension by restricting symmetry operations to an interval and comparing their composition near its endpoints. We also construct explicit qubit symmetry actions in $d=1,2,3$ spatial dimensions for a $2$-group with $G=\Pi_2=\mathbb{Z}_2$. These actions share the same nontrivial Postnikov class but include both anomaly-free and anomalous realizations. Their cohomological anomalies are classified by $H^{d+2}(B\mathcal G,U(1))$, which is $\mathbb{Z}_2$ for $d=1,2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ for $d=3$, and our constructions realize every class in these dimensions. Our results connect higher-group symmetry and its anomalies to concrete lattice operations, providing a microscopic framework for studying anomalous symmetries.

papers.title: Coherent errors, syndrome extraction and the Robustness of Magic in stabiliser codes
papers.summary: Coherent errors leave stabiliser-code-encoded magic states in superpositions of syndrome sectors. We ask how much magic these coherent errors add, and whether syndrome extraction depletes logical magic. Using Robustness of Magic, we show that, for a unitary error U on a correctable region which supports no stabiliser, the encoded state has the same robustness as the logical state plus one copy of the Choi state of U , in every stabiliser code encoding. Syndrome extraction removes this copy, returning the logical robustness. The removed magic is positive for every non-Clifford error: adding a non-stabiliser state to any state multiplies one plus the robustness by a (tightly- bounded) factor above one. The magic capacity of two-qubit gates Clifford-equivalent to diagonal or single-qubit gates is equal to their Choi-state robustness. We give a linear-algebraic test for when a Clifford error makes syndrome extraction measure a logical operator, and give magic lifetimes of stored single-qubit magic states under Pauli noise. Choosing the plane of the stored state extends these lifetimes about 1.5x on rotated surface codes under low code-capacity depolarising noise. We identify states and channels in odd-prime dimension for which Wigner negativity and robustness show equal lifetimes.

papers.title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
papers.summary: We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays. Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results: 1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill. 2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead. 3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{\Omega(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.

papers.title: Equilibria of Replicator Dynamics in Quantum Games
papers.summary: We analyse two-population replicator dynamics for asymmetric $2\times2$ games implemented with the Marinatto--Weber (MW) identity/bit-flip protocol. The effective payoff matrices are explicit convex combinations of relabelled classical matrices. Consequently, the dynamics depends on the initial state only through its four computational-basis probabilities: quantum phases, coherences and entanglement cannot be distinguished from classical shared randomness by the payoffs or trajectories in this protocol. At each pure-strategy vertex, the local eigenvalues equal the negatives of the corresponding unilateral payoff advantages; a vertex is asymptotically stable precisely when it is a strict Nash equilibrium, and thus an evolutionarily stable strategy pair in the asymmetric-game sense. Explicit examples show how varying the initial distribution changes which vertex is stable. When an isolated interior rest point exists, it is a saddle or a nonlinear centre according to the sign of the product of the classical payoff cross-differences; the sign cannot change under the MW mapping, although the point can enter or leave the strategy square. We give all four vertex-stability conditions explicitly in a single table, obtain a closed-form logistic solution on the parity-balanced hyperplane $S=0$, classify the degenerate cases, and give a first integral for the nondegenerate flow. All results concern the MW payoff protocol and its classically simulable family of bimatrix games; none constitutes evidence of an inherently quantum evolutionary advantage.

papers.title: IterTestQ: Assembly-Level, Cross-Platform Testing of Quantum Computing Platforms
papers.summary: Quantum computing platforms are susceptible to quantum-specific bugs, such as incorrectly ordering qubits or incorrectly implementing quantum abstractions. These bugs are difficult to detect and require specialized expertise. The field faces challenges due to a fragmented landscape of platforms and rapid development cycles that often prioritize new features over thorough testing, severely hindering the reliability of quantum software. To address these challenges, we present IterTestQ, a novel cross-platform testing approach for quantum computing platforms. The key technical contribution is our novel ITE process, which generates equivalent quantum programs by iteratively (I)mporting them into platform-specific representations, (T)ransforming the program via optimizations and gate conversions, and (E)xporting the program again. To transfer programs across platforms and test cross-platform consistency, IterTestQ leverages QASM, an assembly-level representation supported by most platforms. The approach uses a crash oracle to detect failures during cross-platform transformations and an equivalence oracle to validate the semantic consistency of the generated assembly programs, which are expected to be equivalent by construction. We evaluate IterTestQ on widely-used quantum computing platforms, including Qiskit, PennyLane, Pytket, BQSKit, and Cirq, revealing 23 bugs, 17 of which are already confirmed or fixed. Our results also demonstrate that IterTestQ complements existing quantum fuzzers (covering tens of thousands of otherwise uncovered lines), is efficient (with 0.00089 seconds per generated program), and that the ITE process is crucial for its effectiveness.

papers.title: Symmetry-Protected Topological Structures in Quantum Many-Body Scar Subspaces
papers.summary: We investigate how symmetry-associated topological properties, originally defined for ground states, can be consistently extended to dynamically isolated subspaces of quantum many-body systems. Focusing on quantum many-body scars (QMBS), we show that a scar subspace is invariant under the relevant symmetries, and it can support well-defined topological properties inherited from an underlying symmetry-protected topological (SPT) ground state, even though individual scar states need not themselves be symmetric. We refer to such structures as SPT-like scar subspaces, emphasizing that the topological properties are defined at the level of the symmetry-invariant subspace rather than on a state-by-state basis. As a concrete example, we analyze the spin-$1$ Affleck--Kennedy--Lieb--Tasaki (AKLT) model, where a restricted spectrum-generating algebra (rSGA) generates a tower of QMBS on top of a nontrivial SPT ground state admitting a matrix product state (MPS) representation. We demonstrate that the resulting symmetry-invariant scar subspace inherits well-defined topological characteristics, encoded in bond-space symmetry representations, expectation values of symmetry-twist operators, and long-range string order in the dilute regime. We further show that these features persist in a broader class of models, including deformations and higher-spin generalizations that preserve the relevant symmetries and admit nontrivial SPT ground states with MPS representations. Our results provide a general framework in which symmetry-associated topological properties, while inherited from the ground state, are consistently realized at the level of symmetry-invariant nonthermal subspaces. This perspective clarifies how topological structures can be meaningfully defined beyond individual eigenstates.

papers.title: Transversal gates for quantum CSS codes
papers.summary: In this paper, we focus on the problem of computing the set of diagonal transversal gates fixing a CSS code. We determine the logical actions of these gates and characterize the subgroups that induce tensor products of single-qubit logical gates and logical identities. We describe these groups through explicit linear equations given by componentwise products of basis vectors of the underlying classical codes, which is the key difference from previous approaches. We compute the complete set of diagonal transversal gates fixing the code, and of transversal logical gates, for any CSS code arising from monomial codes, a family that includes decreasing monomial codes and polar codes. As a consequence, we recover and extend some results in the literature on CSS-T codes, triorthogonal codes, and divisible codes. We also extend these results to diagonal gates acting transversally on several code blocks and use them to characterize addressable gates.
