papers.title: A Vibrated Compacting Granular System: A DEM Light Scattering Comparison
papers.summary: We perform Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations of granular particles (polystyrene spheres) vibrated inside a cubic container. The study investigates the evolution of the packing fraction with and without rotational friction at different shaking amplitudes. The mean-squared displacement (MSD) is used to analyze the particles' diffusive, subdiffusive, and superdiffusive behavior. By monitoring both the dynamics and density evolution, one can observe the system's glassification. The comparison with experiments shows that the MSDs from the simulations are significantly higher than the MSDs measured by Diffusing Wave Spectroscopy (DWS) \cite{kunzner2025dynamics}. Following our finding that the rotational MSD is of the same order of magnitude as the MSD measured in DWS experiments, we propose that the experimental signal is not dominated by translational motion but rather by rotational particle dynamics. This provides access to a relevant particle property that has previously been difficult to measure directly. Finally, we conclude that the system reaches a dynamically constrained state well before random close packing, with particle displacements already below the Lindemann length.

papers.title: Circular dichroism in second- and third-harmonic generation in the chiral topological semimetal CoSi
papers.summary: We theoretically investigate circular dichroism (CD) in second- and third-harmonic generation (SHG and THG) in the chiral topological semimetal CoSi. We demonstrate that both SHG and THG exhibit dichroic responses of order unity, while their robustness against spectral broadening is strikingly different. Specifically, while SHG-CD is strongly suppressed by dissipation, THG-CD remains robust over a wide frequency range. We show that this qualitative difference originates from the phase structure of the nonlinear current, where SHG-CD arises from subleading interference processes that are sensitive to dephasing, whereas THG-CD emerges already at the leading nonlinear order and is therefore protected against spectral broadening. As a result, THG-CD provides a robust probe of chirality encoded in nonequilibrium electronic dynamics. We further reveal non-monotonic frequency dependences and pronounced sensitivity of harmonic emission to the polarization state and crystallographic orientation of the driving field. Our results provide a representative example of robust nonlinear chiroptical responses in chiral topological semimetals and highlight the potential of high-harmonic spectroscopy as a probe of phase-resolved electronic dynamics.

papers.title: Probing bilayer topological order with layer-resolved transport
papers.summary: Shot noise has been used to measure fractional charges of anyons. The value of the charge imposes constraints on fractional statistics but does not determine it. This limitation is particularly important in multi-component systems. For example, the zero charge of neutral anyons in bilayer graphene gives no information about their statistics at all. We propose a way to shed light on the statistics of charged and neutral anyons in multi-component systems with layer-resolved or spin- resolved noise. The protocol applies to the fractional quantum spin Hall effect in MoTe$_2$, topological states in multi-layer graphene and bilayer GaAs, and to recently discovered fractional excitons in bilayer graphene. The approach relies on the relation between statistics and the distribution of the anyon charge over the components. Information about statistics can also be extracted from a simpler measurement of the layer-resolved electric current through a narrow constriction in a Hall bar even in the presence of long-range interactions and other non-universal effects.

papers.title: Nonintegral Flux Trapping in Frustrated Josephson Networks of Triplet Superconductors
papers.summary: In a Josephson junction network, anisotropic coupling between spin triplet pairing correlations can lead to frustrated $d$ vector textures that support spontaneous Josephson currents and nonintegral flux trapping. Such networks can appear in superconducting polycrystals, as well as single-crystal superconductors. In analogy to classical spin systems, in which the presence of geometric frustration and anisotropic superexchange can lead to nontrivial spin textures, Josephson networks with anisotropic Josephson couplings cannot simultaneously optimize their $\mathrm{U}(1)$ superconducting phase differences and relative $d$ vector orientations. The internal pairing structure of Cooper pairs twists as they tunnel across the Josephson junction, and the $d$ vector texture enters as an emergent geometric phase which can spontaneously trap fractional flux. For real-valued Josephson couplings between unitary $d$ vectors, the emergent geometric phase reduces to a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ structure, allowing for spontaneous $\pi$-flux trapping above a critical antisymmetric coupling, distinct from usual half-quantum vortices. Further, we demonstrate a continuously tunable nonintegral flux for complex Josephson couplings. The results of this work reveal new routes to engineer frustrated Josephson networks from the interplay of magnetic textures and spin triplet superconducting pairing order.

papers.title: Spatial statistics for screening molecular structures
papers.summary: The dominant paradigm in computational materials discovery relies on heavily parameterized deep architectures, including message-passing graph networks and equivariant models, that require millions of DFT-labeled training structures and produce non-convex latent representations that complicate continuous optimization for inverse design. These architectures are impractical in data-scarce regimes, which is the typical case in molecular screening, and exhibit well-documented limitations in capturing chemically disordered configurations and chiral geometries. This review presents feature engineering based on spatial statistics as a physically rigorous and immediately deployable alternative. Molecular structures are encoded as voxelized scalar fields, and two-point auto- and cross-correlations are evaluated deterministically via Fast Fourier Transforms, explicitly transferring the burden of spatial pattern recognition from the learning algorithm to a closed-form, physics-informed operation. Principal component analysis of the resulting correlation maps yields low-dimensional, strictly convex representations that support lean neural networks (<100k trainable parameters) and non-parametric surrogate models, achieving sub-2% prediction error with as few as 10 training samples. Demonstrated across periodic crystals, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys, and non-periodic organic molecules, this framework enables Bayesian active learning and zero-shot extrapolation on commodity hardware, which current large-scale architectures cannot replicate at equivalent data budgets.

papers.title: Band Structure and topology of a periodically deformed Kitaev honeycomb model
papers.summary: Motivated by the growing interest in spin liquids and topological phases, as well as the rise of deformation engineering, we study the combined effects of deformation and magnetic fields on the honeycomb Kitaev model. The Kitaev model, as one of the prototypical and exactly solvable spin liquid-hosting models, serves as a simple platform that demonstrates the rich physics one can expect at the intersection of deformation physics and quantum spin liquids. Our work builds on a simplified solution to the undeformed base model that we present. This simplified solution allows for a straightforward extension of our analysis to the deformed case. After incorporating periodic deformations into the Kitaev model (chosen for its similarity to moir\'e physics), we investigate the effects of a hexagonally symmetric deformation on the band structure. We find that deformation leads to a smaller Brillouin zone with new band gaps at the edges, indicating the potential for topological transitions. Finally, we introduce a magnetic field to break time-reversal symmetry and thereby allow for non-trivial topology. We find that, under specific parameter conditions, the magnetic field leads to multiple band-gap closings and openings. An investigation into topological properties reveals nontrivial Chern numbers and a plethora of topological transitions. The resulting nontrivial band topology may motivate future investigations of thermal Hall or related transverse responses, which are not calculated here. We also propose a bulk-measurement approach to the Chern numbers and a possible path to their physical realization. Most importantly, our results demonstrate the rich phenomenology that can arise from the interplay between deformation and spin-liquid physics.

papers.title: First-Principles Study of Fe Adsorption and Its Effects on the Mechanical and Electrical Properties of Monolayer and Bilayer Biphenylene Networks
papers.summary: Biphenylene network (BPN), a two-dimensional carbon allotrope, has attracted interest for its potential applications. Here, we systematically investigate Fe adsorption on monolayer and bilayer BPN using first-principles calculations, focusing on structural stability, mechanical properties, and electronic transport. On monolayer BPN, the average Fe adsorption energy generally becomes more negative with increasing Fe coverage, accompanied by nonmonotonic variations and increasingly pronounced Fe aggregation, eventually favoring three-dimensional growth. In bilayer BPN, the interlayer four-membered ring center is the most favorable adsorption site, with a single-Fe adsorption energy of -4.3 eV. Both pristine monolayer and bilayer BPN exhibit high in-plane Young's and shear moduli. Fe adsorption induces nonmonotonic changes in the in-plane stiffness of monolayer BPN, without systematic enhancement. In contrast, interlayer Fe incorporation dramatically enhances the out-of-plane stiffness of bilayer BPN. The effective out-of-plane elastic constant C33 increases from 24.59 GPa in pristine bilayer BPN to 515.63 GPa at an Fe/C ratio of 25%. Furthermore, the transport calculations reveal pronounced in-plane conductivity anisotropy, with substantially different conductivity values normalized by the relaxation time ({\sigma}/{\tau}) along the two crystallographic directions.

papers.title: Multipolar exchange in a many-body homonuclear mixture of atoms in different internal states
papers.summary: We develop a general method for constructing the many-body Hamiltonian of pairwise interactions describing homonuclear mixtures of atoms occupying states with different total angular momenta or other quantum numbers. This Hamiltonian explicitly accounts for isotropic interactions governed by low-energy s-wave scattering. The advantage of the irreducible spherical tensor operator formalism is demonstrated: these operators give the Hamiltonian an explicit physical structure, account for all scattering channels, and include multipolar exchange interactions. The latter correspond to the exchange of both angular-momentum projections and the total angular momentum. Particular realizations of the general Hamiltonian, widely used in the physics of ultracold gases, are also analyzed. The resulting Hamiltonian provides a universal framework for investigating a broad range of quantum many-body phenomena in bosonic and fermionic atomic gases.

papers.title: Application and Performance Assessment of Annealing Methods for Electrostatic-Energy-Based Configuration Search in Mixed Crystals
papers.summary: In first-principles design of solid solutions and disordered materials, exhaustive evaluation of all possible substitutional configurations is often impractical because the number of site occupations increases exponentially. Here, we develop a framework for pre-screening mixed-crystal configurations using annealing methods, where the Ewald electrostatic energy is used as the objective function. Substitutional occupations are represented by binary variables, allowing the Ewald energy to be mapped onto an Ising-type Hamiltonian and the search for low-energy configurations to be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem. We implement this formulation using simulated annealing (SA) and quantum annealing (QA), and benchmark their performance against exhaustive search. For the small-scale system CaYAlO$_4$, SA achieved a speed-up of about 30 times, while QA achieved a speed-up of more than 100 times; both methods identified all lowest-energy configurations. For the medium-scale system $\beta$-KSbF$_4$ and the large-scale Ba-doped SiAlON system, SA achieved speed-ups of about 200--300 times while stably identifying the lowest-energy structures. In contrast, QA showed limited speed-up for the medium-scale $\beta$-KSbF$_4$ system and missed some low-energy configurations, likely due to chain breaks. These results indicate that, among the approaches examined here, SA showed comparatively robust performance for Ewald-energy-based configuration search in mixed crystals. The proposed formulation can be implemented using publicly available libraries and provides a practical route for accelerating candidate-structure generation before first-principles calculations.

papers.title: Magnon bandstructure and topology in a periodically deformed Kagome lattice with DM interaction
papers.summary: We study the band structure and topology of magnons for a Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction on a deformed Kagome lattice. For simplicity, we focus on a periodically deformed lattice with hexagonal symmetry and an enlarged unit cell. This enlarged unit cell gives rise to a more complex band structure than in the undeformed case. Analyzing band topology, there is a distinction between the topologically trivial case with anti-ferromagnetic coupling and the topologically non-trivial case with ferromagnetic coupling. In the anti-ferromagnetic case, a spin-space symmetry, also present in the classical ground state, enforces these topologically trivial states. In the ferromagnetic case, this symmetry is spontaneously broken by the classical ground state. Consequently, the band structure also hosts numerous topological features. Specifically, we observe many topological transitions and bands with Chern numbers ranging from $+2$ to $-2$, which makes the system richer than in the undeformed case. This emergent topological structure demonstrates that deformed magnets can host new and exciting physics.

papers.title: Same worst case, different risk: how transient response shapes failure probability
papers.summary: The smallest disturbance that can push a dynamical system into failure is a standard measure of stability, but it does not determine how likely failure is under randomly directed disturbances of a given size. The geometry of the transient response connects the two. In the linearized dynamics, each failure boundary and each time after the disturbance define a response vector along the most damaging disturbance. The convex hull of these vectors, the response hull, determines the linear failure-probability curve through its support function. The longest vector sets the worst-case threshold. The mean and spread of the support function set where the curve rises and how steeply, but the mean does not rank systems by risk in general. Under mild regularity conditions, an exact linear-response relation shows how a parameter change shifts the disturbance size at which a given fraction fails: through the mean susceptibility of the directions on that threshold. For weakly damped oscillators, the susceptibility to damping is approximately proportional to the time of a direction's dominant response. Damping thus acts mainly on late failure routes rather than on the early one that sets the worst case, changing the failure probability substantially while barely moving the worst-case threshold. At fixed power imbalance, lowering the inertia instead nearly rescales the hull, moving worst case and risk together. In benchmark power-grid models, the linear predictions agree closely with nonlinear simulations. Strong nonlinear coupling, invisible to linear response, can break this picture; we show how it enters at second order.

papers.title: Controllable Quantum Spin Hall Phases in Bi$_2$Te$_3$-Family van der Waals Heterobilayers
papers.summary: The tunability and control of topological edge/surface states are crucial for the development of new device applications. In this work, by combining first-principles calculations and Wannier-based tight-binding methods, we show the emergence of quantum spin Hall phases in van der Waals heterostructures formed by stacking two trivial quintuple layers from the Bi$_2$Te$_3$ family. We demonstrate the tunability of the edge states under interlayer strain and external electric field effects, suggesting the possibility of switching topological edge states on/off by external control. Additionally, the quantum spin Hall edge channels remain robust against interlayer twist, highlighting their stability against external perturbations. Our results provide a new way to create and manipulate two-dimensional topological phases in systems based on Bi$_2$Te$_3$ family, which can be valuable for practical applications, such as topological field effect transistors and spintronic devices.

papers.title: Helical Domain-Wall-Ring Networks Reshape Superconducting Correlations
papers.summary: Extended domain-wall networks that emerge in moir\'e materials provide a distinct platform for quasi-one-dimensional electronic states. However, the interaction-driven orders in confined networks remain largely unexplored. Here, we discuss superconducting (SC) correlations in interacting helical domain-wall-ring networks in the closed topological domains formed within the moir\'e patterns of an underlying twisted bilayer honeycomb lattice. We first analyze the system within the framework of an infinite-size theory and show that inter-ring SC-pair tunneling is renormalization-group relevant in an appropriate interaction regime, favoring enhanced SC correlations through inter-ring phase locking. To address finite-size effects resulting from the ring-network geometry, we present a self-consistent variational approach. Our analysis shows that even in the regime where the infinite-size theory predicts strongly coupled pair tunneling, the induced phase-locking scale remains strongly suppressed. In contrast, the SC scaling dimension is governed mainly by density-density interactions and ring geometry, decreasing modestly with decreasing twist angle while remaining insensitive to the pair-tunneling strength. This discrepancy demonstrates that ring networks cannot generally be understood as simple finite-size truncations of their infinite-size counterparts but can exhibit qualitatively distinct collective behavior. Our study highlights how the interplay of confinement effects and ring-network geometry can reshape SC correlations.

papers.title: Quantum phase fluctuations quench chiral superconductivity in twisted overdoped cuprate bilayers
papers.summary: Twisted cuprate bilayers have been proposed to host chiral superconductivity at temperatures comparable to their large pairing scale, yet experimental signatures of broken time-reversal symmetry remain unclear. We show that quantum phase fluctuations strongly suppress chiral order in twisted overdoped cuprate bilayers despite robust intralayer pairing. At a $45^\circ$ twist, we analytically demonstrate that the chiral transition temperature obeys $T_\chi\propto t^4$ when the single-electron interlayer tunneling amplitude $t$ is weak. This collapse originates from competition between the small Josephson energy scale supporting chirality and the temperature-dependent collective zero-point energy. Chirality consequently survives only in a narrow angular window at ultralow temperatures, with relative-phase plasma softening above the chiral transition. A distinct transport signature arising from the quantum phase fluctuations is a pronounced low-temperature enhancement of the critical current near a magic angle. These findings separate pairing and chiral ordering scales and offer a possible explanation for the difficulty of observing robust chiral superconductivity in twisted cuprates.

papers.title: Modification of Damon-Eshbach magnetostatic mode spectra in ferromagnet/paramagnet bilayer
papers.summary: Using the magnetostatic approximation, we calculate the spectra of bulk and surface spin waves in an in-plane magnetized ferromagnet/paramagnet bilayer. Due to the dipolar coupling between the layers, the paramagnet becomes polarized, which in turn modifies the spectrum of the Damon-Eshbach magnetostatic modes. We assume that the paramagnet is characterized by a magnetic susceptibility, $\chi \propto 1/(T-T_C)$, which reaches large values when the system temperature $T$ is close to the Curie temperature $T_C$. We find the conditions under which surface spin waves become unidirectional, i.e., capable of carrying energy in only one direction, and determine the magnitude of their frequency nonreciprocity. We demonstrate the possibility of switching the unidirectional wave regime on and off by varying the external magnetic field or temperature, making the ferromagnet/paramagnet system an attractive platform for tunable magnonic logic devices.

papers.title: Unconventional Mixed-Parity Magnetism in Rare-Earth Tetraborides
papers.summary: Altermagnetism has advanced the study of compensated magnets by revealing non-relativistic spin splitting, traditionally classified into strictly even- or odd-parity spin textures. Here, we establish component-resolved mixed-parity spin splitting in a fully three-dimensional compensated magnet and identify its microscopic origin. Using first-principles calculations, tight-binding and $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{p}$ models, along with spin-group symmetry analysis, we demonstrate that the non-coplanar ground state of $\mathrm{TbB}_4$ enforces odd-parity $p$- and $f$-wave-like textures for the in-plane spin components while the out-of-plane component retains an even-parity $d$-wave altermagnetic character. Crucially, the $p$-wave texture is driven not by relativistic spin-orbit coupling but by a staggered emergent flux arising from the scalar spin chirality of the non-coplanar order. This mixed-parity structure dictates distinct transport fingerprints, including bulk non-relativistic Edelstein and spin Hall responses that respond characteristically to reversal of the chirality domains. Spin-orbit coupling additionally enables a Berry curvature dipole. These results establish the rare-earth tetraborides as a robust platform for engineering complex spin-charge conversion phenomena.

papers.title: Compatibility of Martensitic Microstructures in Polycrystals
papers.summary: The paper studies martensitic microstructures in polycrystals, focussing on their compatibility across grain boundaries. After a reduction to the case of a planar grain boundary, the case when the grain boundary separates two constant gradients of zero energy is considered. It is shown that for cubic-to tetragonal transformations such a configuration can occur when the relative grain rotation is not in the cubic group. Then the case when the grain boundary separates two simple laminates of zero energy is considered, it being shown using a computer-assisted symbolic calculation that in the cubic-to-tetragonal case compatibility is only possible for a closed set of measure zero in the manifold of grain boundary normals and relative grain rotations, and that a similar slightly weaker result holds for cubic-to-orthorhombic transformations. The results suggest why higher-order laminates are often observed for such transformations. The Taylor set of deformation gradients is defined and studied, this set having the property that any deformation whose gradient belongs to it corresponds to a zero-energy microstructure for the polycrystal independent of grain geometry and grain rotations. New upper bounds for the Taylor set are proved for cubic-to-tetragonal and cubic-to-orthorhombic transformations, generalizing those of Bhattacharya and Kohn using the geometrically linearized theory. We give a simple proof of a related result of Peigney characterizing the positive diagonal matrices in the quasiconvex hull of the energy wells for cubic-to-tetragonal transformations.

papers.title: Dipolar mixtures in checker-board optical bilayers
papers.summary: Ultra-cold dipolar mixtures in component-dependent optical potentials constitute an interesting platform for the study of the interplay between intra- and inter-component anisotropic long-range interactions. papers.title: Particle-scale structure of granular suspensions
papers.summary: Granular suspensions are intrinsically nonequilibrium systems in which dissipative grain-grain collisions coexist with solvent-induced forcing. We study the particle-scale structure of a granular suspension modeled by smooth inelastic hard spheres immersed in a thermal bath and compare Langevin-dynamics simulation results for the radial distribution function $g(r)$ and the static structure factor $S(q)$ with predictions of an equilibrium-inspired rational function approximation (RFA). The equilibrium hard-sphere RFA is supplied with nonequilibrium input for the contact value and a reduced isothermal-compressibility-like quantity, yielding analytical expressions for $g(r)$ in Laplace space and for $S(q)$. We find that the RFA gives a very good description of the short- and intermediate-range structure of the suspension over a broad range of densities, drag coefficients, and inelasticities. It reproduces $g(r)$ substantially better than the Percus-Yevick approximation in inelastic states, especially near contact, and gives a good account of $S(q)$ except at the smallest wave numbers. There, simulations show a drag-dependent enhancement over the RFA prediction, indicating additional long-wavelength nonequilibrium correlations beyond the present equilibrium-like description. These results show that an equilibrium-based hard-sphere approach provides an accurate description of the particle-scale structure of the present Langevin model with inelastic hard spheres (except in the smallest-$q$ region), and suggest that similar equilibrium-inspired approaches may also be useful for related nonequilibrium hard-sphere suspension models, including multicomponent systems.

papers.title: Differentiable Inverse Design of Two-Body Interactions for the Moore-Read State
papers.summary: Designing interactions that stabilize target quantum states is a central challenge in strongly correlated physics. For fractional quantum Hall states, identifying suitable two-body interactions remains difficult even when a target wave function is known. Here we implement a differentiable inverse-design approach that combines automatic differentiation with exact diagonalization to optimize two-body interactions, using the Moore--Read Pfaffian state as a benchmark. The optimized ground states achieve overlaps exceeding 99\% with the target for systems containing up to 12 electrons. Excitation and entanglement spectra provide complementary finite-size diagnostics. A common exponential pseudopotential profile retains an overlap of 91.1\% at 14 electrons without further optimization, supporting its transferability beyond the optimization sizes. These results demonstrate the approach on a non-Abelian quantum Hall benchmark and motivate its application to other numerically accessible trial states for which suitable approximate parent Hamiltonians remain unknown.

papers.title: Theory of phonon-magnon hybridization and angular momentum in CrI$_3$ and CrBr$_3$
papers.summary: In magnetic materials angular momentum can be mediated by different carriers, including electrons, magnons, and phonons. The magnons can interact with circularly polarized phonons which are close in energy, provided specific symmetry conditions are met. If the interaction is strong enough the phonons and magnons shift in frequency and start to mix to form hybrid magneto-elastic quasi-particles. In this paper, we develop a constrained Hamiltonian framework which incorporates hybrid stiffness matrices and Berry curvatures. We quantify the degree of hybridization between phonons and magnons (up to 8% in CrI$_3$ and 25% in CrBr$_3$) using a decomposition of the total energy, which is a generalization of the norm decomposition for atomic contributions to phonons used in the literature. We also explore how the total angular momentum is conserved but shared between the phononic and magnonic subsystems upon hybridization.

papers.title: Fluctuation electrodynamics of quantum capacitance in electron bilayers
papers.summary: Capacitance provides a thermodynamic probe of interacting electrons. It characterizes the energy cost of transferring charge between conductors, which, in low-dimensional systems, is governed by exchange and correlation effects in addition to electrostatic contributions. We develop a theory of the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells as well as monolayer and bilayer graphene devices, focusing on the contribution generated by interlayer correlations. Within a functional-integral formulation we show that the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy is, at the level of ring diagrams, exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for the van der Waals energy of two conducting sheets, with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer correction to the inverse capacitance is the second density derivative of this energy: a Casimir compressibility. The zero-point fluctuations that generate Casimir forces between mirrors are here the coupled plasmons of the bilayer, and their contribution to the capacitance is obtained in closed form; its sign shows that interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis gives the high-density limit in terms of universal functions. For graphene we find that monolayers behave like the electron gas, while bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and, within the two-band model, can even reverse its sign in the experimentally relevant range of separations. We delineate the limits of the theory, identifying the dilute Wigner-crystal regime and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where the capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing.

papers.title: Bulk-Boundary Correspondence in Semi-Infinite Chains from Sublattice Zeros
papers.summary: We provide an alternative derivation of the bulk-boundary correspondence for semi-infinite chains. To describe edge states, we analytically continue the usual Bloch Hamiltonian to complex wave vectors k. To start, we note that the zeros of a Bloch wavefunction are related to edge states, at least in systems with nearest-neighbour hoppings. We show that an analytically continued Bloch Hamiltonian with chiral symmetry has exceptional points, where two different states coalesce. These special points are related to the adiabatic protection of edge states. We derive a winding number that counts the exceptional states which, together with the boundary conditions, give a lower bound on the number of edge states protected by chiral symmetry. This bound is saturated in the models we consider.

papers.title: Transport coefficients in hard-sphere fluids: thermodynamic versus kinetic descriptions
papers.summary: A thermodynamic theory for transport coefficients in hard-sphere fluids is developed from a general expression for the Onsager matrix. The theory predicts the ratio $\sigma/\sigma_{\rm id}$, where $\sigma$ is a transport coefficient and $\sigma_{\rm id}$ denotes its dilute-gas value. This ratio depends exclusively on equilibrium thermodynamic properties and can therefore be computed directly from the equation of state. Compact expressions are obtained for the thermal conductivity, viscosity, and self-diffusion coefficient. These expressions agree closely with simulation data at low and intermediate densities and remain useful across the fluid range, although deviations increase near freezing, particularly for viscosity. The self-diffusion prediction substantially improves upon Enskog theory. These results support a thermodynamic description of transport coefficients relative to their dilute-gas values.

papers.title: Thermal Hall tomography of superconducting topology in rhombohedral graphene
papers.summary: Chiral superconductors should carry Majorana modes along their edges, yet three decades of work on candidate materials have not measured the integer that counts them. Rhombohedral graphene offers a new route, because its superconductivity coexists with magnetic domains that can be imaged and rewritten. Here we show how heat transport can read this integer and test it against the domain pattern. Warping and finite pair momentum can close the excitation gap while the band Chern number stays fixed. An exact two-band thermal kernel shows how quantization is then lost and bounds the plateau error when the gap survives. Real-space calculations with disorder show that the integer survives disorder several times larger than the gap, because a mobility gap remains. Bogoliubov pockets instead turn the bulk into a heat conductor, and disorder does not restore quantization. Time-reversed domains should show opposite plateaux, and with ideal contacts a wall between them should carry twice either plateau. In microscopic calculations, a written wall carries this number of Majorana channels even when its core is metallic. Writing, moving and erasing such walls would test superconducting topology, its link to magnetism, and protected heat flow in one device.

papers.title: Benchmarking the flow of epithelial cell monolayer with self-aligning deformable active membranes
papers.summary: Collective cell migration emerges from the interplay between motility, deformability and mechanical interactions, yet incorporating these ingredients into computationally efficient tissue models remains challenging. Here, we benchmark self-aligning deformable active membranes in a confined-flow geometry that mimics epithelial monolayer migration around a circular obstacle. In this model, cells are represented as deformable, adhesive membranes whose self-propulsion direction relaxes towards their velocity. By systematically varying the self-alignment timescale, cell-cell adhesion and inlet forcing, we characterize the resulting flows through collective alignment, relative density, neighbor rearrangements and spatial velocity fields. The model captures a broad spectrum of tissue behaviors, ranging from disordered, liquid-like flows to highly aligned, solid-like states. Compared with a related multiparticle model, self-aligning active membranes achieve stronger collective alignment, exhibit a more systematic density response and access states closer to both limits of the solid-liquid spectrum. We further show that increasing the target shape index promotes cell elongation and accelerates tissue flow, directly linking cell-scale deformability to tissue-scale transport. Finally, we compare simulated velocity profiles with experimental measurements from in vitro migrating MDCK epithelial cell monolayers and find qualitative agreement across multiple horizontal and vertical transects around the obstacle. These results establish self-aligning deformable active membranes as a versatile framework for connecting cell mechanics, shape adaptation and self-alignment to collective tissue migration in confined geometries.

papers.title: Automated Analysis to Reveal Grain Boundary Phase Microstructures
papers.summary: We develop a method for analyzing grain boundary (GB) microstructures that identifies distinct interfacial phases and the dislocation line defects separating them. Similar to bulk materials, GBs can adopt multiple distinct interfacial phases and undergo first-order phase transitions. When these phases coexist, their spatial arrangement and phase junctions constitute a GB microstructure, characterized by variations in excess properties and line defects with associated dislocation content. Despite this intrinsic heterogeneity, our ability to quantitatively characterize GB microstructures remains limited, as it requires identification of individual GB phases, phase-resolved excess properties, and the Burgers content of phase junctions, capabilities not available in existing automated methods. Here, we present an automated tool that performs interfacial microstructure mapping for planar coincidence site lattice GBs. The method identifies the spatial distribution of GB phases, quantifies phase-specific excess properties, and estimates the Burgers content of GB phase junctions. We demonstrate the approach using three representative cases: (i) quantification of mass transport during diffusion-limited GB phase transformations; (ii) identification of structurally indistinguishable phases formed by vacancy and interstitial loops; and (iii) characterization of GB microstructures containing phase nuclei. More broadly, this framework enables quantitative studies of GB evolution processes, including spinodal decomposition and coarsening with direct implications for GB deformation, creep, and migration.

papers.title: Irreversibility of many-body harmonic oscillators characterized by generalized Husimi's adiabaticity parameter
papers.summary: In a classical paper [K. Husimi, Prog. Theor. Phys. 9, 381 (1953)], Husimi showed that, for a single harmonic oscillator with a time-dependent angular frequency and initial conditions sampled from an equilibrium distribution, the averaged energy cannot decrease after a cyclic operation. This irreversibility is quantified by Husimi's adiabaticity parameter constituted with adiabatic invariants. In this work, we generalize Husimi's framework to a many-body system of one-dimensional harmonic oscillators coupled on an arbitrary connected network, with all spring constants sharing a common time dependence. For a system attached to a fixed wall, the dynamics can be decomposed into independent normal modes by transforming to mass-weighted coordinates and diagonalizing the resulting positive definite matrix, with each mode characterized by its own Husimi's adiabaticity parameter. By defining the generalized Husimi's adiabaticity parameter as their arithmetic mean, we derive the exact time evolution of the averaged energy and establish its non-decrease under cyclic operations. Numerical simulations confirm these results for both a uniform nearest-neighbor chain and a heterogeneous network.

papers.title: Quantifying translational and bond-orientational order metrics in hyperuniform and nonhyperuniform many-particle systems
papers.summary: Quantifying the degree of order/disorder in many-particle systems remains an outstanding problem in physics, materials science, and mathematics. To this end, we consider the translational order metric $\tau_T$, defined as the squared $L^2$ norm of the total correlation function $h(\mathbf{r})$, and introduce its bond-orientational analogue $\tau_O$, defined from the weighted total correlation function $h_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{r})$ using local orientational weights (S. Torquato et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 011042 (2026)). The pair $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ places both forms of order on a common two-point statistical footing. We compute both metrics for two nonhyperuniform sphere-packing models in 2D and 3D as functions of packing fraction $\phi$: 1) equilibrium hard particles and 2) nonequilibrium random sequential addition (RSA) packings. For the nonhyperuniform systems, bond-orientational order remains subdominant along the equilibrium-fluid and RSA configurations; however, its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases near the upper end of the equilibrium-fluid branches, much more strongly in 2D than in 3D, and the two metrics become comparable along the sampled crystal branches. At common packing fractions, equilibrium fluids and RSA packings trace distinct $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ trajectories, revealing preparation-dependent differences in structural order. As a representative hyperuniform family, we study 2D disordered stealthy hyperuniform (SHU) ground states for $0<\chi<1/2$, where $\chi$ is the stealthiness parameter. Within the disordered SHU phase, bond-orientational order remains subdominant, but its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases toward the disorder-to-order threshold. In all three models, $\tau_T$ and $\tau_O$ are positively correlated beyond the Poisson-reference regime: $\tau_O$ increases monotonically with $\tau_T$ across the sampled state points.

papers.title: One-Dimensional Type-IV Collinear Magnetism
papers.summary: Two-dimensional type-IV collinear magnets combine nonrelativistic spin degeneracy with spin-orbit-coupling-enabled magnetic responses. Here we establish a one-dimensional counterpart through altermagnetic confinement. A Lieb-based construction connects three-dimensional altermagnets to two-dimensional type-IV magnets and extends the same principle to one-dimensional ribbons. In a symmetric $[110]$ ribbon, a sublattice-exchange operation preserves the longitudinal momentum and enforces nonrelativistic spin degeneracy. {Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) ties spin to the lattice, so the N\'eel orientation determines whether the remaining symmetries protect the doublets or allow them to split.} First-principles-derived Wannier calculations for Ta$_2$TeSeO ribbons reveal spin-polarized propagating channels with an ideal right-moving-mode polarization of approximately $35\%$ at finite conductance for the parent easy-axis orientation $\mathbf N\parallel[100]$. Direct DFT calculations of Ta$_2$Te$_2$O ribbons resolve the contrast between spin-split $[100]$ and spin-degenerate $[001]$ SOC spectra. Assembling the same isolated Ta$_2$Te$_2$O ribbons into a transversely periodic array restores spin splitting without SOC. This conversion parallels the recovery of three-dimensional altermagnetism through suitable periodic stacking of two-dimensional type-IV magnets. One-dimensional type-IV magnetism thus provides a route to spin splitting through the interplay of antiferromagnetic order and SOC, distinct from conventional Rashba splitting driven by structural inversion asymmetry.

papers.title: Sub-kelvin cryogenic wafer probing verified by on-wafer primary Coulomb blockade thermometry
papers.summary: Scalable cryogenic wafer level testing is emerging as an essential tool for the development of quantum devices and cryogenic microelectronics, but the main motivation, the actual operational on-wafer temperature, remains largely unverified. In this work, utilizing a cryogenic wafer prober (CWP) enables wafer-scale electrical testing of Coulomb blockade thermometers (CBTs), while the CBTs simultaneously provide an independent static and dynamic assessment of the prober's thermal performance through primary and in situ calibrated secondary electron thermometry, realizing a reciprocal characterization approach. Using recently introduced scalable normal metal TiW-based CBTs, which require no superconductivity suppressing magnetic fields, we have measured on-wafer electron temperatures of 630-660 mK across a full 150 mm wafer, representing, to our knowledge, record-low electron temperatures measured in a CWP. These exceed the nominal 600 mK chuck setpoint by approximately 40 mK on average, demonstrating the necessity of direct on-wafer thermometry. Self-calibrated secondary CBT thermometry resolves the thermal transients caused by chuck movement and reveals a thermal settling time within 5 minutes after probe touch down. This reciprocal wafer-scale approach simultaneously evaluates the device under test and the thermal performance of the measurement environment, providing a practical methodology for scalable sub-kelvin characterization of quantum devices and cryogenic microelectronics.

papers.title: Spin splitting without symmetry: a nearly compensated ferrimagnet and the origin of altermagnetism
papers.summary: The spin splitting of collinear altermagnets is usually attributed to the crystal symmetry relating the opposite-spin sublattices --- a rotation or mirror in place of the translation or inversion of a conventional antiferromagnet. We show that this symmetry organizes the splitting but does not produce it; its origin is the anisotropic arrangement of the magnetic orbitals and their ligands, which also fixes the symmetry itself. Two results establish this. A triclinic ($P1$) \ce{Mn} oxide, a fully compensated ferrimagnet whose two inequivalent sublattices are related by no symmetry, is spin split throughout the Brillouin zone; repositioning the same ligands, atom for atom, to restore an inversion centre relating the two metal sites collapses the splitting to a residual two orders of magnitude smaller, so the splitting follows from the arrangement rather than the symmetry. Symmetry, we show formally, can only ever reverse or forbid a splitting that already exists: it cannot create one between sublattices an arrangement has left electronically identical, nor where the underlying orbitals carry no anisotropy to arrange in the first place. Organizing the analysis through an operation-resolved symmetry hierarchy and reading the crystal classes as a single axis, the enforced nodal planes fall from two to one to zero across the orthorhombic, monoclinic, and triclinic classes while the arrangement-generated splitting persists to the base. The altermagnet and the fully compensated ferrimagnet are thus the two ends of one axis --- the same splitting, organized by symmetry at one end and unorganized at the other --- and the search for compensated spin-split magnets is a search over orbital arrangements rather than symmetry labels.

papers.title: Geometry-Driven Suppression of Fermionic Pairing on a Spherical Surface
papers.summary: We investigate the ground-state properties of a two-component attractive Fermi gas confined to a spherical surface. In the strongly attractive regime, the system forms a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of tightly bound dimers, yielding a gap and chemical potential that approach flat-space results with leading-order geometric corrections. As the attraction decreases, the system crosses over into a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) regime, the sphere radius $R$ constrains the Cooper pair size and shell effects emerge. For closed shells, corresponding to magic particle numbers set by the single-particle spectrum, pairing is suppressed above the scattering length $a^*=4R$, whose value is universal in the spherical geometry in contrast with box-trapped fermionic gases. Our results highlight a fundamental interplay among geometry, quantum statistics, and interactions, motivating future experiments with shell-trapped ultracold fermions and inspiring geometry-controlled condensed matter devices.

papers.title: Hierarchical Fourier Phase Projection for Local Electronic Observables
papers.summary: We develop hierarchical Fourier phase projection (HPP) to evaluate electronic observables without explicitly constructing occupied eigenstates. Nested Fourier probes progressively cancel nearby cross terms, while exponential or algebraic density-matrix decay suppresses distant contributions. Refinement reuses all previous matrix-function responses to evaluate diverse electronic observables. Electron density and nonlocal forces illustrate diagonal extraction and off-diagonal contraction, respectively. A locality-based decay model fitted to changes across completed levels estimates residual errors from the unresolved pairs without additional matrix-function applications. Tests using fixed Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians for semiconductors, metals, and thermally perturbed silica cover different decay ranges and periodic cell geometries. About 90% of the assessed density and nonlocal force predictions lie within a factor of two of the reference errors. The probing requirements for a prescribed local accuracy show weak size dependence. This work thus provides a scalable framework linking electronic locality, observable accuracy, and computational effort in large-scale electronic-structure calculations.

papers.title: Anisotropic wavevector-dependent damping of thickness-quantized magnons
papers.summary: Magnon damping is a key factor governing spin-wave transport and nonlinear dynamics of multimode magnon systems. However, many descriptions rely on the assumption of an effective mode-independent parameter, which can mask wavelength-dependent relaxation processes that depend on propagation geometry and mode profile. The instability threshold exhibits a regular sawtooth dependence on the magnetic field, arising from switching between discrete thickness modes. Comparison with dipole--exchange theory reveals anisotropic wavevector-dependent damping that increases with mode number and depends differently on the in-plane and out-of-plane wavevector components.

papers.title: Time-temperature-composition equivalence of the glass transition in digitally mixed 3D-printed polymers
papers.summary: For more than seventy years, time-temperature equivalence (TTE) has enabled a few measurements to describe the linear viscoelasticity of polymers over many decades of frequency. Multimaterial 3D printing now combines elastomeric and glassy resins voxel by voxel into digitally mixed polymers. Composition shifts the glass transition along the frequency axis, as temperature does, but also broadens it and increases the rubbery plateau modulus. A translation, the only operation of TTE, cannot capture these changes. Here we establish a time-temperature-composition equivalence (TTCE) from dynamic mechanical measurements of five compositions of a printed family. A shift of the transition along the reduced-frequency axis, a stretch of its breadth and a normalization between its plateaus collapse the storage modulus onto one master curve. The collapse holds at every measured temperature, frequency and composition, through a single reduced variable. The position and breadth of the transition change linearly with the volume fraction of the glassy resin. The phase angle and the relaxation spectrum superpose with the same parameters, so the family shares one distribution of relaxation times. The resulting closed form gives the storage and loss moduli continuously in composition, temperature and frequency, and quantitatively predicts two further mixtures withheld from the calibration. The same shift, stretch and normalization also collapse published temperature sweeps of a patterned composite family of different resins, pointing to broader applicability. Composition thus joins temperature and frequency as a third variable of one equivalence, and the closed form can guide the design of graded and architected printed structures.

papers.title: Emergent Spinorial Structure in Mesoscopic Irreversible Thermodynamics
papers.summary: Can transport coefficients determine both the coherent evolution of a mesoscopic system and distances between its thermodynamic states? We establish this connection within a canonical operator framework. Thermodynamic coordinates and conjugate forces obey commutation relations governed by a reduced constant ${\kbar}_B$. Requiring coordinate evolution to reproduce self-adjoint flux observables fixes a compatible generator up to an additive multiplication operator, set to zero in the minimal realization. The resulting equation describes coherent mesoscopic amplitudes, with transport fixing its coefficients and the reduced constant setting the evolution scale. An exact first-order factorization gives a geometry through Connes' spectral-distance prescription, including for coordinate-dependent transport. The metric is twice the inverse of the symmetric transport matrix. Coordinate derivatives of the antisymmetric part can change the dynamics without changing distances. Published thermoelectric data illustrate the geometry. A separate quadratic entropy-production observable has adjacent entropy levels separated by the reduced constant under the stated canonical and finite-mode matching assumptions. This conditional prediction offers a possible experimental signature. The evolution is unitary; irreversible relaxation requires additional mechanisms, such as environmental coupling or coarse-graining.

papers.title: Transport Determines Spectral Distance in Mesoscopic Thermodynamics
papers.summary: We derive a distance between thermodynamic states from a positive Hermitian transport tensor within a mesoscopic canonical model. An exact first-order factorization of the evolution generator gives a commutator norm and the metric $G=2g$, where $g$ denotes the symmetric transport tensor. Gradients of the antisymmetric tensor can change the evolution, but they leave this distance unchanged. The construction allows coordinate-dependent coefficients. For constant Onsager coefficients, a Clifford representation gives the same metric. In a two-channel thermoelectric system, the ratio of normalized principal distances is $\sqrt{1+ZT}+\sqrt{ZT}$. Transport coupling thus fixes the anisotropy of this metric. The construction requires neither an independent metric nor a physical spin variable.

papers.title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2
papers.summary: Nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations of small-polaron hopping are demanding because nuclear motion is coupled to a self-consistent localized electronic state. Near the charge-transfer region, slow self-consistent-field convergence, localization switching, and competing electronic solutions complicate surrogate-assisted optimization. We develop a Gaussian-process-assisted NEB workflow for this regime and demonstrate electron small-polaron hopping in rutile TiO2 using spin-polarized density functional theory with a Hubbard U correction (DFT+U ) with SIESTA. A joint energy-force Gaussian process (GP) with a Mat\'ern covariance model advances the elastic band, while active-atom root-mean-square and maximum-atom displacement limits constrain surrogate motion relative to evaluated configurations. Reaching these limits triggers first-principles sampling without requiring full surrogate convergence. Three independently DFT-verified 96-atom [001] calculations using 11, 13, and 15 images and different surrogate settings and GP parameterizations yield barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, respectively, spanning 0.793 meV. In the 15-image calculation, repeated central-image sampling activates a separately calibrated local GP during surrogate optimization. Final full-band DFT verification gives a maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/{\AA}. A 324-atom calculation yields a lower barrier of 0.1302 eV, indicating supercell sensitivity and demonstrating feasibility at larger GP observation dimension. The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.

papers.title: Structural characterization of the rutile-GeO2/TiO2 (001) heterointerface
papers.summary: Rutile-GeO2 (r-GeO2) has emerged as a promising ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) semiconductor for future high-power device applications because of its favorable combination of physical and electrical properties. This study has used high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) to compare heterointerfaces between thin films of GeO2 grown by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition on closely-lattice-matched rutile TiO2 (r-TiO2) substrates at temperatures of 840{\deg} C and 925{\deg} C. Cross-sectional TEM observations reveal interfaces with two entirely different structures: an amorphous GeOx/r-TiO2 heterostructure with an abrupt, highly faceted and non-planar interface, or a fully epitaxial r-GeO2/r-TiO2 heterostructure characterized by a more wavy but often facetted interface. Structural analysis of the latter sample revealed a high density of strain-relieving interfacial dislocations, identified primarily as Lomer-type or 60{\deg}-type, that accommodated the ~4% lattice mismatch between the two materials, while chemical analysis showed very limited interfacial intermixing. Crystallographic analysis showed that the interface faceting was associated with rutile {101} facets, with characteristic facet angles of ~114{\deg}; these observations support thermally driven TiO2 (001) substrate faceting rather than an interface reconstruction resulting from GeO2 epitaxy. Overall, these findings provide useful insights into the mechanisms governing interface formation and strain relaxation in r-GeO2/r-TiO2 heterostructures and suggest that further refinement of growth conditions should enable improved epitaxial growth of r-GeO2 for future ultrawide-bandgap electronic device applications.

papers.title: Momentum-selective graphene spectroscopy of moir\'e excitons
papers.summary: Far-field photoluminescence probes only the light-cone corner of an exciton's momentum content, whereas energy transfer to nearby graphene integrates in-plane momenta up to the inverse spacer thickness $1/z$. For a WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer we build the transition polarization $\bm{P}_n(\qv)$ of each localized moir\'e exciton from the registry-dependent vector dipole texture and use each $\bm{P}_n$ for both baths. The two baths rank the states differently: the graphene-rate ratios differ from the optical ones, their ordering inverts with spacer thickness, and the distance exponents at $z=10$\,nm spread by more than two units. These ratios are independent of the transition-dipole prefactor. Within the $C_3$-symmetric leading-harmonic model the chiral $p_+$ and $d_-$ states are also dark at normal incidence yet transfer to graphene at rates comparable to the bright ground state. Their graphene rate depends on the sign of the texture phase, a quantity invisible in far-field emission, which we determine from first principles. In a device this prediction requires a splitting, larger than the symmetry-breaking mixing, that protects the chiral partners. Graphene proximity thus acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe of moir\'e excitons, and we propose its use as a practical spectroscopy.

papers.title: Simplified Parisi Ansatz III: Constructive Cavity Method and Ultrametricity
papers.summary: We present a physical explaination of the Constructive Cavity Method (CCM) for the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model, which identifies the decomposition of the cavity variables into layers with the random overlap structure of Aizenman--Sims--Starr. We describe the low-temperature excitations through a dilute gas of defects relative to the ground state. The sharing of these defects among the descendants and the renewal of the fluctuations along new branches produce the GREM structure and the ultrametricity of the overlaps. This mechanism is developed first with a finite number of defects and then extended to exponential populations of states. At fixed kernel, the Gaussian covariances of the fresh fields connect the complete cavity variables, including their common components, to the same hierarchy that determines the Gibbs masses. We also correct some ambiguities of earlier formulations.

papers.title: Temperature-dependent magnetic properties of the antiferromagnet Mn$_2$Au
papers.summary: Mn$_2$Au is one of the most promising materials for antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its high N\'eel temperature, moderate anisotropy, layered spin structure allowing current induced spin-orbit-torques, and ultrafast spin dynamics. Further understanding and control of the magnetic order in Mn$_2$Au for ultrafast spintronics applications via ultrashort electric/optical means requires accurate understanding of how its magnetic properties depend on temperature. Here we present atomistic spin dynamics simulations of the temperature-dependent macroscopic magnetic properties of Mn$_2$Au single crystals. We introduce a spin Hamiltonian based on previous ab initio calculations which produces temperature-dependent scaling of the anisotropy constants with magnetisation consistent with Zener-Akulov-Callen-Callen power laws. The calculated temperature dependence of exchange stiffness follows a scaling law with magnetisation of $m^{1.83}_e$ , and predicts a temperature-dependent domain wall width that agrees very well with direct simulation. Our model provides an understanding of temperature-dependent magnetic properties of Mn$_2$Au that enables large-scale simulation of the working conditions of spintronic devices.

papers.title: Large superconducting diode effect indicates nonuniform triplet pairing in UTe2
papers.summary: The superconducting diode effect (SDE) is characterized by unequal critical current magnitudes for opposite-polarity current flow, owing to broken spatial-inversion and time-reversal symmetries. For a superconducting pair wavefunction to spontaneously break inversion symmetry implies the formation of Cooper pairs with nonzero momentum, yielding a nonuniform superconducting state. For singlet superconductors, the formation of such a (FFLO) state has long been understood to provide an escape from high field Pauli pair-breaking -- how and why such an effect might occur for equal spin pairing is an open question. Here we report the observation of a large SDE in bulk specimens of the three-dimensional heavy-fermion triplet superconductor UTe$_2$, with a peak diode efficiency of 33% at the high magnetic field strength of 33.6 T, representing the highest-field observation of the SDE to date. Crucially, this nonreciprocal transport is strictly confined to a narrow field regime where superconductivity coexists with a field-induced spin-polarized state near a first-order metamagnetic phase boundary. The absence of the SDE away from this slender phase-intersection argues strongly against purely extrinsic vortex pinning asymmetries. Instead, our findings indicate spontaneous inversion symmetry breaking accompanied by finite-momentum Cooper pairing. We model this behavior using a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau theory, demonstrating that the intertwining of magnetic and triplet superconducting orders can stabilize an odd-parity FFLO state.

papers.title: Nano-Nb Superconducting 3D Josephson Junctions Arrays in Cu-Normal Matrix: Superconducting Phase Coherence and Quantum Fluctuations Properties
papers.summary: We investigate the superconducting behavior, phase coherence, and quantum fluctuation properties of three-dimensional arrays of nanometric Nb Josephson junctions embedded in a normal Cu matrix ($\text{Cu-}x\text{ wt}\%\text{Nb}$, $x = 3, 5, 15,$ and $20$), with emphasis on the $5$ and $15$ compositions. Magnetic properties were measured by dc magnetization as a function of temperature and magnetic field using a SQUID magnetometer and by ac susceptibility. Transport properties, including magnetoresistance, $V(I)$ curves, and the critical current $I_c(H,T)$, were measured at fields up to $90\text{ kOe}$. A micro-Hall sensor with ten transverse voltage bridges ($5.0 \times 0.2 \times 0.01\text{ }\mu\text{m}^3$) was used to calibrate the magnetic field actually applied to the sample. Magnetization and transport measurements reveal a double superconducting transition that depends on the applied field and current: $T_c(H)$, with $T_c(0) = 8.2\text{ K}$, is associated with the intragranular response of the Nb grains, whereas the lower $T_c(H)$ is associated with Josephson coupling between grains through the Cu matrix. The response combines that of bulk Nb with signatures of weakly coupled grains, consistent with a collection of superconducting grains embedded in a nonsuperconducting matrix. The characteristic fields $H_{c1} = 400.03\text{ Oe}$ and $H_{c2} = 15\text{ kOe}$ (grains), and $H_{c1j} = 99.93\text{ Oe}$ and $H_{c2j} = 199.25\text{ Oe}$ (intergranular coupling), were determined. The critical current $I_c(H,T)$ exhibits a central maximum at low fields, followed by a long tail and small oscillations with a period of $\Delta H \approx 24\text{ Oe}$, attributed to quantum interference between coupled grains. At higher fields, magnetic flux gradients destroy phase coherence and randomize the phase $\theta$ of the order parameter $\psi = |\psi|e^{i\theta}$, suppressing the oscillations.

papers.title: The Flexoelectric Twist: Persistence of Heavy Fermion Picture in Small-Angle Twisted Bilayer Graphene
papers.summary: Twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) near the first magic angle ($\theta\approx1.05^{\circ}$) hosts topological flat bands that provide a fertile ground for exploring strongly correlated phases. At smaller twist angles ($\theta<1^{\circ}$), lattice relaxation profoundly alters the moir\'e landscape. The extent to which moir\'e lattice reconstruction at different length scales affects the electronic structure through electro-mechanical coupling remains unresolved. Using scanning tunneling microscopy on small-angle TBG devices with different twist angles $\theta\approx0.3-0.7^{\circ}$, we observe a pronounced $dI/dV$ peak at the AA site of the moir\'e lattice on top of a spectrum that is asymmetric about the charge neutrality point; we visualize lattice reconstruction at moir\'e lattice length scales (20-45\,nm); and we detect a dilation of the atomic lattice at the AA sites at Angstrom length scale. We demonstrate that the inclusion of moir\'e lattice reconstruction supports compact localized heavy fermion $f-$states at AA sites whereas the inclusion of atomic lattice dilation generates a strong flexo-electric response that breaks particle-hole symmetry, pushing the $f$-states down in energy. Consequently, these heavy fermion states energetically coexist with itinerant $c$-electrons at the AB/BA sites. Our spatially resolved spectroscopic measurements visualize this coexistence, confirming the persistence of the heavy fermion model in the small-angle regime $\theta<1^{\circ}$. Our findings show that flexo-electric responses can realize qualitatively distinct electronic landscapes in moir\'e materials beyond the single-particle picture. Looking ahead, small-angle TBG could prove an ideal platform to explore the interacting large-$N$ Kondo lattice problem with high tunability of the $f-$occupation and $c-$density through twist-angle and electrostatic back gates, respectively.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Linear Response Theory for Nonautonomous Systems
papers.summary: Linear Response theory aims to predict how added forcing alters the statistical properties of a system. This has been predominantly studied for autonomous dynamical systems, yet many systems in the physical, natural, and social sciences are inherently nonautonomous. In such settings, one would like to understand how the system's time-dependent statistical properties change when additional infinitesimal forcings are applied. This question is of clear practical relevance, but from a rigorous mathematical viewpoint it has been addressed only for a few specific classes of systems and perturbations. Here we provide a rigorous linear response theory for a rather general class of deterministic and random nonautonomous systems satisfying a specific set of assumptions that are the counterpart of the standard assumptions used in the autonomous setting. A central ingredient is rapid loss of memory along the nonautonomous evolution. Our main strategy is to reformulate the sequential dynamics as a fixed-point problem for a global transfer operator acting on an extended sequence space of measures. This yields explicit and readily implementable causal response formulas for predicting the effect of small perturbations on time-dependent statistical states. We illustrate the theory on two representative classes: sequential compositions of expanding maps and sequential compositions of noisy random maps. We also establish linear response for reflected Euler-Maruyama discretizations of dissipative nonautonomous stochastic differential equations with nondegenerate additive Gaussian noise, on fixed compact domains. As a physical application, we study the response of a Ghil-Sellers climate energy balance model, discretized in latitude and time to a time-dependent perturbation of the greenhouse parameter.

papers.title: Fluctuations of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick free energy at critical temperature
papers.summary: We consider the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model at the critical inverse temperature $\beta = 1$ with zero external field. We prove that the free energy $F_N = F_{N,\beta=1}$ of this model has variance \[ \mathrm{Var}(F_N) = \frac16 \log N + O(1)\,, \] confirming a physics prediction of Aspelmeier \cite{aspelmeier2008free}, and that the centered and scaled $F_N$ satisfies a Gaussian CLT. We also identify the critical two-replica overlap scale, proving \[ \mathbb{E} \langle R_{1,2}^2\rangle \asymp N^{-2/3}\,, \] as conjectured by Talagrand \cite{talagrand2011mean2}, together with a uniform exponential moment bound for $N^{1/3} |R_{1,2}|$. The key input is a critical reweighted moment method, in the spirit of the ``small subgraph conditioning'' technique from probabilistic combinatorics, but capable of capturing diverging fluctuations. Through this reweighting, we relate the critical SK model to the BBP critical edge, which determines the overlap and fluctuation scales.

papers.title: Coarse-to-Fine Diffusion with Residual Prior for Low-Dose CT Denoising
papers.summary: Low-dose CT (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but often introduces severe noise and streak artifacts that obscure subtle anatomical structures. Existing diffusion-based denoising methods commonly rely on implicit assumptions about the noise distribution, which may not hold in practical LDCT scenarios and can degrade denoising performance. To address this limitation, we propose a Residual-Guided Diffusion framework that effectively incorporates an explicit difference prior to inform the diffusion process of noise distribution. The difference prior is computed as the residual between the LDCT image and a coarse clean estimate, constraining diffusion sampling to a plausible residual space. We further adopt a coarse-to-fine strategy in which a pre-trained RED-CNN provides the coarse estimate to anchor global anatomy, and the diffusion model refines the remaining details under the prior guidance. For efficiency, we employ accelerated sampling with 20 steps at inference. Experiments on three representative datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both quantitative and qualitative performance measures.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Airlight-Aligned Dual-Gain Recovery with Exact RGB Feasibility for Training-Free Single-Image Dehazing
papers.summary: The inverse atmospheric-scattering model amplifies transmission, airlight, and sensor-noise errors when a scalar gain $1/t$ is applied in dense haze. We introduce A$^2$CR, a training-free recovery operator that decomposes the airlight-centered RGB residual into components parallel and perpendicular to the airlight vector. Two gains are obtained from analytic quadratic risks containing transmission, airlight, and noise uncertainty. Each gain pair is constrained by the exact convex polygon induced by the six RGB-cube inequalities and gain bounds. An edge-aware joint total-variation problem is solved with a primal-dual algorithm and exact polygon projection. On a controlled DIODE RGB-D evaluation comprising 500 frames and 22,500 reproducible haze recipes, the full variant improves over scalar inversion by $2.951$ dB PSNR (95% bootstrap CI $[2.900,3.001]$), $0.191$ SSIM $[0.187,0.196]$, and $-0.978$ CIEDE2000 $[-1.074,-0.883]$, while eliminating post-recovery RGB violations. Results on four real paired datasets are mixed and were not blind: the method is strongest on Dense-Haze but does not dominate RFEP, DCP, and Haze-Lines elsewhere. We therefore claim an interpretable constrained recovery study, not state-of-the-art dehazing. Code, 64 executable numerical and regression tests, manifests, and statistical artifacts accompany the paper.

papers.title: Feedback Stability of Discrete-Time LTI Systems via Frequency-Wise Scaled Relative Graphs
papers.summary: This paper studies the stability of negative-feedback interconnections of proper, stable discrete-time multivariable linear time-invariant (LTI) systems using scaled relative graphs (SRGs). We propose a frequency-wise condition that compares the SRGs of the two subsystems'frequency-response matrices only at the same frequency along a feedback-scaling homotopy. We prove that this condition guarantees well-posedness along the homotopy and $\ell_2$-stability for both single-input single-output (SISO) and multi-input multi-output (MIMO) subsystems, without requiring the chord property or nonsingular frequency-response matrices. An equivalent form exchanges scaling and geometric inversion. We also derive an operator-level condition from the SRG closures of the convolution operators and show that it implies the frequency-wise condition. Numerical examples show that the operator-level condition is more conservative because it depends on intersections between responses at different frequencies.

papers.title: Short-Circuit Current Calculation in DC Shipboard Microgrid Using Operational Admittances
papers.summary: The increasing adoption of DC shipboard power systems is driven by the need to integrate energy storage systems seamlessly onboard. In this context, accurate calculation of short-circuit current transients is critical for sizing fast-acting protection devices. This paper proposes a methodology to calculate short-circuit current transients based on operational admittance modelling of network elements and power converters. The superposition principle is then applied to calculate current contributions and voltage time profiles. The methodology is validated with a detailed EMT model of a notional LVDC shipboard microgrid section consisting of an active front end, a bidirectional buck-boost converter and two special loads. Results demonstrate that the methodology accurately tracks nodal voltages and the fault current contributions dynamics up to the prospective fault current peak, thus providing a computationally efficient tool for fault analysis and protection coordination in LVDC microgrids.

papers.title: Dataset and Experimental Testbed for Deep Learning-Based Bluetooth Device Fingerprinting
papers.summary: AI-enabled wireless networks have emerged as vital components of future-generation wireless communication systems. Among various wireless architectures, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) networks have attracted significant research interest due to their widespread adoption and low cost. In these networks, deep learning (DL) models can be integrated directly into the physical-layer infrastructure to perform diverse tasks, including environment sensing, localization, radio frequency fingerprinting (RFFP), and signal denoising. While highly effective under their original training configurations, these DL models often fail significantly when deployed in unseen environments---such as different rooms, varying temperature conditions, or altered carrier frequencies. Addressing this limitation requires rigorous benchmarking of models and algorithms against unseen configurations to evaluate their generalization and robustness. To bridge this gap, this paper makes two key contributions: i) we introduce a comprehensive, large-scale wireless BLE dataset consisting of raw IQ transmissions from 31 distinct commercial devices captured across diverse days, locations, environments, temperatures, receiver hardware, and frequency channels; ii) we present a case study evaluating state-of-the-art techniques for domain-robust RFFP to advance real-world AI reliability.

papers.title: Wideband Channel Measurements in the Lower FR3 Band (6-12 GHz) for Industrial Environments
papers.summary: The upper mid-band, also known as Frequency Range 3 (FR3), spans 7.125-24.25 GHz and is a key candidate band for sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications. However, channel measurements in industrial environments remain scarce, and the 3GPP indoor-factory (InF) channel model, developed for omnidirectional antennas, has yet to be validated across the FR3 band. This paper presents a wideband channel measurement campaign in an industrial production hall, covering 135 line-of-sight (LOS) positions at 1-18 m and 30 non-line-of-sight (NLOS) positions behind an industrial robot at 2.5-16.5 m across 6-12 GHz. In LOS, the path-loss exponent ranged from 1.87 to 2.12, and the close-in fits agreed with the 3GPP InF-LOS model to within approximately 2 dB. However, shadow fading was only 1.4-1.7 dB, compared with the model's 4.3 dB. In NLOS, the robot caused an excess loss that increased from 10.3 to 13.0 dB between 6.5 and 11.5 GHz, consistent with diffraction. Blocking the direct path raised the mean directional delay spread from approximately 5 to 25 ns, close to omnidirectional values. These results indicate that the 3GPP InF model captures mean LOS path loss well but overestimates the variability of beam-aligned FR3 links, and that blockage loss in FR3 is frequency dependent. The dataset and processing code are publicly available.

papers.title: Sense Less, Miss Less: Evidence-Driven Sensing Schedules for ISAC
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) lets a base station detect human motion with the same signals it uses for data, but every sensing transmission takes resources from users. Sensing rarely while nothing moves saves resources, yet a brief hand gesture by an otherwise still person can then start and end between two transmissions and go unnoticed. We propose an evidence-driven schedule, based on data-efficient cumulative-sum (CuSum) change detection, that pauses sensing while measurements indicate no motion and senses continuously once they suggest motion. It is adapted to orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) sensing, where requests can be blocked by data traffic and measurements arrive late, and evaluated with an articulated human model of limb motion. In simulations without wall reflections, with the same monitoring budget and below one false alarm per minute, it detects 1.5--4.2 times as many limb movements within 200~ms as periodic sensing. A tuned two-rate trigger performs similarly, and the gain over periodic sensing persists, without retuning or cost matching, in a simulated room with wall reflections. Under a small budget, measurements should decide when to sense.
